By the rays of His consciousness, which extend pervading the host of moving and non-moving things, having pervaded the worlds, having enjoyed the gross objects of enjoyment, and again the subtle ones illumined by the intellect and produced by desire, having drunk in all particulars, He sleeps, the relisher of the sweetness of bliss, while making us taste through māyā. To Him, the Brahman beyond the count of māyā, the turīya, the supreme, the immortal, the unborn, I bow down. (1)

He who is the Self of all (Viśvātman), having tasted the gross enjoyments which are the objects of enjoined activity, and afterwards the subtle ones, the offspring of His own intellect's expansion, by His own light, and again, having gradually established all these in His own Self, having abandoned all particulars, devoid of the host of attributes — may He, the turīya, protect us. (2)
MK_C01_INTRO1::block-1:
"Om, this syllable, is all this; its detailed exposition follows." This treatise consisting of four chapters (prakaraṇas), being the very essence of the import of the Vedānta, is begun with "Om, this syllable" and so on. For this very reason, the connection (sambandha), subject-matter (abhidheya), and purpose (prayojana) need not be stated separately. Whatever connection, subject-matter, and purpose obtain in the Vedānta, those very ones must obtain here as well; nevertheless, the expounders hold that they should be stated in brief by one who wishes to comment on the prakaraṇa.

Now, a śāstra is connected with its subject-matter by manifesting the means that yield the purpose, and thus through that connection it possesses a definite sambandha, abhidheya, and prayojana. What then is that purpose? It is stated — just as for one afflicted by disease there is restoration to health upon the cessation of the disease, so for the Self, which is of the nature of suffering, there is restoration to its own state upon the cessation of the manifold appearance of duality (dvaita-prapañca); the state of non-duality (advaita-bhāva) is the purpose. And since the manifold of duality is produced by avidyā, its cessation will result through vidyā (true knowledge); therefore this work is begun for the disclosure of the knowledge of Brahman.

The establishment of this meaning is from such Śruti passages as: "For where there is duality as it were" (Bṛ. Up. 2.4.14; 4.5.15), "For where there is something else as it were, there one sees another, one knows another" (Bṛ. Up. 4.3.31), "But where for him all has become the very Self, by what should one see whom, by what should one know whom?" (Bṛ. Up. 4.5.15), and the like.

Among these, the first prakaraṇa, predominantly scriptural (āgama-pradhāna), serves as the means for the comprehension of the truth of the Self for the purpose of ascertaining the Oṃkāra. The second prakaraṇa is for establishing, by reasoning, the unreality (vaitathya) of duality on the ground of its cause — for upon the cessation of that duality whose cessation yields the comprehension of non-duality, just as the comprehension of the reality of the rope follows upon the cessation of the alternatives such as the snake superimposed on the rope. Likewise, when the suspicion of unreality might be raised against non-duality itself, the third prakaraṇa establishes by reasoning that non-duality is truly so. The fourth prakaraṇa is for the refutation, by their very reasonings, of those non-Vedic doctrines which stand opposed to the comprehension of non-duality as truth, on the ground that, being mutually contradictory, they signify what is not true.
MK_C01_V01: Om, this syllable, is all this. Its detailed exposition is as follows: all that is past, present, and future is verily Oṃkāra. And whatever else is beyond the three times, that too is verily Oṃkāra. (1)
MK_C01_V01::block-0:
How, again, does the ascertainment of the Oṃkāra come to be the means of comprehending the truth of the Self? It is stated — from such Śruti passages as: "That syllable Om" (Kaṭha Up. 1.2.15), "This is the support" (Kaṭha Up. 1.2.17), "This indeed, O Satyakāma, is both the higher and the lower Brahman, namely Oṃkāra. Therefore the wise, by this very support, attains either of them" (Praśna Up. 5.2), "By Om one should join oneself with the Self" (Nārāyaṇa Up. 79), "Om is Brahman" (Tait. Up. 1.8.1), "Oṃkāra alone is all this" (Chānd. Up. 2.23.3), and the like.

Just as the rope and the like, being non-dual and existing in their true nature, are the locus of the alternatives of the snake and the rest, so too is the non-dual Self, existing in absolute reality, the locus of the alternatives such as prāṇa; in the same way, the entire expansion of speech, having for its content the alternatives of prāṇa and so forth which are imagined upon the Self, is verily Oṃkāra. And that very Oṃkāra is the Self's own form, since it denotes the Self.

And every alternative of the Self in the form of prāṇa and the rest, denoted by the modifications of the Oṃkāra in the form of words, does not exist apart from its name; this is from such Śruti passages as: "Modification is a beginning of speech, a name only" (Chānd. Up. 6.1.4), "All this is bound by speech as a cord, by names as ropes; for all this is but names" (Ait. Ār. 2.1.6), and the like.

Therefore he says — "Om, this syllable, is all this." Whatever this aggregate of meanings is, that which is to be denoted, since it is non-different from its denoting word, and since the difference of the denoting word is non-different from the Oṃkāra, all this is verily Oṃkāra. And the supreme Brahman is comprehended only through the means of the denoter and the denoted; hence it is Oṃkāra alone. "Its detailed exposition" (upavyākhyānam) — of this very imperishable Om, which is of the nature of the higher and lower Brahman, the upavyākhyāna, that is, the clear declaration in close proximity to Brahman, since it is the means for the comprehension of Brahman; the remainder of the sentence is "is to be known here as that which is being undertaken."

"Past, present, future" — whatever is delimited by the three divisions of time, that too is verily Oṃkāra by the reasoning stated. And whatever else is beyond the three times, knowable only as cause, not delimited by time — namely the unmanifest (avyākṛta) and the rest — that too is verily Oṃkāra.
MK_C01_V02: All this is verily Brahman; this Self is Brahman; this very Self has four quarters (pādas). (2)
MK_C01_V02::block-0:
Although the denoter (abhidhāna) and the denoted (abhidheya) are one, the statement was made with predominance to the denoter — "Om, this syllable, is all this," and so on. The fresh statement, with predominance to the denoted, of what was indicated with predominance to the denoter, is for the comprehension of the oneness of the denoter and the denoted. Otherwise the doubt would arise that the comprehension of the denoted depends upon the denoter, and that the status of the denoted as denoter would be only secondary (gauṇa).

And the purpose of comprehending the oneness of the denoter and the denoted is this — that, dissolving them both simultaneously by a single effort, one may attain Brahman which is distinct from them both. And so it will be said — "The pādas are the mātrās and the mātrās are the pādas" (Mā. Up. 8). Therefore he says — "All this is verily Brahman." All that was spoken of as merely Oṃkāra, that is this Brahman. And that Brahman, indirectly mentioned, he now points out directly and specifically — "This Self is Brahman." By "this" (ayam), pointing as it were by gesture, he refers to the inner Self that is being divided into four quarters — "this Self."

This Self, denoted by Oṃkāra, established as the higher and the lower, has four pādas — like the kārṣāpaṇa coin which is divided into four parts, not like a cow which has four feet (as separate limbs). The word pāda in the case of the three — Viśva and the rest — has the sense of an instrument (karaṇa-sādhana), since the comprehension of the turīya is by the successive dissolution of the preceding ones; whereas the word pāda in the case of the turīya has the sense of an object (karma-sādhana), since it is that which is to be attained (padyate).
MK_C01_V03: The first quarter is Vaiśvānara, whose seat is the waking state, who is conscious of what is external, who has seven limbs, nineteen mouths, and is the enjoyer of gross objects. (3)
MK_C01_V03::block-0:
How is it of four quarters? He says — "Whose seat is the waking state" (jāgaritasthāna). The waking is his seat — hence jāgaritasthāna. "Conscious of what is external" (bahiḥprajñaḥ) — he whose consciousness is on objects other than the Self; that is, whose consciousness, being illumined through avidyā, appears as if directed to outer objects.

Likewise, "having seven limbs" — as in the description of the Vaiśvānara as the remainder of the imagination concerning the agnihotra oblation: "Of this Self, Vaiśvānara, the head verily is the well-resplendent (heaven), the eye is the multiform (sun), the breath is that which moves variously (wind), the body is the abundant (sky), the bladder is verily wealth (water), the feet are verily the earth" (Chānd. Up. 5.18.2); and the āhavanīya fire is mentioned as the mouth. Thus he is the one who has these seven limbs, hence saptāṅga.

Likewise, "having nineteen mouths" — the ten organs of cognition and action, the five vital airs beginning with prāṇa, and manas, buddhi, ahaṅkāra, citta — these are like mouths, that is, gateways for apprehension. He, thus distinguished, the Vaiśvānara, enjoys the gross objects of sound and the rest through these gateways — hence "enjoyer of gross objects" (sthūla-bhuk).

Because he leads (nayanāt) all men (viśveṣāṃ narāṇāṃ) variously into pleasure and the like, he is Viśvānara; or, he is both the universal (viśvaḥ) and the man (naraḥ), hence Viśvānara; Viśvānara himself is Vaiśvānara, since he is non-different from the Self of all bodies (sarva-piṇḍātman); he is the first quarter. Since the comprehension of the subsequent quarters is preceded by this one, his being first is established.

How, when the four-quartered nature of the inner Self is being discussed by "This Self is Brahman," can the heavenly worlds and the rest be the head and other limbs? This is no defect, for the four-quartered nature is intended to belong to the entire manifold, with its adhidaivika aspect, through this Self. And thus, on the cessation of the entire manifold, non-duality is established. The Self, abiding in all beings, will be seen as one, and all beings (as abiding) in the Self.

Thus the meaning of Śruti passages such as "But he who (sees) all beings" (Īśa Up. 6) is summed up. Otherwise, the inner Self, delimited by his own body alone, would be seen as the Sāṅkhyas and others see it; and in that case, the distinction made by Śruti — namely "non-duality" — would not exist, since there would be no difference from the Sāṅkhya and similar views. And the upaniṣads desire the establishment of the oneness of the Self with all; hence it is fitting that the body-Self of the individual, in the adhyātmika aspect, has its oneness with the Virāj-Self of the adhidaivika aspect, with the heavenly worlds and the rest as its limbs — this is the intent of the statement "having seven limbs." And the inferential mark from "Thy head would have fallen" (Chānd. Up. 5.12.2) and the like supports this.

The oneness with Virāj is meant to indicate also the Hiraṇyagarbha-Self and the avyākṛta-Self. This has been said in the Madhubrāhmaṇa: "He who is in this earth, the resplendent and immortal puruṣa, and he who is in the body adhyātmically" (Bṛ. Up. 2.5.1) and so on. The oneness of suṣupti and the avyākṛta is established of itself, since both are without distinction. And in this way, what was stated will be established: that on the cessation of all duality, there is non-duality.
MK_C01_V04: The second quarter is Taijasa, whose seat is the dream state, who is conscious of what is internal, who has seven limbs, nineteen mouths, and is the enjoyer of subtle objects. (4)
MK_C01_V04::block-0:
Dream is the seat of this Taijasa — hence svapnasthāna. The waking consciousness, having multiple instruments, appearing as if directed to outer objects, being merely a vibration of the manas, deposits in the manas an impression (saṃskāra) of that very form; and that manas, thus impressed, like a painted cloth, when impelled by avidyā, kāma and karma without dependence on external instruments, appears as if waking. So it has been said — "Taking a portion of the all-encompassing material of this world" (Bṛ. Up. 4.3.9) and so on. Likewise, having begun with "When it becomes one with the supreme deity, the manas" (Praśna Up. 4.2), it is said in the Atharvana — "Here this deity experiences his greatness in dream" (Praśna Up. 4.5).

Since the manas is internal in relation to the sense-organs, and since in dream the consciousness is in the form of the impressions of the manas, he is antaḥprajña; in a consciousness empty of (external) objects, of the nature of mere illumination, he becomes as it were the subject — hence Taijasa. For Viśva, on account of consciousness having objects, the gross is the object of enjoyment; but here, the consciousness consisting merely of impressions is the object of enjoyment, hence the enjoyment is "distinct" or "refined" (pravivikta). The rest is as before. The second quarter is Taijasa.
MK_C01_V05: Where one, asleep, desires no desire whatever, sees no dream whatever — that is suṣupti. The third quarter is Prājña, whose seat is suṣupti, who is unified, a mass of consciousness only, full of bliss, the enjoyer of bliss, the gateway of cognition. (5)
MK_C01_V05::block-0:
Since sleep, in respect of seeing and not-seeing, is alike (in dream and deep sleep), the qualifying clause "where, asleep," and so on, is for distinguishing suṣupti. Or, since in all three states there is sleep characterized as the non-awakening to reality, which is undistinguished, he distinguishes suṣupti from the previous two — "where, in which place or time, asleep, one desires no desire whatever, sees no dream whatever." For in suṣupti there is no dream-vision in the form of apprehending things otherwise (than they are), as in the previous two, nor is there any desire whatever.

That very suṣupti is the seat of this one — hence suṣuptasthāna. The duality, divided into the two states (waking and dream), the brood of mind-vibrations, having attained non-discrimination without abandoning that very form, is said to be "unified" (ekībhūta), as the day along with its expanse seems unified when grasped as it were by the night-darkness. Hence the cognitions, which are the vibrations of manas in waking and dream, are as it were condensed; this very state, being of the nature of non-discrimination, is called prajñāna-ghana. As at night everything, undivided by night-darkness, appears as a mass, even so it is verily a mass of consciousness. By the word "only" (eva), it is meant that there is no other category apart from consciousness.

Since in the manas there is no toil and pain of vibration in the form of subject and object, he is ānandamaya — abounding in bliss; not bliss itself, since (this bliss) is not absolute. Just as in the world one stationed at ease is called "happy, an enjoyer of bliss," so this state, of the nature of utter freedom from toil, is experienced by this Self — hence "enjoyer of bliss" (ānandabhuk), as per Śruti: "This is his supreme bliss" (Bṛ. Up. 4.3.32).

He is the gateway (cetomukha) for the awakening to dream and the rest, since (the manas which is) consciousness becomes the door; or, his door is the manas in the form of cognition, the entrance for the coming forth of dream and the rest — hence cetomukha. Knowing the past and the future, knowing all objects — this belongs to him alone, hence prājña. For even in suṣupti, by reference to a previously held state, he is called Prājña. Or, mere consciousness alone is his unique form — hence prājña; in the other two there is also distinct cognition. He, this Prājña, is the third quarter.
MK_C01_V06: He is the Lord of all, the all-knowing, the inner controller; he is the source of all; he is verily the origin and dissolution of beings. (6)
MK_C01_V06::block-0:
This one, established in his own form, is sarveśvara — Lord, ruler of the entire collection of differences along with the adhidaivika aspect; not different in kind from this, as is held by others, since Śruti says: "For, dear one, the manas has prāṇa as its bond" (Chānd. Up. 6.8.2). For this very one, abiding in all the differentiated states of all, is the knower — hence eṣa sarvajñaḥ.

For this very reason he is antaryāmin — having entered within all beings, he is also the controller and ruler. For this very reason, since he produces the differentiated world as stated, he is the womb (yoni) of all. Since this is so, the origin (prabhava) and the dissolution (apyaya) of beings is verily this one alone.
MK_C01_INTRO2::block-0: Here on this matter, the following verses occur —
MK_C01_K01: Outwardly cognising is Vaiśvānara, the all-pervading; inwardly cognising is Taijasa. The dense-cognition one is Prājña; one alone, abiding in three modes.
MK_C01_K01::block-0: Here, with reference to the meaning previously stated by the Śruti, these verses occur — beginning with bahiḥprajñaḥ. Because the one Self assumes the three stations (jāgrat, svapna, suṣupti) by turns (paryāyeṇa), and because the recognition "this very one am I" (so'ham) reconnects the three by memory upon waking, it is established that the Self is distinct from the three stations, that it is one (ekatva), pure (śuddhatva), and unattached (asaṅgatva). This is the purport, supported by the Śruti's analogy of the great fish (mahāmatsya) which moves freely between the two banks while remaining itself (Bṛ. Up. 4.3.18).
MK_C01_K02: Vaiśvānara is in the right eye; Taijasa is within the mind; Prājña is in the heart-space. Thus the one Self is established threefold within the body.
MK_C01_K02::block-0:
This verse — beginning dakṣiṇākṣi — is meant to display, even in the waking state itself (jāgaritāvasthā), the experience of the three (Viśva, Taijasa, Prājña). The right eye itself is the "face" (mukham); there, predominantly, Viśva, the seer of gross objects, is experienced — as the Śruti says, "His name is Indha, this puruṣa who is in the right eye" (Bṛ. Up. 4.2.2). "Indha" — having the quality of brilliance — is Vaiśvānara, the Vairāja Self present within Āditya, and is the very same seer in the eye; the seer is one.

Objection (pūrvapakṣa): Hiraṇyagarbha is one entity, the kṣetrajña presiding within the right eye is another, and the body's lord (the seer) is yet another. Reply (siddhānta): Not so, for no intrinsic (svataḥ) difference is admitted; "The one Deva hidden in all beings" (Śve. Up. 6.11), and the Smṛti, "Know Me also, O Bhārata, as the kṣetrajña in all kṣetras" (Bh. Gī. 13.2), and "Undivided, yet existing as if divided in beings" (Bh. Gī. 13.16). Although all sense-organs are alike, the keenness of perception is found especially in the right eye, and so Viśva is specifically located there.

Having seen a form via the right eye, when one closes the eyes and recalls that very form, one sees within the mind — as if in a dream — that same form manifested as a vāsanā-impression. As it is there, so it is in the dream; thus Taijasa, who is "within the mind" (manasi antaḥ), is none other than Viśva functioning under a subtler condition.

In the heart-space (ākāśe ca hṛdi), when even the activity called "remembering" subsides, Prājña becomes unified — verily a dense mass of cognition (ghana-prajña) — because mental activity has ceased. Both seeing and remembering require the mind's vibration; in the absence of these, the soul rests in the heart, undifferentiated, as the prāṇa-Self — "Prāṇa indeed absorbs all these" (Chā. Up. 4.3.3). Taijasa is Hiraṇyagarbha, since he abides in the mind, by the Śrutis: "Mind is the liṅga" (Bṛ. Up. 4.4.6); "This puruṣa is mind-formed" (Bṛ. Up. 5.6.1).

Objection: In deep sleep, prāṇa is differentiated (vyākṛta), and the organs are of its nature; how then can it be undifferentiated (avyākṛta)? Reply: This is no fault, for the avyākṛta has no specification of place and time. Though prāṇa, when self-identified as such, is differentiated, yet in deep sleep the limited body-bound self-identification of the embodied dissolves into prāṇa; hence prāṇa is avyākṛta for those who in waking had bounded identification. Just as for those who identified with the limited individual, prāṇa is undifferentiated when their identifications dissolve into prāṇa, even so for prāṇa-identifiers, when there ensues the state of non-distinction, the same undifferentiatedness obtains, together with seedhood for future manifestation. The single overseer (adhyakṣa) abiding in the avyākṛta state, and the overseers of the limited identifications, are one with that; hence the previously stated qualification "having become one, a mass of cognition" (ekībhūtaḥ prajñāna-ghanaḥ — Mā. Up. 5) is fitting.

How can the avyākṛta be denoted by the word "prāṇa"? Because the Śruti says, "Mind is bound to prāṇa, dear one" (Chā. Up. 6.8.2). Objection: There the Sat-Brahman, introduced by "Sat alone, dear one" (Chā. Up. 6.2.1), is what is denoted by "prāṇa." Reply: This is no fault, since Sat is admitted to be of the nature of seed. Although there Sat-Brahman is denoted by "prāṇa," yet without abandoning its character as the seed for the production of jīvas, both the designation "prāṇa" for Sat and the term "sat" for it are appropriate. For if Brahman were to be spoken of as wholly seedless, the Śrutis would say, "Not this, not this" (Bṛ. Up. 4.5.3); "Whence words turn back" (Tai. Up. 2.9.1); "Other indeed than the known, and beyond the unknown" (Ke. Up. 1.4); and the Smṛti, "It is called neither sat nor asat" (Bh. Gī. 13.12). [Thus the term prāṇa here points to Sat-Brahman in its seed-aspect, not in its absolute nirbīja form.]
MK_C01_K03: Viśva is ever the experiencer of the gross; Taijasa is the experiencer of the subtle (pravivikta); and Prājña is the experiencer of bliss. Know thus the threefold enjoyment.
MK_C01_K04: The gross satisfies Viśva; the subtle satisfies Taijasa; bliss satisfies Prājña. Know thus the threefold satisfaction.
MK_C01_INTRO3::block-0: These two verses convey a meaning already stated.
MK_C01_K05: In the three abodes, that which is enjoyed and the one declared as the enjoyer — whoever knows both these as one is not tainted, even while enjoying.
MK_C01_K05::block-0:
In the three abodes — waking and the rest (jāgrat, svapna, suṣupti) — there is one enjoyable (bhojya) which has become threefold as gross, subtle (pravivikta), and bliss; and there is one enjoyer (bhoktā) declared under the names Viśva, Taijasa, Prājña — declared as one because of the recognition "this same I" (so'ham) and because the seer-character (draṣṭṛtva) does not differ across the states. He who knows both these — though appearing variously divided as enjoyed and enjoyer — as one, even while enjoying is not tainted, for all that is enjoyed is the very enjoyable of the one enjoyer.

For a thing's own object does not diminish or increase it. Fire is not consumed by burning its own fuel of wood and the like; just so, the one Self, in whose own field of objects all enjoyable things stand, is not tainted by enjoying them. Knowledge of this non-duality (advaita) is liberation (mokṣa) even amidst apparent enjoyment.
MK_C01_K06: There is the firm conclusion: the origination of all existing entities is from this. Prāṇa generates all; the Puruṣa sends forth the conscious rays separately.
MK_C01_K06::block-0:
Of the existing (sat) — that is, those subsisting in their own nature as māyā shaped by avidyā into name and form — of all the entities (sarva-bhāvānām) namely the divisions Viśva, Taijasa, Prājña, the prabhava, the origination, is from Brahman. The author will himself say: "A barren woman's son is not born either really or even by māyā" (Mā. Kā. 3.28). For if origination were from the utterly non-existent (asat), then since Brahman is beyond all transactional grasp, there would arise the wrong consequence that Brahman itself is asat, due to the absence of any approach by which to grasp it.

It is observed that rope-snake and the like, arisen from the seed of māyā fashioned by avidyā, possess being (sattva) only as the rope-Self and so on. Indeed a rope-snake, mirage, and similar appearances are nowhere apprehended without a substratum (anāspadāḥ). Just as before the snake's appearance the snake already existed in the rope as the rope-Self, so before the origination of all entities they exist in the seed-Self that is prāṇa. The Śruti also declares: "All this is verily Brahman" (Mu. Up. 2.2.12); "This was, in the beginning, the Self alone" (Bṛ. Up. 1.4.1).

Therefore, prāṇa generates all. As to ceto-aṃśūn — "the rays of consciousness" — these are like rays (aṃśavaḥ) of the sun: from the Puruṣa, who is of the nature of pure consciousness, the rays in the form of cit, comparable to suns reflected in water (jalārka), are conceived as the divisions Prājña, Taijasa, Viśva manifest in the various bodies of gods, men, animals, and the rest. The Puruṣa sends these forth (pṛthak sṛjati) as distinct from the field of objects, of his own nature like sparks from fire (agni-visphuliṅga-vat) and like reflected suns in water for the jīva-aspect; while the prāṇa as seed-Self generates the other entities (the objective realm). The Śruti supports this: "As the spider… as from fire the small sparks" (Bṛ. Up. 2.1.20).
MK_C01_K07: Other thinkers on creation hold that origination is the manifestation (vibhūti) of Īśvara. Yet others have imagined creation to be of the nature of dream and māyā.
MK_C01_K07::block-0:
Vibhūti — the expansion — is Īśvara's creation: so the thinkers on creation hold. But for those who reflect on the supreme reality (paramārtha-cintaka) there is no preoccupation with creation — that is the meaning. As the Śruti says, "Indra by his māyās appears in many forms" (Bṛ. Up. 2.5.19).

Suppose a magician throws a rope into the sky, climbs it with weapons in hand, passes beyond the range of sight, is hewn to pieces in battle and falls down, and then rises up again. To those who watch, no real preoccupation with the truth of the magic-show arises. Just so is this expansion of the deep-sleep, dream, and other states — like the magician's stretching out of the rope. Like the magician on the rope are Prājña, Taijasa, and the rest standing in those states. Distinct from both rope and the climber is the real magician (paramārtha-māyāvī) standing on the ground; just as he, hidden by māyā, remains invisible while really standing there, so does the supreme Reality named turīya. Hence the noble seekers of liberation (mumukṣūṇām āryāṇām) take interest only in reflection upon That; they have no interest in pointless reflection upon creation.

Therefore these alternatives belong only to the cosmologists. Hence he says — "of the nature of dream and māyā" — meaning of the form of dream (svapna-sarūpā) and of the form of māyā (māyā-sarūpā). The schools refuted here are those of the cosmologist ritualists and creation-theorists (sṛṣṭi-cintakāḥ) who treat the world as Īśvara's vibhūti, and those who treat creation as svapna or māyā as ultimately to be analysed; from the standpoint of pravṛtti such accounts have their place, but in the path of nivṛtti aimed at liberation only the turīya is the proper object of inquiry.
MK_C01_K08:
The creation is the mere will of the Lord — thus the cosmologists who are decided about creation hold; whereas the meditators on Time consider that the origination of beings proceeds from Time.

Meaning: Some teachers, accepting the Lord (Īśvara) as one whose resolve is unfailingly true, declare that the universe is nothing more than His will, just as a potter wills the pot. Others, holding Time itself to be the supreme cause, maintain that beings are produced from Time, not from any conscious agent.
MK_C01_K08::block-0:
Bhāṣya: Because the Lord is one of unfailingly true resolve (satya-saṅkalpa), creation is His will alone — that is, pots and the like are nothing other than His mere conception, and not anything over and above that conception. Others, however, hold that creation arises from Time itself.

Thus the ācārya cites two views: one ascribing creation to the Lord's will, the other ascribing it to Time as the universal cause. Both are recorded here only to be examined and ultimately set aside in the light of the non-dual truth that admits of no real origination at all.
MK_C01_K09:
Some say creation is for the Lord's enjoyment, others say it is for sport; but this is the very nature of the Deity — for one whose desires are wholly fulfilled, what longing can there be?

Meaning: Various theorists assign different motives — bhoga (experience), krīḍā (play), or svabhāva (innate nature) — to explain why the Lord projects the world. Gauḍapāda answers that none of these can apply to the Self that is āptakāma, of whom every desire is already satisfied; hence creation cannot stand as a real, motivated act.
MK_C01_INTRO4::block-0: Auxiliary bhāṣya: "Thus" — this concluding particle gathers up the foregoing series of opinions on the cause of creation, signalling that the enumeration of these views is now complete and that the discussion is about to turn to its final disposition in the light of the non-dual truth.
MK_C01_V07:
Not inwardly cognitive, not outwardly cognitive, not cognitive both ways, not a mass of cognition, not cognitive, not non-cognitive; unseen, beyond empirical dealings, ungraspable, devoid of distinguishing marks, unthinkable, indescribable; the essence of the conviction of the one Self, the cessation of all phenomena, tranquil, auspicious, non-dual — such, they hold, is the Fourth (Turīya). That is the Self; That is to be known.

Meaning: This mantra describes Turīya, the Fourth, by a sustained chain of negations. It is not the waking experiencer (viśva), not the dreamer (taijasa), not the deep-sleeper (prājña), not anything between, beyond, or other than these. It is the very Self, in which all duality subsides and which alone is to be realised as one's own true nature.
MK_C01_INTRO5::block-0: Auxiliary bhāṣya: "Here, on this very topic, occur these verses" — with this transitional remark, Śaṅkara introduces the kārikās of Gauḍapāda which now follow, expounding the import of the seventh mantra concerning Turīya in metrical form.
MK_C01_K10:
He is the Lord (Īśāna) of the cessation of all sorrows; the Master, imperishable, non-dual amidst all entities — that resplendent Fourth, all-pervading, is so declared.

Meaning: Turīya is praised as the sovereign through whose realisation every form of suffering — that of viśva, taijasa, and prājña alike — is brought to an end. Being one without a second and never deviating from its own nature, it is the all-pervading, self-luminous Deity, the Fourth.
MK_C01_K10::block-0:
Bhāṣya: Here these verses occur. Of all sorrows characterised by prājña, taijasa, and viśva, Turīya, the Self, is the Lord (īśāna) of their cessation. The word "Īśāna" is glossed as prabhu — meaning that He is the master with regard to the cessation of sorrow, since the cessation of sorrow is brought about by the knowledge of Him.

Avyaya means he does not pass away — he never deviates from his own nature, never falls from it. And why? Because he is non-dual amidst all entities. Just as the rope is the one true reality underlying the appearance of snake and the like, even so is Turīya; for the śruti declares, "Verily, there is no cessation of the seeing of the seer" (Bṛ.U. 4.3.23) — and so the world, like rope-snake, is unreal. That very deva, by reason of his self-effulgence, is called turya, the fourth, and is recorded in tradition as vibhu, the all-pervading.
MK_C01_K11:
Viśva and Taijasa are held to be bound by both effect and cause; Prājña is bound by cause alone; in Turīya, however, neither of these two is established.

Meaning: The waker and dreamer labour under two limitations — non-apprehension of the truth (cause) and misapprehension of it as something else (effect). The deep-sleeper has only the first, the seed of non-apprehension. In the Fourth, neither seed nor sprout exists, for it is utterly free of the bondage of avidyā.
MK_C01_K11::block-0:
Bhāṣya: The general and particular characters of viśva and the rest are now set forth in order to determine the true nature of Turīya. "Effect" means the state of fruit — that which is produced; "cause" means the state of seed — that which produces. Through the two — non-apprehension of the truth and misapprehension as something else — which are themselves seed and fruit, the said viśva and taijasa are held to be bound, that is, comprehended.

Prājña, however, is bound by the seed-state alone; for in his case the mere non-awakening to the truth is the cause of his being prājña. Therefore those two — seed and fruit, non-apprehension and misapprehension — do not arise, do not exist, are not possible in Turīya. Turīya thus stands wholly outside the round of causal bondage.
MK_C01_K12:
Prājña knows nothing — neither self nor other, neither truth nor untruth; Turīya, however, is ever the seer of all.

Meaning: The deep-sleeper, though seedless of distinct cognitions, lies covered by the darkness of non-apprehension and so cognises nothing. Turīya, by contrast, is the eternal, changeless Witness, in whose self-luminosity neither the seed of non-apprehension nor any of its sprouts can ever take root.
MK_C01_K12::block-0:
Bhāṣya: How then is Prājña said to be bound by the cause, and how is it that the bondage of non-apprehension and misapprehension is not established in Turīya? Because Prājña does not cognise anything whatsoever — neither the Self, nor that which is distinct from it, nor any external duality born of the seed of avidyā — as do viśva and taijasa; therefore he stands bound by that darkness which is non-apprehension of the truth, the seed of misapprehension.

And because that Fourth is sarvadṛk sadā — ever the seer of all — being other than nothing else and existing always, and being all and at once the seer of all, in him there is no seed of non-apprehension. Where the seed is absent, its offspring, misapprehension, is also absent for that very reason. Just as in the sun, whose nature is unceasing illumination, the contrary — non-illumination or other-illumination — is impossible, so it is here, as the śruti affirms: "There is no cessation of the seeing of the seer" (Bṛ.U. 4.3.23). Or alternatively, since in waking and dream the Fourth alone, abiding in all beings, appears as the seer of all things, it is sarvadṛk sadā, in accord with the śruti, "Other than this, there is no seer" (Bṛ.U. 3.8.11).
MK_C01_K13: The non-apprehension of duality is equally common to both Prājña and Turīya. Yet Prājña is conjoined with seed-sleep (the latent cause of duality), and that seed-sleep does not exist in Turīya.
MK_C01_K13::block-0: This verse is meant to dispel a doubt that arises from another consideration. The doubt that arises is this: how is it that, when the non-apprehension of duality is equal in both, only Prājña is bound by causality and not Turīya? This doubt is now removed. Because Prājña is conjoined with seed-sleep — the non-awakening to Reality is sleep, and that very sleep is the seed of the birth of particular cognitions; that is seed-sleep; with it Prājña is conjoined. But because Turīya is by its very nature ever-seeing (eternal Consciousness), the seed-sleep characterised by non-awakening to Reality does not exist in it. Hence there is no causal bondage in It — this is the purport.
MK_C01_K14: The first two (Viśva and Taijasa) are conjoined with both dream and sleep; Prājña is conjoined with sleep alone, devoid of dream. The firmly established knowers see neither sleep nor dream in Turīya.
MK_C01_K14::block-0: Dream is the apprehending of a thing as other than what it is — like the snake on a rope; sleep is what was described as the darkness characterised by non-awakening to Reality. With both these — dream and sleep — Viśva and Taijasa are conjoined; hence they were said to be bound by both effect and cause. But Prājña is conjoined with sleep alone, free of dream; therefore he was said to be bound only by the cause. The firmly established ones — that is, the knowers of Brahman — do not see either of the two in Turīya, because the two are opposed to it as darkness is to the sun. Hence Turīya was declared to be bound neither by effect nor by cause.
MK_C01_K15: Dream belongs to him who apprehends otherwise; sleep belongs to him who knows not Reality. When the inversion of these two is destroyed, one attains the state of Turīya.
MK_C01_K15::block-0:
When does one become firmly established in Turīya? It is now told. For him who apprehends Reality otherwise — like the snake on a rope — in the waking and dream states, dream arises. Sleep — characterised by not knowing Reality — is equally present in all three states. Because dream and sleep are equal there, Viśva and Taijasa form one group. And since misapprehension predominates and sleep is subordinate, in dream state the inversion is dream itself.

But in the third state (deep sleep) the inversion is solely sleep — characterised by non-apprehension of Reality. Therefore, when in those two stations of effect and cause the inversion characterised by misapprehension and non-apprehension of Reality, taking the form of bondage of effect and cause, is destroyed by the awakening to the supreme Reality, one attains the state of Turīya. Then, not seeing therein the bondage of either form, he becomes firmly established in Turīya — this is the meaning.
MK_C01_K16: When the jīva, asleep through beginningless māyā, is awakened, then he awakens to the unborn, sleepless, dreamless, non-dual.
MK_C01_K16::block-0:
This jīva caught in saṁsāra is asleep — by the seed-form of non-awakening to Reality (in deep sleep) and by the māyā-shaped slumber of misapprehension running from beginningless time (in dream and waking). In both stations he sees such dreams as: 'this is my father, this my son, this grandson, this field, house, cattle; I am their owner, happy, miserable; I am ruined by this one, I have prospered through that one' — thus dreaming, he sleeps. When, however, he is awakened by a most compassionate teacher, knower of the truth of Vedānta, who instructs: 'You are not such a being made of cause and effect; you are That' — then he awakens.

How? In It there is no modification of birth and the rest, neither external nor internal; therefore It is unborn, as the śruti says, 'Unborn, with nothing within or without' (Muṇḍ. 2.1.2) — meaning, devoid of all modifications of being. Since sleep, the seed of avidyā-darkness which is the cause of birth and the rest, does not exist in It, It is sleepless; that Turīya is indeed sleepless; and for that very reason It is dreamless, since dream depends on it (sleep). Because It is sleepless and dreamless, therefore It is unborn, non-dual; and Turīya as the Self — that he awakens to then.
MK_C01_K17: If the world of plurality existed, it would surely cease — there is no doubt. This duality is mere māyā; in the highest sense, all is non-dual.
MK_C01_K17::block-0: If awakening occurs by the cessation of the world of plurality, then how can there be non-duality so long as the world has not ceased? It is replied: it would indeed be so if the world existed. But like the snake on a rope, it is mere imagination and does not really exist. If it did exist, it would have to cease — there is no doubt. But the snake imagined on a rope through deluded perception, being non-existent, does not really cease through discrimination. Nor does the māyā produced by a magician, when the bewilderment of the spectators' eyes ceases, cease as a really existent thing. Just so, this duality called the world is mere māyā; like the rope and the magician, in the highest sense it is non-dual. Therefore there is no world that has either come into being or that ceases — this is the purport.
MK_C01_K18: The distinction would cease if it had been imagined by anyone. This discourse is for the sake of instruction; once Reality is known, no duality remains.
MK_C01_K18::block-0: But how is the distinction 'teacher, scripture, disciple' itself negated? It is replied: this distinction would cease if it had been imagined by someone. Just as this world is imagined like the rope-snake or magic, so this distinction of disciple and the rest is also a construct prior to awakening, occasioned by the need for instruction. Hence this discourse — 'disciple, teacher, scripture' — is for the sake of instruction. When the knowledge that is the fruit of instruction has been accomplished and the supreme Reality has been known, no duality remains.
MK_C01_V08: This very Self, considered with reference to syllables, is Om; considered with reference to its mātrās, the pādas are the mātrās and the mātrās are the pādas — namely, the letters a, u, and m.
MK_C01_V08::block-0: The praṇava, with primacy of the signified, was explained as the four-footed Self. That very Self is now described with primacy of the signifier, with reference to the syllable — hence 'adhyakṣaram', the Self regarded as the syllable. What then is that syllable? It is Om. This Om, when divided pāda by pāda, exists with reference to its mātrās — hence 'adhimātram'. How? The pādas of the Self are the mātrās of Om. Which are they? The letters a, u, and m.
MK_C01_V09: Vaiśvānara, whose seat is the waking state, is the letter 'a', the first mātrā (measure) of Om — by reason of pervasion, or because of being first. He who knows thus verily attains all desires and becomes the foremost.
MK_C01_V09::block-0:
Here a particular correlation is set forth — the Vaiśvānara whose locus is the waking state is the letter 'a', the first mātrā of the praṇava (Om). By what common feature? The text answers: by 'pervasion' (āpti). Pervasion means all-pervadingness. The whole of speech is pervaded by the letter 'a', as the śruti declares: 'The letter a is verily all speech' (Ai. Ār. 2.3.19).

Likewise the world is pervaded by Vaiśvānara, as is shown by the śruti: 'Of this Self that is Vaiśvānara, the head indeed is the heaven of fine effulgence' (Chā. Up. 5.18.2) and so on. We have already stated that the name and the named are one.

'Possessed of a beginning' (ādimat) — that which has a beginning. Just as the syllable named 'a' is itself the beginning, so too is Vaiśvānara; therefore by virtue of this very common feature of being-the-beginning, Vaiśvānara has the nature of 'a'.

The fruit of knowing this oneness is now declared: 'He attains verily all desires, and he becomes the first, the foremost among the great' — namely he who knows thus, that is, who realises the oneness as stated.
MK_C01_V10: Taijasa, whose seat is the dream state, is the letter 'u', the second mātrā — by reason of superiority, or because of being intermediate. He who knows thus verily increases the flow of knowledge and becomes equal-minded; none in his lineage will be ignorant of Brahman.
MK_C01_V10::block-0:
Taijasa, whose seat is the dream state, is the letter 'u', the second mātrā of Om. By what common feature? The text answers: 'by superiority' (utkarṣa). For the letter 'u' is, as it were, superior to (above) 'a'; likewise Taijasa is superior to Viśva.

Or 'by being both' (ubhayatva) — the letter 'u' stands midway between 'a' and 'm'; similarly Taijasa stands between Viśva and Prājña. Hence by the common feature of partaking of both extremes.

The fruit for the knower is now stated: 'He verily increases the flow of knowledge', that is, he augments the continuum of cognition. He becomes 'equal' (samāna), of even regard — even those of the hostile camp become non-hostile to him as do those of the friendly side. And in his lineage, no one ignorant of Brahman is born — for him who knows thus.
MK_C01_V11: Prājña, whose seat is deep sleep, is the letter 'm', the third mātrā — by reason of measuring, or because of merging. He who knows thus verily measures (knows the truth of) all this, and becomes the merging (the cause of the universe).
MK_C01_V11::block-0:
Prājña, whose seat is deep sleep, is the letter 'm', the third mātrā of Om. By what common feature? The common feature here is 'mitiḥ' (measuring). Miti means measure. For Viśva and Taijasa are, as it were, measured by Prājña at the times of dissolution and origination, by entering and emerging — like grains of barley by a measuring-pot. Likewise, when the utterance of Om concludes and is taken up again, the letters 'a' and 'u' enter into and emerge from 'm'.

Or 'by merging' (apīti). Apīti means absorption, becoming-one. For at the final letter when Om is uttered, 'a' and 'u' become as it were one; similarly Viśva and Taijasa become one in Prājña during deep sleep. Hence by this common feature too there is identity between Prājña and the letter 'm'.

The fruit for the knower is now declared: 'He verily measures all this' — that is, he knows the true nature of the universe. And he 'becomes the merging' — that is, he becomes the very Self that is the cause of the universe. The mention of subordinate fruit here is for the sake of praising the principal means (of meditation).
MK_C01_INTRO7::block-0: On this matter, these verses are stated —
MK_C01_K19: When the identification of Viśva with the letter 'a' is intended, the common feature of being-first stands out prominently; and in the determination of (its being) a mātrā, the common feature of pervasion is also evident.
MK_C01_K19::block-0:
On this, these verses occur. When the 'a-ness' of Viśva — that is, its being merely the letter 'a' — is intended to be expressed, then by the reasoning already stated the common feature of being-first (āditva) is seen to stand out prominently; this is the meaning.

The phrase 'when a-ness is intended' is explained by the words 'in the determination of the mātrā'. That is: when one ascertains Viśva to be the letter 'a', (this common feature emerges). 'And the common feature of pervasion as well' — the word 'prominently' is to be carried over, by force of the conjunction 'ca'.
MK_C01_K20: When Taijasa is recognised as the letter 'u', superiority is clearly seen. And in the determination of its mātrā, the quality of being-both is similarly (evident).
MK_C01_K20::block-0: When Taijasa is recognised in its 'u-ness' — that is, when its being the letter 'u' is intended — superiority is seen distinctly, clearly; this is the meaning. And being-both is itself manifest. All else is as before.
MK_C01_K21: When Prājña is taken as the letter 'm', the common feature of measuring stands out prominently; and likewise in the determination of the mātrā, the common feature of merging (laya) too is evident.
MK_C01_K21::block-0: In the case of Prājña's being the letter 'm', the two common features — measuring (miti) and merging (laya) — are the prominent ones; this is the meaning.
MK_C01_K22: He who, with conviction, knows the equal common feature in all three states — he, indeed, the great sage, is worthy of worship and adoration by all beings.
MK_C01_K22::block-0: He who knows in the three states aforesaid the equal common feature as stated, being firmly convinced that 'verily it is so' — he becomes the knower of Brahman, worshipped and venerated in the world.
MK_C01_K23: The letter 'a' leads (the meditator) to Vaiśvānara (the Universal); the letter 'u' similarly to Taijasa (the Luminous); and the letter 'm' once more to Prājña (the Knower). But for the matraless (Oṃkāra), there is no further movement, no goal beyond.
MK_C01_K23::block-0:
Having effected, by means of the common features already stated, the identity between the quarters of the Self and the mātrās (sound-units), the meditator who attains the aforementioned Oṃkāra is led by the letter 'a' to Viśva — that is, made to reach the Universal. The meaning is: he who knows Oṃkāra with the letter 'a' as its support becomes Vaiśvānara himself.

In the same way, the letter 'u' leads him to Taijasa; and the letter 'm' once more to Prājña. The word 'ca' (and) carries forward the verb 'leads' from the previous clauses. But when the letter 'm' too is dissolved, then, the seed-state being itself destroyed, no further course or goal whatsoever is found in the matraless Oṃkāra — this is the meaning.
MK_C01_V12: The matraless (fourth) is Turīya — beyond all empirical dealings, in which the phenomenal world is dissolved, the auspicious, the non-dual. Thus is Oṃkāra verily the Self. He who knows this enters the Self with the Self.
MK_C01_V12::block-0:
Amātra means 'that which has no mātrās'; such is Oṃkāra, the fourth, the Turīya, the Self alone. Because both speech and mind, which are of the nature of the named and the name, have ceased there, it is avyavahārya — beyond all empirical transaction; it is prapañcopaśama, that in which the phenomenal world is utterly stilled; it is auspicious (śiva); it has become the non-dual (advaita). Thus the Oṃkāra of three mātrās and three quarters, when employed by one possessed of the knowledge stated, is itself the Self.

He who knows thus enters the Self by the Self alone — his own supreme Self. Through the vision of the supreme Reality, the knower of Brahman, having burnt up the third (causal) seed-state, has entered the Self and is not born again, since the Turīya is seedless. For when the rope and the snake have been discriminated, the snake that has 'entered' the rope does not, by force of mental impressions, rise again as before for those who have so discriminated.

But for those of dull and middling intellect who have taken up the role of aspirants — for the saṃnyāsins walking the right path who have grasped the established commonality of mātrās and quarters — the Oṃkāra duly meditated upon becomes the support for the realization of Brahman. Thus indeed it will be said: 'There are three āśramas' (Mā. Kā. 3.16) and so on.
MK_C01_INTRO9::block-1: Here on this (subject) occur these verses —
MK_C01_K24: One should know Oṃkāra quarter by quarter; the quarters are the mātrās — there is no doubt. Having known Oṃkāra quarter by quarter, one should think of nothing else whatsoever.
MK_C01_K24::block-0: Just as before, here too these verses occur. By means of the common features already stated, the quarters themselves are the mātrās, and the mātrās themselves are the quarters; therefore one should know Oṃkāra quarter by quarter — this is the meaning. When Oṃkāra is thus known, one should think of no further purpose, whether seen or unseen, since one has accomplished all that is to be accomplished — this is the sense.
MK_C01_K25: One should fix the mind on Praṇava; Praṇava is Brahman, the fearless. For one ever absorbed in Praṇava, fear exists nowhere.
MK_C01_K25::block-0: One should yoke — that is, concentrate — the mind upon Praṇava as already explained, in its supreme essential form. Because Praṇava is Brahman, the fearless. For one who is ever yoked therein, fear exists nowhere, in accordance with the śruti, 'The knower fears nothing whatsoever' (Tai. Up. 2.9.1).
MK_C01_K26: Praṇava is the lower Brahman; Praṇava is also remembered as the higher. Praṇava is without a prior, without anything within (different from itself), without anything outside, without a subsequent — Praṇava is imperishable.
MK_C01_K26::block-0: Praṇava is both the higher and lower Brahman. In ultimate truth, when the mātrās and quarters have dissolved, the higher Self alone is Brahman. There is no prior cause for it — hence apūrva (without a prior); nothing of a different kind exists within it — hence anantara (without an interior other); likewise nothing exists outside it — hence abāhya (without an exterior); no posterior effect issues from it — hence anapara (without a successor). For it is unborn, both within and without, like a solid mass of salt, a homogeneous mass of pure consciousness — this is the meaning.
MK_C01_K27: Praṇava is verily the beginning, the middle, and likewise the end of all. Having thus known Praṇava, one attains That immediately thereafter.
MK_C01_K27::block-0:
The beginning, middle, and end — that is, the origination, sustenance, and dissolution — of all are Praṇava alone. Just as the magician and the like are (the support) for the elephant of magic, the rope-snake, the mirage, the dream, and so on which arise (apparently), even so for the phenomenal world of space and the rest which arises (in like manner), Praṇava — the Self which corresponds to the magician and his kin — is the substratum.

Having thus known Praṇava as the Self standing in the place of the magician (in relation to all this manifestation), at that very moment one attains identity with That — this is the meaning.
MK_C01_K28: One should know Praṇava as Īśvara seated in the heart of all. Knowing Oṁkāra to be all-pervading, the wise one does not grieve.
MK_C01_K28::block-0: One should know that Praṇava — Īśvara — is seated in the heart, the seat of memory and of all cognitions, of every living being. The wise and intelligent one (dhīraḥ), having understood the Self that is Oṁkāra to be all-pervading like ākāśa and untouched by saṁsāra, does not grieve. There is no occasion for grief for such a one, since the Śruti texts such as 'The knower of the Self crosses over sorrow' (Chān. Up. 7.1.3) declare this very fruit of Self-knowledge.
MK_C01_K29: He who knows Oṁkāra — measureless, of infinite measure, the auspicious cessation of all duality — he alone is the muni; no one else, however learned.
MK_C01_K29::block-0:
Amātraḥ — without measure — is the turīya Oṁkāra. 'Mātrā' is that by which something is measured, that is, delimitation; he whose measure is endless is anantamātraḥ — meaning that his magnitude cannot be circumscribed in this or that fashion. Precisely because in him all duality has come to rest, he is śivaḥ, the auspicious.

He by whom Oṁkāra has been known just as has been expounded — he alone, by reason of his contemplation (manana) of the supreme Reality, is the muni; no other person is, even though he be versed in the śāstras. This is the meaning.
MK_C02_K01: The wise declare the unreality of all objects in dream, on account of their being located within, and on the ground that they are confined.
MK_C02_K01::block-0:
It has already been stated that 'when It is known, no duality remains' — on the strength of Śruti texts such as 'One only, without a second' (Chān. Up. 6.2.1). But that was based on Āgama alone. Here it can also be ascertained by reasoning that duality is unreal; hence the second prakaraṇa is begun with the words 'vaitathyam' and so forth.

The state of being vitatha is vaitathya — that is, unreality. Of what? Of all objects, both external and internal, that are perceived in dream — so the manīṣiṇaḥ, those skilled in the means of valid knowledge, declare. The reason for the unreality is given as 'antaḥsthānāt': their location is inside the body, in its midst — for there alone are the objects, mountains, elephants and the rest, perceived in dream, and not outside the body; therefore they must be unreal.

Apprehending the doubt, 'But this reason is inconclusive, since pots and the like are also perceived inside a closed chamber,' he adds 'saṁvṛtatvena hetunā' — meaning, on the ground of being a confined inner location. For within the body's enclosed nāḍīs there is no possibility of mountains, elephants and so forth, since a mountain certainly does not exist inside the body.
MK_C02_K02: Also, on account of the shortness of the time, one does not go from the body and see; and everyone, on waking, is not present in that place.
MK_C02_K02::block-0:
It might be objected: 'It is not established that the place of the dream-objects is the inner, confined location, since one who sleeps in the east appears to be seeing dreams in the north.' Anticipating this, he answers: the dreamer does not go out of the body to some other region and see dreams. For no sooner is he asleep than he is seen as if seeing dreams in a place a hundred yojanas distant from where his body lies, requiring a month's journey to reach. Yet there is no long stretch of time available for travelling to that place and returning; therefore, on account of the shortness of the time, the dreamer does not go to another place.

Further, every dreamer, when he wakes up, is not found in the place where the dream was seen. Were he indeed to go to another region in the dream, he would wake up there, in the very place where he saw the dream. But this does not happen. One who sleeps at night sees objects as in the daytime; he meets with many people; and those whom he meets ought to recognise him — but they do not. If they had seen him, they would say, 'We met you there today.' This too does not occur. Hence, in dream the seer does not go to another place.
MK_C02_K03: And the non-existence of chariots and the like is heard, supported by reasoning. The unreality thus established, they say, is what Śruti has revealed in the case of dream.
MK_C02_K03::block-0: On this further ground also, the objects perceived in dream are unreal: the non-existence of chariots and the like, perceived in dream, is heard with supporting reasoning in the Śruti — 'There are no chariots there' (Bṛ. Up. 4.3.10). Therefore, the unreality already arrived at by the reasons of inner location, confinement and the rest is — as the knowers of Brahman declare — also revealed by that very Śruti, which, while restating the same point, has for its purport the establishment of the self-luminous nature in the dream state.
MK_C02_K04: On account of being inside, and on account of confinement, there is a difference of these from what is recalled in the waking state. As is there, so in dream — the difference is only by way of confinement.
MK_C02_K04::block-0:
The proposition is that the objects perceived in the waking state are unreal. The reason is 'because they are perceived' (dṛśyatvāt). The example is 'like the objects perceived in dream'. The application of the reason: just as there, in dream, the perceived objects are unreal, so in the waking state too the property of being perceived is the same — there is no difference. The conclusion: therefore, in the waking state too, unreality is taught.

The difference of dream-objects from waking-objects is only on the score of inner location and confinement. The fact of being perceived, and the fact of being unreal, are alike in both.
MK_C02_K05: The wise declare the dream and the waking states to be one, on the well-known ground of the sameness of the differences in both.
MK_C02_K05::block-0: On the well-known ground that the differences in both are alike objects of cognition, and so equal, the discriminating ones declare the oneness of the dream-state and the waking-state. This is simply the fruit of what was already established by the previous reasoning.
MK_C02_K06: What is not at the beginning and not at the end is even so in the present. Resembling the unreal, they yet appear as if real.
MK_C02_K06::block-0: Furthermore, the unreality of the differences perceived in waking is established by their non-existence at the beginning and end. Whatever is non-existent at the beginning and at the end — like a mirage and the like — is determined in the world to be non-existent in the middle as well. Just so, these waking-perceived differences, by reason of their absence at the beginning and at the end, are like a mirage and the rest, and hence resemble unreal things; therefore they are themselves unreal. Yet they are regarded as if real by the deluded who do not know the Self.
MK_C02_K07:
The purposefulness of those (waking objects) is contradicted in dream; therefore, on account of having a beginning and an end, they are surely remembered as merely false.

In waking, food, drink, conveyances and the like serve evident purposes — quenching hunger, slaking thirst, enabling movement — yet that very utility is overturned in dream. Hence, having a beginning and an end like dream-objects, the objects of waking too are unreal.
MK_C02_K07::block-0:
It was said that, like dream-objects, waking-objects also are unreal; this, the opponent contends, is improper. For waking-objects such as food, drink and conveyances are seen to be purposeful — they remove hunger, thirst and the like, and accomplish such effects as going and coming — whereas dream-objects do nothing of the sort. Hence, to declare waking-objects unreal like dream-objects is mere fancy.

This objection does not stand. Why? Because the very purposefulness seen in food, drink and the rest is contradicted in dream. In waking one eats and drinks, becomes satisfied, with thirst quenched; yet the moment one falls asleep one finds oneself, in the dream, afflicted by hunger and thirst as though one had fasted day and night and had eaten nothing — just as in dream one rises unsatisfied after having eaten and drunk.

Thus the purposefulness of waking-objects is itself overturned within dream. Therefore we conclude, beyond all doubt, that waking-objects too are unreal exactly like dream-objects. Since the property of having a beginning and an end is common to both, they are remembered as nothing but false.
MK_C02_K08:
The unprecedented (in dream) is indeed a property belonging to the dweller of that state, just as four-armed forms and the like are peculiar to dwellers in heaven. He, the dreamer, beholds them on going there, even as one well-trained here perceives objects in another country.

Though strange forms appear in dream, this is no defect: such novelty belongs to the dream-dweller's state itself, like the thousand eyes of Indra to heaven-dwellers. The dreamer, entering his own dream-realm, sees them as a traveller perceives the lands he reaches.
MK_C02_K08::block-0:
It might be objected: since waking and dream are equated, the assertion of the unreality of waking-distinctions through the dream-example is wrong, because the example is not established. For the very distinctions seen in waking are not seen in dream; rather, in dream one beholds something altogether unprecedented — one's own self mounted upon a four-tusked elephant, possessed of eight arms, and other such things never met with before. Such a novel content cannot be equated with the unreal, and so must be real. Hence the example fails, and the unreality of waking like dream is unwarranted.

This is not so. That which you take to be unprecedented in dream is not self-established. Rather, the unprecedented is the property of the dweller of that state — that is, of the seer himself who possesses the dream-condition. Just as the thousand eyes and other peculiarities belong to Indra and the rest who dwell in heaven, so this unprecedented character belongs to the dream-seer's state, and is not something self-existent like the seer's own essential nature.

The dreamer, who is the dweller of that state, going to the dream-realm, beholds these unprecedented mental constructions as his own. It is just as a man here, well trained in the route to a distant land, traverses that road, reaches that land, and there beholds its objects. Hence, just as the rope-snake, the mirage-water and the like are unreal — being mere properties of their respective substrate — so the unprecedented dream-objects, being properties of the dream-state, are likewise unreal. Therefore the dream-example is by no means unestablished.
MK_C02_K09:
Even in the dream-state, that which is imagined inwardly by the mind is unreal; while what is grasped outwardly by consciousness is held to be real — yet the falsity of both is seen.

Within dream itself, what mere wishful thought constructs is rejected as unreal, while pots and the like apprehended through the senses are taken as real. Both, however, being equally mental constructions, are equally false.
MK_C02_K09::block-0:
Having dispelled the doubt about novelty, the kārikā now expounds further the parity of waking-distinctions with dream by elaborating the dream-example itself.

Even in the dream-state — that is, even within the dream-realm — what is imagined inwardly by the mind, in the form of wishful thought, is held to be unreal; for it disappears the very moment after the wish-thought, simultaneously with it. There in the same dream, what is grasped outwardly by consciousness — apprehended through the eye and the other senses, such as pot and cloth — is taken to be real. Thus a division into real and unreal is seen, even though all of it has actually been determined to be false.

Hence, although both alike are imagined by the inward and outward mind, the falsity of both is seen. The seeming difference between the inwardly-imagined and the outwardly-grasped is itself a construction; in truth both stand on the same footing of unreality.
MK_C02_K10:
Even in the waking-state, what is imagined inwardly by the mind is unreal; what is grasped outwardly by consciousness is held to be real. The falsity of both is reasonable.

In waking too, mere thought-constructs are deemed unreal, while perceived objects are taken as real; yet since both alike arise as mental constructions, both are equally false.
MK_C02_K10::block-0:
The falsity of both the seemingly-real and the seemingly-unreal is reasonable, since there is no difference between them in being constructions of the inward and outward mind. The rest has already been explained.

Thus, just as in dream both inwardly-imagined and outwardly-grasped objects are alike false, so in waking too both stand equally as mental constructions, and equally as unreal.
MK_C02_K11:
If the falsity of the distinctions in both states be admitted, then who knows these distinctions, and who indeed is their imaginer?

If both waking and dream are equally false, what is the basis of memory and knowledge of these distinctions? Who perceives them, and who constructs them?
MK_C02_K11::block-0:
The objector speaks: If the distinctions belonging to both the dream-state and the waking-state are equally false, then who knows these distinctions imagined by the inward and outward mind? And who, indeed, is their imaginer? What is the support, the substratum, of memory and knowledge?

The import is: unless one is willing to embrace the doctrine of no-self, some abiding knower must be admitted. Falsity cannot apprehend falsity; cognition and recollection must rest upon something. Hence either there is a real knower, or the Buddhist position of soullessness must follow.
MK_C02_K12:
The Self, the resplendent Ātman, by His own māyā imagines Himself through Himself; He alone knows the distinctions — such is the conclusion of Vedānta.

Ātman the luminous, by His own māyā, projects within Himself all the differentiated forms and Himself cognizes them, just as a rope appears as snake. This is the firm conclusion of the Upaniṣads — there is no other ground for knowledge and memory.
MK_C02_K12::block-0:
By Himself, through His own māyā, Ātman the resplendent imagines His own Self in His very Self in the form of distinctions about to be expounded — just as one imagines snakes and the like in a rope. He Himself, again, cognizes those distinctions — exactly in that very same manner. Such is the firm conclusion of Vedānta.

There exists no other support for knowledge and memory than the Self. Nor can knowledge and memory hang upon nothing at all, as the nihilists (vaināśika) hold; cognition without a cogniser is impossible. Hence the one Ātman, by māyā, both projects and apprehends the manifold — and this alone resolves the difficulty raised.
MK_C02_K13:
He variously fashions other entities established within the mind, and the determinate ones outside the mind — thus does the Lord imagine.

The Lord, by becoming inward-minded, projects the impressions of word and the rest as latent within; by becoming outward-minded He projects the determinate world of earth and the like. In both modes, the imaginer is none other than the Self.
MK_C02_K13::block-0:
How does He, by imagining, fashion forth? It is now told. He variously fashions, makes manifold, the other worldly entities — that is, words and other objects of experience — that are established within the mind in the form of latent impressions, unmanifest, by becoming outward-minded; and likewise the determinate ones such as earth and the rest, which are limited to the time of imagining.

In the same way, becoming inward-minded, He fashions the wishful thoughts and the like. Thus does He imagine — He, the Lord, the īśvara, that is, the Self. The whole manifold is thus seen to be a sport of the one Ātman, who in His sovereignty projects both the inner mental states and the outer enduring objects.
MK_C02_K14:
Those inner objects which last only as long as the thought, and those outer ones which are bounded by mutual duration — all alike are mere imaginations; their distinction has no other cause than the imagination itself.

Inner thoughts last only while thought of; outer objects mutually delimit each other's duration. Yet both are equally constructions, and the difference between them is itself part of the construction — without further reality.
MK_C02_K14::block-0:
It might be feared that not everything can be a mere mental construction like dream, since wishful thoughts and other inner constructions are limited only by the mind that conceives them, while outer objects are mutually delimited and so seem of a different order — possessing an independent measure. This apprehension is unwarranted.

Those that are inner — that is, are bounded only by the mind — have no measurer apart from the time of the mind itself; they are time-of-thought, perceived only in the act of thinking. The two-time ones — that is, the outer differentiated objects — are mutually delimited: as in 'while he sits, he milks the cow; while he milks the cow, he sits' — so that the sitting and the milking each measure and are measured by the other. So much of the one corresponds to so much of the other; this is the mutual measurer-measured relation among outer distinctions, and these are the two-time ones.

Both — the inner thought-time objects and the outer two-time objects — are alike mere constructions. The supposed difference of being two-time, possessed by the outer, has no cause apart from imagination itself: it is a feature of the imagining, not an independent real. Here too the dream-example holds good: in dream as well, both inner mental imaginings and outer apparently mutually-delimited objects are alike unreal.
MK_C02_K15: Those that are unmanifest within, and those that are clearly manifest without — all of these are merely imagined; the difference lies only in the sense-organ (through which they are perceived).
MK_C02_K15::block-0:
The supposed distinction here — that within, the things manifest only through mental impressions are unmanifest, while without, in another sense-organ such as the eye, they are clearly manifest — is not produced by any real existence of the differences themselves; for in dream too the very same kind of inner-and-outer distinction is observed.

What then is it caused by? It is caused solely by the difference of sense-organs. Hence it stands established that the objects of the waking state are likewise mere imaginations, exactly as the objects of dream are.
MK_C02_K16: First the (Self) imagines the jīva, and thereafter the various objects, both external and internal; as is one's knowledge, so does one's memory become.
MK_C02_K16::block-0:
What, it may be asked, is the root of this imagining of external and internal entities as mutually causes and effects? It is now stated. First — upon the pure Self, which is in truth devoid of such characteristics — there is imagined, as a serpent upon a rope, the jīva, marked by the form of being agent and enjoyer: 'I act; mine are pleasure and pain.'

Thereafter, conformably with that (jīva-notion), and through the distinctions of action, instrument, and fruit, are imagined the manifold entities — prāṇa and the rest — both external and internal. And what, it is asked, is the cause of this imagining? It is this: that very jīva, itself imagined and made the locus of all imagination, is yathāvidya — that is, of such a kind as is his vidyā or cognition; and his memory becomes correspondingly tathā-smṛti, of the same kind.

Hence: from the cognition of imagined causes arises the cognition of effects; therefrom the memory of cause and effect; therefrom further cognition; therefrom the cognitions of the corresponding action, instrument, and fruit-distinctions; therefrom the memory of these; and from that memory, again, the cognitions thereof. Thus, in this manner, both external and internal entities, in the relation of mutual cause-and-effect, are imagined manifoldly.
MK_C02_K17: Just as a rope, when not definitely ascertained in the dark, is variously imagined as a serpent, a stream of water, a staff and so on, even so is the Self (Ātman) variously imagined.
MK_C02_K17::block-0:
It was stated that the imagination of the jīva is the root of all imaginations. By what cause this very imagination of the jīva itself comes about is now expounded by means of an illustration. As in the world a rope, when its true form is not ascertained — when one has not determined 'this is just thus' — comes, in dim darkness, to be variously imagined as a serpent, or a stream of water, or a staff, owing in the first instance to the non-determination of its real nature; for had the rope been at the very outset definitely known in its own form, the imaginations of serpent and the rest would not have arisen, just as they do not arise about one's own hand or fingers — this is the illustration.

In the same way, because the Self, distinct from the painful properties of saṃsāra such as cause-and-effect and so on, has not been ascertained in its own nature as pure intelligence, mere existence, and non-duality, it is imagined through the endless distinctions of jīva, prāṇa, and the rest. This is the established conclusion of all the Upaniṣads.
MK_C02_K18: As, when the rope is definitely ascertained, the imagination ceases and there remains the non-duality 'it is rope alone' — even so is the ascertainment of the Self.
MK_C02_K18::block-0:
As, upon the ascertainment 'it is the rope itself,' the imaginations of serpent and the rest cease and there abides the non-duality 'it is rope alone' — even so does there arise the ascertainment of the Self, brought about by the sunlight of the knowledge generated by the scriptures which expound the Self as void of all properties of saṃsāra, in the form 'neti neti.'

That ascertainment is: 'All this is the Self alone — without a prior, without a posterior, without an interior, without an exterior, having outside and inside (as itself), unborn, undecaying, immortal, fearless, one alone, non-dual.'
MK_C02_K19: By these endless entities such as prāṇa and the rest is (the Self) imagined; this is the māyā of that resplendent (Self), by which it is itself, as it were, deluded.
MK_C02_K19::block-0:
If the ascertainment is that the Self is one alone, how then is it imagined through these endless entities such as prāṇa and the rest, which constitute saṃsāra? It is now answered — listen.

This is the māyā of that resplendent Self. Just as a magician's deployed magic makes the perfectly clear sky appear as if filled with trees that are flowering and bear leaves, even so is this māyā of the Lord, by which He, though Himself unaffected, becomes as it were deluded. As has been said, 'My māyā is hard to overcome' (Bhagavad-Gītā 7.14).
MK_C02_K20: The knowers of prāṇa say it is prāṇa; the knowers of bhūtas say it is the (gross) elements; the knowers of guṇas say it is the guṇas; the knowers of tattvas say it is the tattvas (categories).
MK_C02_K21: The knowers of pādas (quarters) call it pādas; the knowers of objects call it objects; the knowers of worlds call it worlds; the knowers of devas call it devas.
MK_C02_K22: The knowers of the Vedas call it Vedas; the knowers of yajñas call it yajñas; the knowers of the enjoyer call it the enjoyer; and the knowers of the enjoyed call it the enjoyed.
MK_C02_K23:
Those who know the subtle declare It as the subtle; those who know the gross hold It to be the gross. Those who know the formed call It the formed, while those who know the formless declare It to be the formless.

The one Self, devoid of all such distinctions, is variously imagined according to the predilections of those who superimpose upon It their favoured categories, just as a rope is taken to be a snake or a stick.
MK_C02_K24:
Those versed in time speak of It as time; those versed in the directions speak of It as the quarters. Those who know disputations call It the disputations; those who know the worlds call It the worlds.

Each class of theorists projects upon the partless Self the very category in which they are most expert, mistaking their own conception for the ultimate truth.
MK_C02_K25:
Those who know the mind call It mind; those who know the intellect call It the intellect. Those who know the citta call It citta; those who know dharma and adharma call It these two.

Thus, depending on the vāsanā of the speaker, the one Self is named after the inner instrument or after merit and demerit, though It transcends them all.
MK_C02_K26:
Some say It is composed of twenty-five principles, others of twenty-six. Yet others speak of It as constituted of thirty-one categories, while still others declare It to be infinite.

Thus the Sāṅkhyas, Pāśupatas, Pāñcarātrins and others, each according to their own system of enumeration, fasten upon the one Self the limited number of tattvas they have postulated.
MK_C02_K27:
The knowers of worlds declare It to be the worlds; the knowers of the āśramas call It the stages of life. Those versed in genders speak of It as masculine, feminine, and neuter; while still others speak of It as the higher and the lower.

In this way every school, gripped by its own preferred category, projects that very category upon the Self which is in truth attribute-less and beyond all such divisions.
MK_C02_K28:
Those versed in creation call It creation; those versed in dissolution speak of It as dissolution. Those versed in sustenance call It sustenance — and yet all these (categories) reside here always (in the Self).

Thus the cosmologists, fixated each upon his preferred phase of the world-process, name the unborn Self after creation, dissolution, or sustenance, though all such notions abide nowhere but in the Self itself.
MK_C02_K28::block-0:
Prāṇa is Prājña, the seed-Self, and the rest — beginning with the gross and ending with sustenance — are but the differentiated effects of that very seed. All the other distinctions, conceived by the world and imagined by every kind of being, are like the snake, the stick, and the streak of water that are projected upon the rope.

These are imagined in the Self — which is in truth empty of them all — owing to avidyā, the cause of which is the failure to ascertain the true nature of the Self. This is the gist of the matter.

Since it would yield only meagre fruit, and since the meanings of the words are themselves well established, no effort has been made here to comment upon each padārtha of the verses on prāṇa and the rest individually.
MK_C02_K29:
Whatever object one shows to a man as the truth, that very object he proceeds to behold (as himself or his own); and that object, having become him as it were, protects him; and the grasp of that object lays hold of him.

Thus, identifying himself with whatever notion has been impressed upon him, the seeker is bound by that very notion as if it were the ultimate reality.
MK_C02_K29::block-0:
What more need be said?
