Whichever bhāva — that is, whichever entity, whether one of the categories beginning with prāṇa already mentioned, or some other not mentioned at all — an ācārya or any other authoritative person points out to a disciple, saying "this alone is the truth," the disciple then beholds that very entity as himself, thinking "I am this," or thinking "this is mine."

And that bhāva which has been thus shown protects him, that is, the very entity now beheld as the Self enshrouds him on every side, sealing him off with itself. The grasping of that — tadgrahaḥ, the fixed conviction "this alone is the truth" — then lays hold of him, the grasper, and reaches him in turn: meaning, the entity attains the status of his very Self.

Thus the disciple becomes whatever Reality has been displayed to him, and the limited conception which he was taught becomes for him the whole of his being.
MK_C02_K30:
By these (prāṇa and the rest), which are not in truth distinct from the Self, this Self is yet apprehended as though distinct. He who knows it thus, in truth, may speak (of these as separate) without misgiving.

The deluded, perceiving the imagined as real, take the modifications to be other than the Self; but the discerning, recognising them as mere superimpositions like the snake on the rope, behold them as nothing but the one Self.
MK_C02_K30::block-0:
By these — by prāṇa and the rest — which are in truth not separate from the Self (apṛthag-bhāvaiḥ), this Self is yet apprehended (lakṣitaḥ), determined, as though separate, in the form of imagined modifications resembling the snake projected upon the rope. So is It taken to be by the deluded.

For the discerning, however, just as the snake and the rest imagined upon the rope have no being apart from the rope, so prāṇa and the rest have no existence apart from the Self. This is the import — and it is supported by the śruti, "all this is what this Self is" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka 2.4.6).

He who knows in truth, both from śruti and from reasoning, that what is superimposed upon the Self has no existence apart from the Self — like the snake upon the rope — and who knows the Self alone as one without modification, he, being free from misgiving, can rightly distribute the meaning of the Vedas into its sections (vibhāgataḥ kalpayet): "this passage has such-and-such purport, that one a different one."

For without the knowledge of the inner Self, no one can know the Vedas in truth. As the Mānava text says: "None who is ignorant of the inner Self ever attains the fruit of his actions" (Manu 6.82).
MK_C02_K31: As dream and māyā are seen, and as the city of the gandharvas, so this entire universe is seen by those proficient in the Vedānta. (31)
MK_C02_K31::block-0:
What was earlier established by reasoning, namely the unreality of duality, is now declared to be ascertained from the Vedānta as the means of valid knowledge. "Svapna" (dream) and "māyā" (illusion) — these two, "svapnamāye," though by their very nature unreal entities (asadvastvātmike), are taken by the undiscerning to be real, as if they were of the nature of real things (sadvastvātmika iva).

Just as a city of the gandharvas, appearing as if filled with the bustle of spread-out wares, market-shops, houses, palaces, women, troops of men and rural settlements (prasārita-paṇyāpaṇa-gṛha-prāsāda-strī-puñja-janapada-vyavahārākīrṇam iva), is seen, while being perceived, suddenly to lapse into nothingness; and just as dream and māyā are perceived as having an unreal form (asadrūpe); so too is this entire duality of the universe seen as wholly unreal.

Where is it so seen? — In the Vedāntas, namely in such passages as "There is no diversity whatsoever here" (Kaṭha 2.1.11), "Indra by his māyās" (Bṛhad. 2.5.19), "This was the Self alone in the beginning" (Bṛhad. 1.4.1), "This was Brahman alone in the beginning" (Bṛhad. 1.4.10), "From a second indeed arises fear" (Bṛhad. 1.4.2), "Yet there is no second to It" (Bṛhad. 4.3.23), "When for him all has become the very Self" (Bṛhad. 4.5.15), and the like, by "vicakṣaṇaiḥ" — by the most acute seers of reality, that is, by the wise. So too the Vyāsa-smṛti: "It (the world) is seen as resembling a pit of darkness, like a bubble in the rain, prone to destruction, devoid of happiness, and after destruction reduced to non-being" (Mokṣadharma 301.60).
MK_C02_K32: There is no dissolution, no origination, none bound, none striving, none seeking liberation, and none liberated — this is the supreme truth. (32)
MK_C02_K32::block-0:
This verse is for the conclusion of the topic of the chapter. When duality is unreal and the Self alone is one, real in the highest sense, then this becomes established — that this entire worldly and Vedic activity is solely within the sphere of avidyā. Then there is no "nirodha" — "nirodhana" being dissolution; no "utpatti" — origination; no "baddha" — the bound transmigrating soul; no "sādhaka" — one possessed of the means to mokṣa; no "mumukṣu" — one desirous of release; no "mukta" — one whose bondage has been loosed. Because of the absence of origination and dissolution, the bound and the rest do not exist — this is the supreme truth.

How is there absence of origination and dissolution? It is replied: because of the unreality of duality. From numerous śrutis such as "Where there is, as it were, duality" (Bṛhad. 2.4.14), "He who sees here as if many" (Kaṭha 2.1.10), "All this is the Self alone" (Chānd. 7.25.2), "All this is Brahman alone," "One only, without a second" (Chānd. 6.2.1), "All this is what this Self is" (Bṛhad. 2.4.6), the unreality of duality is established. For only of an existent thing could there be origination or dissolution, not of a non-existent like the horns of a hare. Nor does the non-dual originate or dissolve. To say "non-dual" yet "with origination and dissolution" is contradictory.

But as for the empirical transactions of duality, that has been said to be imagined upon the Self in the form of the prāṇas etc., like the snake on the rope. Of the mental imagination of the form of rope-snake there is neither dissolution nor origination upon the rope itself; nor in the mind is there origination or dissolution of the rope-snake; nor in both. Likewise, since duality is uniformly mental, in a controlled or sleeping mind duality is not apprehended; therefore it is established that duality is mere mental imagination. Thus it is well said: due to the unreality of duality, the absence of dissolution etc. is the supreme truth.

Objection (pūrvapakṣa): If the operation of the śāstra pertains to the absence of duality and not to non-duality (because of contradiction), then non-duality would have no proof, leading to the doctrine of the Śūnyavādins (the void-theorists), since duality also is absent.

Reply (siddhānta): No. The unworkability of imagination without a basis has already been answered, just as the rope is the basis of the snake imagined upon it. — How then do you revive this objection?

Further objection: Even the rope, being the basis of the snake-imagination, is itself but imagined; thus the example fails.

Reply: No. When the imagination is dissolved, the unimagined remains precisely as the unimagined, and so its reality is established. — "It is unreal like the rope-snake," if so urged — no, because it is not absolutely unimagined; like the un-imagined portion of the rope itself prior to the cognition of the absence of the snake, and because the imaginer is admitted to be established prior to the rise of imagination, there is no possibility of its non-existence.

Further objection: How then, with no operation of the śāstra upon its very nature, can the śāstra cause the cessation of the cognition of duality?

Reply: This is no defect, because duality, like the snake on the rope, is superimposed by avidyā upon the Self. Notions such as "I am happy," "I am sorrowful," "deluded," "born," "dead," "aged," "possessed of a body," "I see," "manifest," "unmanifest," "agent," "enjoyer," "connected," "separated," "diminished," "grown," "these are mine" — all these are superimposed upon the Self. The Self runs through them all without deviation, like the rope through the various cognitions of snake, stream, staff and the like.

And since the cognition of the qualified (the Self as such) is established, there is no need for the śāstra to do anything regarding it. Indeed, the śāstra does not produce what is unproduced; were it merely to imitate what is already produced, it would not be a means of valid knowledge. But since, due to the obstruction of particularities like happiness etc. superimposed by avidyā, the Self does not abide in its own nature, and the abiding in one's own nature is the supreme good — therefore the śāstra removes happiness etc. from the Self by producing in the Self the cognition of "not unhappy" etc., that is, by the "neti neti" method (the bhāṣya is truncated here).
MK_C02_K33: This (Self) is imagined by means of unreal entities and also by the non-dual; the entities too are only by the non-dual. Therefore non-duality is auspicious. (33)
MK_C02_K33::block-0:
He states the reason for the meaning of the previous verse. As upon a rope, by means of the unreal — the snake, the stream, the staff and the like — and also by means of the non-dual real rope-substance, the rope-substance itself is imagined as "this is a snake," "this is a stream," "this is a staff," — even so, by means of unreal — non-existent — prāṇas etc. that are infinite, not in the highest sense real. For when the mind is unstirred, no entity can be perceived by anyone; and there is no stirring of the Self. The entities perceived only by the stirred (mind) cannot be imagined as real in the highest sense.

Therefore, by unreal entities — the prāṇas etc. — and by the non-dual paramārtha-sat (the supremely real) Self, who like the rope is the basis of all imaginations, is this Self imagined by Itself, though It is ever of one nature.

And those entities, the prāṇas and the rest, are also imagined only by the non-dual real Self; for no imagination is possible without a basis. Hence, since the Self is the basis of all imagination, and the non-dual does not deviate by its own being even in the state of imagination, non-duality is auspicious (śivā). The imaginations alone are inauspicious, for they cause fear etc. like the rope-snake. Non-duality is fearless; therefore it alone is auspicious.
MK_C02_K34: This (universe) is not many by way of being the Self, nor in any way by its own being; nor is anything separate or non-separate — thus the knowers of truth know. (34)
MK_C02_K34::block-0:
Why is non-duality auspicious? Where the manifold — the otherness of one from another — is seen, there would be the inauspicious. But here, in the supremely real non-dual Self, this entire universe born of saṃsāra in the form of prāṇas etc., when examined as to its being-the-Self in its supremely real nature, does not turn out to be a manifold separate substance — just as the snake imagined and seen as manifold does not exist when examined by the light of the rope's true form. Nor does it ever exist by its own being as prāṇa etc., precisely because it is imagined like the rope-snake.

Likewise, prāṇa and the like do not exist as separate from one another, in the way a buffalo exists separately from a horse. And because of their unreality, neither do they exist as non-separate from one another or from the supreme. Thus the brāhmaṇas who know the supreme truth understand. Hence, since there is no cause of inauspiciousness, non-duality alone is auspicious — this is the purport.
MK_C02_K35: By the sages, free from passion, fear and anger, who have crossed to the further shore of the Vedas, this (Self) has been seen as devoid of all imagination, as the cessation of the world, as non-dual. (35)
MK_C02_K35::block-0:
This very same right vision is praised. By the sages — those of the nature of constant reflection, the discerning — free from all defects such as passion, fear, anger and the rest, who have crossed to the further shore of the Vedas, that is, who have ascertained the truth of the meaning of the Vedānta, the knowers, this Self is seen — directly apprehended as without any imagination (nirvikalpa), as utterly free from imagination, by those wholly devoted to the meaning of the Vedānta. "Prapañcopaśama" — "prapañca" being the spread of the diversity of duality, in which it is at rest, that is, absent — the Self in which the prapañca is silenced.

For this very reason it is non-dual. Only by the wise, free from defects, and devoted to the Vedānta, namely the saṃnyāsins, is this Self capable of being seen, not by others — those whose minds are sullied by passion etc., dialecticians and the like with views that incline towards their own factions. This is the purport.
MK_C02_K36: Therefore, having known It thus, one should fix one's memory upon non-duality. Having attained non-duality, one should comport oneself in the world as one inert. (36)
MK_C02_K36::block-0:
Since the non-dual is auspicious and fearless because it is of the form of the cessation of all evil — therefore, having known It thus, one should fix one's memory upon non-duality, that is, one should make one's recollection conduce to the apprehension of non-duality.

And having ascertained that non-duality, having known "I am the supreme Brahman," one should comport oneself in the world like one inert, in regard to the Self that is beyond hunger and the rest, immediate and self-revealing, unborn, transcending all worldly transactions — that is, not displaying oneself as "I am of such-and-such a nature." This is the purport.
MK_C02_K37: Free from praise, free from salutation, free from svadhā-rituals (offerings to the ancestors), with both the moving and the unmoving as his abode, the renunciate should live by whatever comes by chance. (37)
MK_C02_K37::block-0:
How should he comport himself in the world? It is replied: free from all rituals such as praise, salutation, and the like, having renounced all external desires, having entered the renunciation of the supreme swan order (paramahaṃsa-pārivrājya). This is the purport, on the strength of such śrutis as "Having known this very Self" (Bṛhad. 3.5.1) and such smṛtis as "Their understanding fixed on That, their self in That, established in That, having That as the supreme goal" (Gītā 5.17).

"Cala" — the body, since it changes every moment; "acala" — the principle of the Self. Whenever, on occasion of eating and the like transactions, the knower forgets the abode of the Self, namely his standing in the unchanging Self-principle which is space-like and motionless, and thinks "I," then the moving body becomes his abode — such a one is "calācalaniketa" (one whose abode is now the moving body, now the unmoving Self), the wise man no longer takes refuge in external objects.

And he should be "yādṛcchika" — that is, of bodily subsistence consisting only of loin-cloth, covering and morsel of food obtained as it chances. This is the meaning.
MK_C02_K38: Having seen the truth as inner, and having seen the truth also as outer, becoming the truth itself, delighting in That, he should never fall away from the truth. (38)
MK_C02_K38::block-0:
The outer — the earth and the rest — and the inner of the form of body etc., are unreal, like the rope-snake and like dream and māyā, on the authority of such śrutis as "It is a transformation that is mere talk, a name" (Chānd. 6.1.4). The Self, on the other hand, is with the outer and the inner, unborn, without a prior, without a posterior, without inside, without outside, whole, like space pervading all, subtle, motionless, devoid of qualities, partless, actionless, on the authority of "That truth, that Self, that thou art" (Chānd. 6.8.7).

Having thus seen the truth, one becomes the truth itself, delighting in That, not delighting in the outer. Just as one who does not see the truth, having taken the body to be the Self, supposing himself to follow the movements of the mind, sometimes thinks "I, fallen from the truth, am now the body etc., a Self that has slipped from the principle"; and when the mind is gathered, sometimes thinks, "I am now established as the truth, of clear nature" — not so the knower of the Self, since the Self is of one form and slipping from one's own nature is impossible.

"I am Brahman ever" — thus he is one not fallen from the truth, that is, his vision of the Self-truth has not slipped at any time. This is the purport, on the strength of smṛtis such as "In a dog and in a dog-eater" (Gītā 5.18) and "the same in all beings" (Gītā 13.27).
MK_C03_K01: The seeker who takes refuge in upāsanā (devout meditation) abides in a Brahman that has been produced. But before its origination, all this is unborn (aja); for that reason such a one is called wretched (kṛpaṇa).
MK_C03_K01::block-0:
In the determination of Om it was stated that 'the cessation of phenomenal plurality, the auspicious and non-dual, is the Self,' merely as a thesis to be proved, and again in the words 'when That is known, duality does not exist' (Mā. Kā. 1.18). Thereafter, in the chapter on Vaitathya (the Unreality of phenomena), the absence of duality was established by means of illustrations such as dream, māyā and the city of the gandharvas, and through reasoning grounded in the marks of being perceived (dṛśyatva), having a beginning and end (ādyantavattva), and the like.

Now the question arises: is non-duality (advaita) to be apprehended only through scriptural testimony (āgama-mātra), or can it also be ascertained through reasoning (tarka)? To this Gauḍapāda answers: it can also be known through reasoning. With the question 'How so?' the Advaita-prakaraṇa is begun.

In the previous chapter it was settled that the entire complex of difference such as the meditator, the object of meditation, and so forth is unreal (vitatha), and that the bare Self alone, non-dual, is the supreme reality (paramārtha). For one who, having taken to upāsanā as a means of liberation for himself with the notion 'I am the worshipper, Brahman is mine to worship,' having performed that worship, is now abiding in a Brahman that has come into being, and thinks: 'after the fall of the body I shall attain the unborn Brahman, and before its origination this all and I myself were unborn.' He whose essence was unborn before origination, having now been born and abiding in a born Brahman, hopes by upāsanā to recover that very state again.

Thus the dharma resting on upāsanā (upāsanāśrita-dharma) makes the practitioner a knower of a petty Brahman (kṣudra-brahma-vit). For this reason such a one is remembered (smṛta) as kṛpaṇa, a destitute, a paltry being, by the great souls who behold the eternal unborn Brahman. This is the import, as is taught in the Talavakāra (Kena) text: 'That which is not uttered by speech, that by which speech is uttered, that alone know thou as Brahman, not this which people here worship' (Ke. U. 1.5).
MK_C03_K02: Therefore I shall declare that which is free from wretchedness (akārpaṇya), unborn (ajāti), having attained complete sameness — the manner in which nothing whatsoever is born though seemingly being born on every side.
MK_C03_K02::block-0:
Unable to apprehend the Self as unborn, both within and without (sa-bāhyābhyantaram aja), and considering himself wretched through avidyā, one who thinks 'I am born; I abide in a born Brahman; resorting to upāsanā I shall attain Brahman' becomes a kṛpaṇa. Therefore I shall declare akārpaṇya — the state free of destitution, namely the unborn Brahman.

What is born is the very seat of wretchedness, as the śrutis teach: 'Wherein one sees another, hears another, knows another — that is the petty (alpa)' (Chā. U. 7.24.1); 'That is mortal'; 'Modification is a mere name, a verbal handle' (Chā. U. 6.1.4). The opposite of that, namely the unborn Brahman both within and without, called the Plenitude (bhūman) and free of wretchedness — on attaining which all the wretchedness wrought by avidyā is dispelled — that akārpaṇya I shall now declare.

'Ajāti' means: that to which no birth (jāti) belongs. 'Samatāṁ gatam' means: it has reached complete sameness on all sides. Why so? Because it is devoid of any inequality of parts. A thing possessed of parts is said to be born when it undergoes inequality among its parts; but this Brahman, being partless (niravayava), has attained sameness, and therefore does not split into any parts. Hence it is said: ajāti, akārpaṇya, samantataḥ — on every side, in no manner does even the smallest fragment come into being. As a rope-snake (rajju-sarpa) seems to be born through the vision created by avidyā, so does this seem; yet by every reckoning Brahman alone, the unborn, remains. Hear, then, the manner in which it is not born.
MK_C03_K03: The Self is, indeed, like ākāśa (space); It appears as it were arisen as the jīvas, just as ākāśa appears arisen as the spaces enclosed in pots. And like the pots and similar aggregates that arise from ākāśa, the bodily aggregates arise from the Self — this is the illustration concerning birth.
MK_C03_K03::block-0:
It was promised that 'the unborn Brahman, free of wretchedness, shall be declared.' To establish that, the kārikā states the reason and the illustration. The Self (ātmā), the supreme one — for It is subtle, partless, and all-pervading — is described as ākāśavat, 'like ākāśa.' By the jīvas, the kṣetrajñas (knowers of the field), It appears arisen, even as ākāśa appears arisen as the spaces in pots (ghaṭākāśa). The supreme Ātman is, in this manner, like ākāśa.

Or alternatively: just as ākāśa is said to be 'born' through the spaces in pots, so the supreme Self is said to be born through the individual selves. The birth of the jīvas from the supreme Ātman that is heard of in the Vedānta texts is comparable to the birth of pot-spaces from the great ākāśa — and is not real (na paramārthatas). This is the import.

Further: just as from that very ākāśa pot-aggregates and the like are seen to arise, so from the supreme Ātman, who stands in the place of ākāśa, arise the aggregates of earth and the other elements outwardly, and the inner aggregates of body and organs (kārya-karaṇa) — all imagined like a snake on a rope. Therefore it is said: 'the Self appears arisen as the aggregates such as pots.'

When, in deference to the slow-witted whom the śruti seeks to teach, scripture speaks of the birth of the Self as that of the jīvas and the rest, then, when birth is provisionally accepted, this — the example of ākāśa — serves as the illustration.
MK_C03_K04: When pots and similar things are dissolved, the spaces within the pots merge back into ākāśa; in the same way, the jīvas here merge back into the Self.
MK_C03_K04::block-0: Just as the origination of pots and the like brings about the origination of the spaces in pots, and the dissolution of the pots brings about the dissolution of the spaces in them, so by the origination of the body-and-organ aggregate the jīva originates, and by its dissolution the jīvas dissolve here in the Self — not on their own (na svataḥ). This is the meaning. The seeming birth and dissolution of the jīva is wholly conditional upon the upādhi (limiting adjunct), and not intrinsic to the Self at all.
MK_C03_K05: Just as when one space within a pot is conjoined with dust, smoke, and the like, not all the pot-spaces become so conjoined, in the same way the jīvas are not all conjoined with pleasures and pains.
MK_C03_K05::block-0:
If the Self were one in all bodies, then because the Self in any one would possess birth, death, pleasure and pain, all selves would be involved with that, and there would arise an admixture of action and result (kriyā-phala-sāṅkarya) — so say the Dvaitins. To them this is the answer: just as when one pot-space is joined with dust, smoke, and the like, not all the pot-spaces and other spaces are joined with that dust and smoke, so it is with the jīvas in regard to pleasures and the rest.

But, the objector continues: surely you yourself hold there is but one Self. Granted; have you not heard that, like ākāśa, the one Self exists in all aggregates? If so, the same Self would, everywhere, be at once happy and miserable.

This objection cannot stand against the Sāṅkhya. For the Sāṅkhya does not allow that pleasure, pain and the rest belong to the Self at all; he assigns them to buddhi, in which they inhere by samavāya. Nor is there any pramāṇa for imagining differences in the Self whose very nature is mere awareness (upalabdhi-svarūpa).

'But if there is no difference, the prakṛti's being for-the-sake-of-another (pārārthya) becomes unaccounted for' — not so. For what prakṛti accomplishes does not inhere in the Self; if bondage and liberation, the fruits of prakṛti's activity, were to inhere severally in different puruṣas, then prakṛti's pārārthya would be unestablished if there were one Self, and the postulating of plurality of puruṣas would be reasonable. But the Sāṅkhyas themselves do not admit that bondage or liberation inhere in the puruṣa as an object; they admit that the puruṣas are mere consciousness, devoid of distinguishing marks. Hence prakṛti's pārārthya is established merely by the bare existence of puruṣa (puruṣa-sattā-mātra-prayuktam), not by any plurality among puruṣas. Therefore, plurality of puruṣa is not to be inferred from pārārthya; nor is there any other pramāṇa for the Sāṅkhya in support of such plurality. Taking only the existence of the Other as occasion, prakṛti binds and frees itself; and the Other, in His being mere awareness, is the cause of prakṛti's activity, without any specifying mark. Hence the postulating of plurality of puruṣas, and the abandonment of the meaning of the Veda, is sheer delusion.

The Vaiśeṣikas and the like say: desire and the rest inhere in the Self by samavāya. This too is unsound. The saṁskāras which are the cause of memory cannot inhere in a Self that has no spatial parts; and if memory arises merely from the contact of Self and mind, the regularity of memory cannot be accounted for, or else all memories would arise simultaneously. Nor is conjunction proper between Selves of a different category — devoid of touch and the rest — and the mind and other things. Nor are qualities such as colour, or motions, generalities and particulars and samavāya, ever distinct from substance.

If, on the opponent's view, desire and the rest were utterly distinct from the substance Self, no relation between them and the substance could be made out. 'But the relation called samavāya is not contradictory in things ayuta-siddha (inseparable in being)' — no; for the eternal Self is established prior to the impermanent desires and the rest, and so cannot be ayuta-siddha with them. And if it were ayuta-siddha with the Self, then desires and the rest would have to be eternal, like the Self's magnitude. That is undesired, since it would entail the Self's never being released.

If samavāya is itself other than substance, another relation would have to be specified between samavāya and substance, just as between substance and quality. 'Samavāya is itself simply a permanent relation, and need not be further related' — then all things in the relation of samavāya would be permanently related, and any separation between them would be unintelligible. And if substance and the rest were utterly separate, the very meaning of the genitive case would fail, as between two substances of which one has touch and the other does not.

Further, if the Self were qualified by adventitious arrival and departure of desires and the like, the Self would become impermanent. Like the body and its fruits, the Self would be saṁśrayed by parts and modifications — and these defects, like those of the body, would be unavoidable. Thus the imagination of plurality of Selves, of inherence of qualities in the Self, and of samavāya as a real relation distinct from substance, all collapse. The Vedāntic teaching that the one Self alone is real, and that the apparent diversity of jīvas is upādhi-borne — like dust on one pot-space and not on others — therefore stands firm.
MK_C03_K06: Form, function, and name differ in this place and that; yet there is no real difference in ākāśa itself. Just so should the conclusion be reached regarding the jīvas.
MK_C03_K06::block-0:
How then can the empirical usage that depends on apparent difference of selves arise in one Self, when in truth that difference is only avidyā-wrought? The answer: just as in the one ākāśa here, the spaces in a pot, water-pot, an inner room and so on are differentiated by smallness, largeness and the like, and likewise their functions — fetching water, holding, lying down — are seen to differ, and the names too, 'the pot-space,' 'the water-pot-space,' and so on, are seen to differ accordingly, in this and that field of usage; yet all this usage in ākāśa, occasioned by differences of form, function and name, is wholly non-ultimate (aparamārtha eva).

In paramārtha there is no difference in ākāśa whatever. Nor does any usage referring to a difference in ākāśa arise apart from the door of an external upādhi. As that is, so is it with the jīvas — the selves likened to pot-spaces, distinguished only by the upādhis of bodies. Upon investigation, the wise reach this nirṇaya (settled conclusion). The diversity belongs to the upādhis; the Self remains undivided.
MK_C03_K07: The space within a pot is neither a modification nor a part of ākāśa; in the same way the jīva is never a modification or a part of the Self.
MK_C03_K07::block-0:
It might be objected that in pot-spaces and the rest the differences of form, function and the like really are of the nature of paramārtha. This is not so. For the pot-space is not a vikāra (modification) of the supreme ākāśa, as a ring or other ornament is of gold, or as foam, bubble and ice are of water; nor is it an avayava (part) of ākāśa, as a branch is of a tree.

Just as the pot-space is neither a modification nor a part of ākāśa, even so the jīva, who corresponds to the pot-space, is never — sadā, at any time — a modification or a part of the supreme Ātman, the paramārtha-sat (truly real), who corresponds to the great ākāśa. Therefore the usage based on the supposed difference of selves is mere illusion (mṛṣaiva). It has no foothold in the real.
MK_C03_K08: Just as for the childlike the sky appears soiled by impurities, so for the unawakened the Self too appears soiled by impurities.
MK_C03_K08::block-0:
Since the empirical usage of differences of form, function and so on rests upon the imagined differences of pot-spaces and the like, and since likewise the empirical usage of birth, death and the rest rests upon the differences of jīvas conditioned by bodies, therefore the impurity of kleśa, karma and phala (affliction, action and result) belongs only to the upādhi, not to the Self in paramārtha. To establish this very point by an illustration, the kārikā says — yathā bhavati bālānām.

As in the world the sky appears soiled by impurities such as dense dust and smoke to children, the unwise (avivekin) — but never to those who possess discrimination of the true nature of the sky — so the supreme Self too, the inner knower (vijñātā pratyak), appears soiled by the impurities of kleśa, karma, and their fruits to the unawakened (abuddhānām), those devoid of discrimination of the inner Self (pratyagātma-viveka-rahita), but never to those who possess such viveka.

As a salt-desert (ūṣara-deśa) does not in truth become endowed with water, foam and waves merely because thirsty creatures superimpose them upon it, even so the Self does not in truth become defiled by the impurities of affliction and the rest superimposed upon it by the unwise. This is the meaning.
MK_C03_K09: In death and in birth, in going and coming, and in the abiding within all bodies, [the Self] is not different from space. (9)
MK_C03_K09::block-0: Gauḍapāda once again elaborates the very same point already established. Just as the space within a pot has its own apparent birth, destruction, going, coming, and abiding [yet is in truth nothing other than the one all-pervading space], even so the Self's so-called birth, death, and the rest, occurring within all bodies, must be cognised as in no way different from [the nature of] space. This is the purport.
MK_C03_K10: All aggregates [of body, etc.], like dream-objects, are projected by the Self's māyā. Whether [we suppose] gradation [in their reality] or complete equality [of all of them as real], no logical ground is found [for either]. (10)
MK_C03_K10::block-0:
The aggregates of body and the rest — which stand in the place of pots in the analogy — are, like the bodies seen in dream and like the bodies fashioned by a magician, projected by the Self's māyā. The Self's māyā is avidyā; by it these aggregates are set forth. They are not real in the highest sense — this is the meaning.

Now, suppose one posits gradation, that is, a higher reality for the bodies-and-organs aggregates of devas and the like as compared with those of animals; or suppose one posits the complete equality [of reality] for all of them. In neither case does logic admit them: a probative reason that would establish their genuine production is simply not to be found. Since this is so, they are wrought by avidyā alone, and not real in the highest sense. This is the import.
MK_C03_K11: The sheaths beginning with the food-essence (rasa), which have been expounded in the Taittirīya, — their innermost Self is the supreme Living-One, even as space [pervading them all] has been disclosed [by us]. (11)
MK_C03_K11::block-0:
In order to show that this Self-principle — non-dual, free of birth and the rest — is established by śruti as its valid means of knowledge, [Gauḍapāda] now adduces scriptural passages. The sheaths beginning with rasa — namely, the annarasamaya, the prāṇamaya, and so forth — are sheaths only by way of analogy, since each outer one envelops the one within it; thus they are clearly expounded in the Taittirīya — i.e., in the [Brahmānanda-]vallī of the Taittirīya-śākhā Upaniṣad. The Self of these sheaths is that innermost Self by which all five sheaths are en-Selfed, possessed of selfhood. He is termed jīva, the Living-One, since He is the cause of life in all.

Who indeed is He? [Gauḍapāda] says: He is the supreme Self alone — the very one introduced earlier as "satyaṃ jñānam anantaṃ brahma" (Tai. Up. 2.1.1). It is from this Self that, through the sequence of space and so forth — like dream and magic — the aggregates characterised as the rasa-sheaths and the rest are projected by the Self's māyā, as already stated. This Self has been disclosed by us as resembling space, in the verse "ātmā hy ākāśavat" (Mā. Kā. 3.3) and the like. The intent is: He is not the kind of self imagined by the logicians — knowable through the inferential reasoning of the human intellect.
MK_C03_K12: In the [Madhu-brāhmaṇa,] the knowledge-of-honey, the supreme Brahman has been revealed in each of the pairs [adhidaiva and adhyātma], — even as the one space is shown [to be present] in earth and in the belly. (12)
MK_C03_K12::block-0:
Furthermore — both adhidaiva and adhyātma, the radiant immortal Puruṣa indwelling earth and the rest, who is the knower, is the supreme Self alone, is Brahman, is All. Thus in each of the pairs — until the dissolution of duality is reached — the supreme Brahman has been revealed.

Where has it been so revealed? He answers: in the "knowledge-of-honey" — that is, in the Madhu-brāhmaṇa — which goes by the name of brahma-vidyā. "Honey" here stands for the immortal: immortality, because it is the cause of bliss; and "madhu-jñāna" is that wherein this immortal is known, namely, the Madhu-brāhmaṇa. Therein, this is the meaning.

And in what manner [is it revealed]? He says: just as in the world it is shown by inference that one and the same space is present in [the cavity of] earth and in [the cavity of] the belly. Even so [is the supreme Brahman shown to be the inner one in each pair]. This is the import.
MK_C03_K13: The non-difference of jīva and Ātman is praised as identity, and any [posited] manifoldness is censured — that alone, in this manner, is the consistent teaching. (13)
MK_C03_K13::block-0:
What has been ascertained both by reasoning and by śruti — namely, the non-difference of jīva and the supreme Self — is praised as identity, lauded by the śāstra and by Vyāsa and the rest. And the perception of manifoldness — natural, common to all beings, fabricated by sham logicians who turn their backs on śāstra — is censured by such passages as: "there is verily no second to it" (Bṛ. Up. 4.3.23); "from a second alone fear arises" (Bṛ. Up. 1.4.2); "if he but make even a slight gap [a sense of otherness], from that there arises fear for him" (Tai. Up. 2.7.1); "all this is verily this Self" (Bṛ. Up. 2.4.6); "from death to death he goes who sees here as it were manifoldness" (Ka. Up. 2.4.10); and by other such passages, and by the knowers of Brahman.

This [identity-teaching] alone is, in this manner, consistent — straightforward and accordant with reason. As for the warped views fabricated by the logicians, they, when scrutinised, being themselves crooked, do not lend themselves to coherent construal. Such is the intent.
MK_C03_K14: The separateness of jīva and Ātman that was proclaimed prior to creation is figurative, [employed] with reference to a future usage; for [taken] as primary it cannot be sustained. (14)
MK_C03_K14::block-0:
Objection: But the separateness of jīva and the supreme Self is also proclaimed by śruti — proclaimed prior to the Upaniṣadic passages on creation, namely in the karmakāṇḍa, manifoldly, according to the variety of desires ("one desirous of this," "one desirous of that," etc.); and likewise in mantras such as "He upheld the earth and the heaven" (Ṛg. 10.121.1) and the rest [where the Lord is treated as other than the worshipper]. In the face of such conflict between the karmakāṇḍa and the jñānakāṇḍa, how can the unity-purport of the jñānakāṇḍa alone be ascertained as the consistent meaning?

Reply: To this it is said. Such Upaniṣadic creation passages as "That from which these beings are born" (Tai. Up. 3.1.1); "Just as from a fire tiny sparks fly forth" (Bṛ. Up. 2.1.20); "From this very Self space arose" (Tai. Up. 2.1.1); "He reflected; that brought forth fire" (Chā. Up. 6.2.3) — prior to such creation passages, what was proclaimed in the karmakāṇḍa as separateness, that is not so in the highest sense.

What then? It is figurative — like the difference between the great space and the pot-space; like "he is cooking the rice," by anticipated future usage. For the passages [seemingly teaching] difference can never have any primary differentiating import, since the [seeming] passages teaching difference of selves merely restate the natural avidyā-bound common perception of difference of beings.

And here in the Upaniṣads, by the passages on creation and dissolution, the very identity of jīva and the supreme Self is what is sought to be expounded — by "That thou art" (Chā. Up. 6.8.7); "He does not know — that one is other, I am other" (Bṛ. Up. 1.4.10); and the like. Hence, [it is as if to say:] "In the Upaniṣads identity is yet to be expounded by śruti as truth"; relying upon, as it were, this future usage, the [karmakāṇḍa's] re-enunciation of the world's perception of difference is figurative alone. This is the intent.

Or again: prior to creation, in "He reflected … that brought forth fire" (Chā. Up. 6.2.3) and the rest, identity itself was proclaimed by "One alone, without a second" (Chā. Up. 6.2.2); and that very identity is to be re-affirmed by "That is the truth, That is the Self, That thou art" (Chā. Up. 6.8.7). With reference to this future usage [of identity], whatever separateness of jīva and Ātman is gleaned in any passage is figurative — like "he is cooking the rice." Even so.
MK_C03_K15: The creation that has been variously declared by [the figures of] clay, metal, sparks, and the rest — that is [merely] a means for [pedagogical] entry; in no manner whatever is there [actual] difference. (15)
MK_C03_K15::block-0:
Objection: Granted that prior to creation all is unborn, one alone without a second, still after creation the multitude of things and the multitude of jīvas have arisen, distinct.

Reply: Not so, for the creation-passages have a [different] purpose. This very fault has already been disposed of: the aggregates are projected by the Self's māyā as in dream; the production-and-difference of jīvas is [no more real] than the production-and-difference of pot-spaces.

For this very reason, drawing on the creation-passages [of difference], here once again, in order to make manifest the [true] purport of the creation-śrutis, the topic is taken up by adducing the illustrations of clay, metal, sparks, and so forth: the creation that has been thus variously declared, illuminated, imagined, in different ways — that whole mode of creation is, for us, a means for the dawning of the cognition of the identity of jīva and the supreme Self. Even as in the prāṇa-saṃvāda the parable of speech and the rest being pierced through with evil by the asuras is fashioned for the purpose of bringing about the cognition of the pre-eminence of prāṇa.

Objection: That [parabolic status] itself is unproven.

Reply: No, since across the various śākhās the saṃvāda of prāṇa and the rest is heard differently. For if the dialogue had been an actual fact, the saṃvāda would have been heard in one and the same form in all śākhās, and not in mutually contradictory manifold modes; but we do hear it [variously]. Therefore, the saṃvāda-śrutis do not have that [literal-fact] purport. Just so are the production-passages to be cognised.

Objection: The variation among the saṃvāda-śrutis and the production-śrutis from one creation-cycle to another is on account of the difference of kalpas and creations.

Reply: No, for that would be purposeless — apart from the said purpose of awakening the cognition [of identity]. It is not possible to imagine for the saṃvāda- and creation-śrutis any other purpose. If one says they are for meditation upon their literal occurrence, no — for the cognition of [actual] strife, of [actual] origination and dissolution, is not desirable [as a meditation]. Therefore, the production-śrutis and the rest are solely for the dawning of the cognition of the identity of the Self, and it is not fitting to imagine other purposes for them. Hence, in no manner whatever is there a difference brought about by [actual] origination.
MK_C03_K16: The āśramins are of three kinds — having lower, middling, and higher vision; this upāsanā has been taught for their sake, out of compassion. (16)
MK_C03_K16::block-0:
Objection: If indeed the supreme Self alone — eternally pure, intelligent, free by nature, one — exists in truth, as established by śrutis like "One alone without a second" (Chā. Up. 6.2.2), and aught else is unreal — then for what purpose is this upāsanā taught by such śrutis as: "The Self, verily, is to be seen" (Bṛ. Up. 2.4.5); "That Self which is free from sin" (Chā. Up. 8.7.1); "Let him exercise volition" (Chā. Up. 3.14.1); "Let one meditate as the Self alone" (Bṛ. Up. 1.4.7); and the rites such as the agnihotra?

Reply: Hear the reason therein. The āśramins — those qualified by [their respective] āśramas, as well as the varṇins traversing the path; for the word āśrama is used illustratively — are of three kinds. How? They are those of lower, middling, and higher vision: "vision" being the capacity for discernment. That is, they are endowed with the capacities of dull, middling, and superior intellect.

This upāsanā has been taught for their sake — for the dull and middling-visioned āśramins and the rest; and the rites likewise. It is not taught for the sake of those of settled superior vision who [already see], "The Self alone is one without a second." By the compassionate Lord, out of pity, [the question arose]: "How may these who, while treading the right path, attain to this supreme one-vision?" — as is shown in: "That which is not thought by mind, by which, they say, mind is thought — know That alone to be Brahman; not this which [men] here meditate upon" (Ke. Up. 1.5); "That thou art" (Chā. Up. 6.8.7); "This Self is verily all this" (Chā. Up. 7.25.2); and the rest.
MK_C03_K17: The dualists, firmly settled in the establishment of their own siddhāntas, mutually contradict one another; with them this view (of non-duality) is not in conflict.
MK_C03_K17::block-0:
Since the vision of the non-dual Self has been ascertained both by śāstra and by reasoning (upapatti), it alone is samyagdarśana — right vision; and any view that stands outside it is mithyādarśana — false vision. There is yet another reason why the dualists' view is false: it is the seat of the faults of rāga, dveṣa and the rest. How so? In their own siddhānta-vyavasthā — the rules established for arranging their respective doctrines — the dualists, following the views of Kapila, Kaṇāda, Buddha, Ārhata and the like, are firmly determined: "Just so is the supreme reality, and not otherwise." Each is attached to his own thesis there, and seeing in the others an opponent of his own (view), he hates that other. Thus, beset by attachment and aversion, owing solely to their adherence to their own siddhānta they mutually — that is, one against the other — contradict each other.

By these mutually contradictory schools this view of ours, the Vaidika thesis of the unity of the Self because nothing is other than (the Self), is not contradicted — just as one's own hand and foot do not stand in mutual contradiction. Thus, since the cognition of the Self's unity is not the seat of the faults of rāga, dveṣa and the like, that very cognition is samyagdarśana — this is the import.
MK_C03_K18: Non-duality is verily the supreme reality; duality is said to be a differentiation of it. For them (the dualists) duality holds in both ways; therefore this (our) view does not conflict with them.
MK_C03_K18::block-0:
By what reason is it not in conflict with them? It is now stated. Non-duality is the supreme reality (paramārtha); for (hi), since duality, namely manifoldness, is a differentiation (bheda) of that non-duality — that is, an effect of it — as the śruti declares: "One only, without a second" (Chā. Up. 6.2.1) and "It projected light" (Chā. Up. 6.2.3); and by upapatti also, since in the absence of the throbbing of one's own thought, in samādhi, in fainting and in deep sleep, (duality) does not exist. Therefore duality is said to be its differentiation (tad-bheda).

But for those dualists, both from the standpoint of supreme truth (paramārthatas) and from the non-supreme standpoint (aparamārthatas), it is duality alone in either way. If the deluded ones hold the vision of duality and we, the undeluded, hold the vision of non-duality, then by this very reason our position is not in conflict with them — as the śruti says, "Indra by māyās…" (Bṛ. Up. 2.5.19) and "There is verily no second to that" (Bṛ. Up. 4.3.23). Just as one mounted upon a rutting elephant, when the unbalanced one standing on the ground says, "I too am mounted on a counter-elephant; drive your elephant against me," does not, with the cognition of non-conflict, drive his elephant against him — even so. Hence, in supreme truth, the very Self of the knower of Brahman is the Self of the dualists also. Therefore, by this reason our position is not in conflict with them.
MK_C03_K19: This is differentiated only by māyā, never otherwise — for the unborn (aja). Were it really differentiated, the immortal would attain mortality.
MK_C03_K19::block-0:
When it has been said that duality is the differentiation of non-duality, someone might suspect: "Then duality too, like non-duality, would be supremely real." Anticipating this the kārikā says: that supremely real non-duality, this — namely the world of duality — is differentiated only by māyā, just as the moon (appears) many to one with eye-disease, or as a rope (appears) as snake, line of water and the rest by such (apparent) divisions; not in supreme truth, because the Self is partless (niravayava). For only that which has parts is differentiated through the otherwise-becoming of its parts, as clay through the differentiations of pot and so on. Therefore the partless, unborn (aja) is in no other way (anyathā) — not differentiated by any mode whatsoever; this is the import.

For, were the immortal, unborn, non-dual, by-its-own-nature existent (svabhāva-sat) really being differentiated, it would attain mortality, as fire would coldness. And that — the going-counter to one's own nature — is undesired, since it is contradicted by every pramāṇa. The unborn, non-dual Self-reality is differentiated by māyā alone, not in supreme truth. Therefore duality is not paramārtha-sat — supremely real.
MK_C03_K20: The (opposing) disputants desire birth (jāti) for what is verily unborn (aja); how shall the unborn, immortal entity attain mortality?
MK_C03_K20::block-0: But certain other expounders of the Upaniṣads, brahmavādins, garrulous in argument, desire — as supreme truth (paramārthata eva) — birth (jāti), origination (utpatti), for the very Ātman-reality which is unborn (aja) and by-nature immortal. For them, if it has come to be (jāta), it would necessarily attain mortality. And how shall that which is unborn (aja), immortal (amṛta), by-nature existent (svabhāvataḥ san), the Self, attain mortality? In no way will mortality, the going-counter to its own nature, ever befall it — this is the meaning.
MK_C03_K21: The immortal does not become mortal, nor likewise the mortal immortal; the otherwise-becoming of (a thing's) very nature (prakṛti) shall in no way occur.
MK_C03_K21::block-0: Since in the world the immortal does not become mortal, nor likewise does the mortal become immortal, hence the otherwise-becoming of one's prakṛti — namely svabhāva — its self-displacement, shall in no way occur, just as the heat of fire (does not displace itself).
MK_C03_K22: For the disputant whose by-nature immortal entity goes to mortality, how shall the (then) immortal-by-something-made remain motionless for him?
MK_C03_K22::block-0: But for that disputant for whom the by-nature (svabhāvena) immortal entity goes to mortality — that is, comes really into being (paramārthato jāyate) — for him the proposition that prior to its origination it (the entity) was by-nature immortal is itself false. How then? Its immortality is then by something made (kṛtaka): such is its svabhāva. (Now) how shall that which is immortal by something made remain motionless (niścala)? It will in no way remain (so) by way of being immortal-by-nature. For the holders of Self-jāti (origination), no aja in any sense exists at all. Everything here is mortal; hence the contingency of the impossibility of liberation (anirmokṣa-prasaṅga) — this is the import.
MK_C03_K23: Whether what is created is created really or unreally, the śruti is alike. What is ascertained (by śruti) and accompanied by reasoning, that prevails — not the other.
MK_C03_K23::block-0:
Objection: "For one who upholds non-origination (ajātivāda), the śruti that propounds creation does not fit." Granted; the śruti propounding creation does exist; but it is paratoward another aim — "It is a means; cause (the disciple) to descend (by it)" (Mā. Kā. 3.15) — as we have already said. Even now, when the answer has been (so) given, this further objection-and-answer is undertaken merely to remove the suspicion of conflict between the literal flow of the śruti's sṛṣṭi-passages and its intended sense. Whether in the case of an entity being really (bhūtataḥ) — paramārthataḥ — created, or unreally (abhūtataḥ) — by māyā, in the manner of a magician — the śruti of creation is alike, equal (to either). Objection: "Among gauṇa (figurative) and mukhya (primary) (senses), the apprehension of the word's sense in the primary is what is proper." Reply: Not so; for any other (mode of) creation is unestablished and purposeless — as we have already said.

All creation, whether figurative or primary, has avidyā-sṛṣṭi alone for its scope, not paramārtha — as the śruti says, "with-outside-and-inside, indeed unborn" (Muṇḍ. Up. 2.1.2). Therefore, what has been ascertained by the śruti — "one only, without a second, unborn, immortal" — and what is endowed with yukti, with reasoning — that alone (prevails); we have already said this in the previous portions. Just that becomes the meaning of the śruti, never the other, ever, anywhere.
MK_C03_K24: By the scriptural tradition "There is no manifoldness here at all", and likewise "Indra by māyās…", He, though never coming to be, is born in many ways — but only by māyā.
MK_C03_K24::block-0:
How is the śruti's ascertainment (so)? It is said: if the creation were really (bhūtata eva), then the (world's) manifoldness would be true; (and in that case) the āmnāya for showing its absence would not exist. But the āmnāya does exist — "There is here no manifoldness whatsoever" (Kaṭha Up. 2.1.11) — for the prohibition (pratiṣedha) of the existence of duality. Therefore the creation, being for the purpose of bringing about the realization of the unity of the Self, has been imagined; it is itself unreal (abhūta), like the prāṇa-saṃvāda (dialogue of the prāṇas). For it is referred to by the word māyā which propounds the unreal in "Indra by māyās" (Bṛ. Up. 2.5.19).

Objection: "The word māyā denotes prajñā (cognition)." Reply: True; but since the cognition of the senses (indriya-prajñā), being avidyā-constituted, is admitted as māyā, there is no fault. The meaning is: by māyās, that is, by the cognitions of the senses which are of the form of avidyā. As the śruti says, "Though never coming to be, He is born many ways" (Tai. Ār. 3.13). Therefore He is born by māyā alone (māyayā tu); the word tu has the force of restriction — "by māyā only." For non-being-born and many-fold birth cannot coexist in one place, like coldness and heat in fire. And because of fruitfulness (phalavattva), the vision of the Self's unity alone is the meaning ascertained by the śruti — as is shown by the mantra-passage "What delusion, what grief is there for one beholding unity?" (Īśā Up. 7) and from the censure "He goes from death to death" (Kaṭha Up. 2.4.10) of the perception of difference such as creation and the rest.
MK_C03_K25: By the rejection of origination and by the censure (of the worship of origination), origination is denied. The cause too is denied by the rhetorical question, "Who indeed could give rise to this?" (25)
MK_C03_K25::block-0:
By the censure of the worship-worthiness of sambhūti (origination), expressed in "Those who worship sambhūti enter into blinding darkness" (Īśā Mantra 9), origination itself is negated. For if origination were existent in the highest sense (paramārtha-sat), the censure of it would not be tenable.

Objection (pūrvapakṣa): The censure of sambhūti is meant to enjoin its conjunction (samuccaya) with vināśa (destruction, i.e. karma), just as in "Those who worship avidyā enter into blinding darkness" (Īśā Mantra 12).

Reply (siddhānta): True indeed; the censure of sambhūti aims at enjoining the combination of the contemplation of deities (which is the sphere of sambhūti) together with karma denoted by the word vināśa. Yet, just as karma called vināśa, which is the natural innate course of activity born of ignorance, serves the purpose of crossing over death, so too the combination of deity-meditation with karma — being the cause of refining the person, taking the form of the activity of attachment to the fruits of karma, characterised by the twin desires for ends and means — serves the purpose of crossing over death. Thus, separated from impurity in the form of death which is the twofold desire (eṣaṇā-dvaya), the person becomes refined.

Hence the conjoint practice of deity-vision and karma, which is itself avidyā, is meant for crossing over death. Just so, for one who has crossed over the death of avidyā in the form of the twin desires, who is dispassionate, and who is intent on the inquiry into the meaning of the Upaniṣadic teaching, there inevitably arises the knowledge of the oneness of the supreme Self (paramātma-ekatva-vidyā). Thus, in relation to the prior avidyā, the subsequent Brahma-vidyā — the means to immortality — being connected to one and the same person, is said to be combined with avidyā.

Therefore, since (avidyā) has another purpose, with reference to Brahma-vidyā which is the means to immortality, the censure of sambhūti is purely condemnatory — even though it is the cause for the removal of impurity, since it does not stand on the same footing (as Brahma-vidyā). Hence, by the censure of sambhūti, the existence of sambhūti is merely relative; therefore, with reference to the supreme reality which is the oneness of the Self, the origination called "immortality" is also denied.

Thus, of the jīva who is fashioned by māyā alone and presented by avidyā, in the destruction of avidyā, since (the jīva) is of the very nature (of the Self), in the highest sense who indeed could give rise to him? For no one would generate the snake superimposed on the rope by avidyā, which has been dispelled through discrimination; likewise, none could give rise to him. Since "who indeed" carries the force of rhetorical refutation, the cause is denied. The intent is: there exists no producing cause of that which has arisen from avidyā and has been dispelled — as the śruti says, "This (Self) was not born from anything, nor did anything arise from it" (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 1.2.18).
MK_C03_K26: Since (the śruti) negates whatever is explained by repeatedly saying "not thus, not thus" — by the principle of being ungraspable, the unborn (Self) shines forth as everything. (26)
MK_C03_K26::block-0:
By the negation of every distinction, in the passage "Now, therefore, the teaching is: not thus, not thus" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.3.6), the śruti, considering the difficulty of comprehending the Ātman thus expounded, repeatedly, with the desire of expounding that very same (Ātman) through other means, denies whatever it has explained. The śruti, with the intent of indicating the imperceptibility of the Self, negates the graspable, the object of the cognising intellect that has origin, by passages such as "That Self is — not thus, not thus" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.9.26; 4.2.4; 4.4.22; 4.5.15).

For one who does not understand that the means (upāya) are intended only for (revealing) what is to be attained (upeya), there might be the apprehension that what is explained as the means becomes graspable like an object to be attained. To prevent this, the śruti negates by means of the cause, namely, the principle of "ungraspability" (agrāhya-bhāva). Thus, for one who knows that the means are wholly subservient to what is to be attained, and that the latter is of an eternal, unitary form, that very Self-reality, unborn within and without, shines forth of itself.
MK_C03_K27: Of the existent (sat) alone is birth fitting through māyā, not in reality. For one who holds birth to be in reality, what is born is born again (and so on, ad infinitum). (27)
MK_C03_K27::block-0:
Thus, by hundreds of śruti-passages, it has been ascertained that the Self-reality, unborn within and without, is non-dual; there is nothing other than it. Now this very same conclusion is to be once more determined through reasoning, hence (the kārikā says): here this (objection) might arise — if the Self-reality were always ungraspable, it would be non-existent (asat). Not so, on account of the perception of effects.

Just as of an existent magician birth (i.e. an effect) takes place through māyā, similarly, the perceived birth of the world, being an effect, leads (us) to recognise the Self — really existent like the magician — as the support (āspada) of the world's birth, which is itself māyā. Hence the birth of the world is fitting only from an existent cause (sat), like the elephant and other māyā-fashioned effects of the magician — not from a non-existent cause. But not in reality (tattvataḥ) is the Self's birth tenable.

Alternatively: just as of an existent thing such as a rope, birth in the form of a serpent and the like takes place through māyā, not in reality, so too of the Self — though ungraspable yet existent — birth in the form of the world is fitting through māyā, like the snake on the rope, but not in reality is there birth of the unborn Self.

Further, for one who maintains (vādin) that the supremely real, unborn Self-reality is itself born as the world: it cannot be said that the unborn is born — that is contradictory. Hence by implication, what is already born is born — this would follow. And from that follows the fault of regress (anavasthā), so birth is not (tenable). Therefore, it is established that the Self-reality is unborn and one alone.
MK_C03_K28: The birth of a non-existent (asat) — neither through māyā nor in reality — is fitting at all. The son of a barren woman is born neither in reality nor even through māyā. (28)
MK_C03_K28::block-0: For the asat-vādins (who maintain that the world is born of the non-existent), the birth of a non-existent entity, either through māyā or in reality, is in no way tenable, on account of its never having been seen. For the son of a barren woman is born neither through māyā nor in reality. Therefore, here the doctrine of the asat-vādin (i.e. the Buddhist Mādhyamika position which posits arising from non-being, refuted along with all other birth-from-asat views) is by far untenable — that is the meaning.
MK_C03_K29: Just as in dream the mind, through māyā, vibrates appearing as duality, so too in waking the mind, through māyā, vibrates appearing as duality. (29)
MK_C03_K29::block-0: How then is it said that the existent's birth is only through māyā? — Just as the snake imagined upon the rope, when seen as the rope, is itself (the rope), so the mind, when seen as paramātma-vijñapti-svarūpa, while really being that, vibrates in dream through māyā as appearing in duality of grasper and grasped (grāhya-grāhaka), like the snake on the rope. Likewise, in waking too, the mind vibrates through māyā — that is, it only seems to vibrate.
MK_C03_K30: The mind, non-dual, appears as dual in dream — there is no doubt. Likewise, non-dual, it appears as dual in waking — there is no doubt. (30)
MK_C03_K30::block-0: Like the serpent (appearing) in the form of the rope, in reality the mind, being non-dual in the form of the Self, in dream appears as dual — there is no doubt. For in dream, the elephant and the like (the graspable), and the eye and the like which apprehend them — these two — do not exist apart from cognition (vijñāna). Likewise it is in waking — there is no difference, since both consist of the highest reality which is mere cognition (paramārtha-sad-vijñāna-mātra).
MK_C03_K31: Whatever duality, with all that moves and is unmoving, is here — that is mind-perceived. For when the mind ceases to be mind (amanībhāva), duality is no more apprehended. (31)
MK_C03_K31::block-0:
It has been said that the mind itself, like the snake-on-rope, is mere imagination appearing as duality. (Question: ) What is the proof here? (Reply: ) An inference characterised by concomitant presence and absence (anvaya-vyatireka) is offered. How? — "This duality, all of it, is mind" is the thesis (pratijñā), since it is seen by, that is, displayed by, the mind that imagines it (manodṛśya). The reason: presence (of duality) when the mind exists, and absence (of duality) when the mind is absent.

For when the mind has reached amanībhāva — i.e. is restrained through the practice of discriminative vision (viveka-darśana) and dispassion (vairāgya), or has dissolved (laya), as the snake into the rope, in deep sleep (suṣupti) — duality is not apprehended at all. Hence, by reason of (its) absence, the unreality of duality is established — that is the meaning.
MK_C03_K32: When, by the realisation of the truth that is the Self (ātma-satya), one no longer imagines, then (the mind) attains the state of being mind-less; in the absence of the graspable, (it becomes) free from grasping. (32)
MK_C03_K32::block-0:
How again does this amanībhāva come about? — It is said: ātma-satya means the Self alone is real (satya), as in the example of clay; as the śruti says, "Modification is a mere name, originating in speech; only the clay is real" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.1.4). The realisation of that, in accordance with the teaching of scripture and the teacher (śāstra-ācārya-upadeśa), is ātma-satya-anubodha.

Through that, on account of the absence of anything to be imagined, one no longer imagines — like fire ceasing to burn in the absence of fuel. When, that is, at that very moment, (the mind) attains amanastā, the state of mind-lessness; in the absence of the graspable, the mind is agraha — devoid of the imagining and grasping (function) — that is the meaning.
MK_C03_K33: They declare that knowledge (jñāna) which is free from imagination (akalpaka) and unborn (aja) is non-different from the knowable. The knowable is Brahman, unborn and eternal; the unborn (Self) is known by the unborn (knowledge) itself.
MK_C03_K33::block-0:
If this duality is unreal, by what means is the truth of the Self rightly known? To this it is replied — "akalpakam" means devoid of every imagination (sarva-kalpanā-varjitam); and precisely for that reason it is "ajam," unborn. "Jñānam," mere intelligence-stuff (jñapti-mātram), is, the knowers of Brahman declare (prachakṣate, kathayanti), non-different (abhinnam) from the knowable, which is Brahman the supremely real. As the śruti says: "For there is no destruction of the seeing of the seer" (Bṛ. U. 4.3.30) — like the heat of fire; "Brahman is consciousness and bliss" (Bṛ. U. 3.9.28); "Brahman is real, knowledge, infinite" (Tai. U. 2.1.1), and the like.

A further qualifying compound: "brahma-jñeyam" — that of which Brahman is the knowable; this Brahman, established in itself, is the knowable, non-different from the knowledge as heat is non-different from fire. By that same essential nature of the Self, by the unborn knowledge, the unborn knowable, the truth of the Self, is itself made known (vibudhyate). The meaning is: just as the sun, whose nature is constant light, requires no other light, so the Self, being a single homogeneous mass of eternal consciousness (nitya-vijñānaika-rasa-ghana), requires no other knowledge.
MK_C03_K34: The activity (pracāra) of the controlled (nigṛhīta) mind, free from imagination (nirvikalpa) and endowed with discrimination (dhīmat), is to be specially known. Different is the state in deep sleep (suṣupti); that is not the same as this.
MK_C03_K34::block-0:
It has been stated that, when by the realisation of the truth of the Self no fresh resolve is formed and external objects are absent, the mind, like a fire without fuel, becomes pacified, controlled (nigṛhītam, niruddham). Thus, in this "non-mind" (amanībhāva) state of the mind, the absence of duality has also been declared. The activity (pracāra), the moving forth (pracaraṇa), of such a controlled, niruddha, nirvikalpa (free from every imagination), and dhīmat (endowed with discrimination, viveka-vat) mind — that activity, indeed, is to be specially known (viśeṣeṇa jñeyo, vijñeyaḥ) by the yogins.

Pūrvapakṣa: But when there is absence of every cognition (sarva-pratyaya-abhāva), the activity of the mind controlled in samādhi is just like the activity of the mind in deep sleep, since in both alike there is absence of cognitions; what then is there to know? Siddhānta — It is replied: not so. For in suṣupti there is a different sort of activity: it is the activity of a mind grasped by the darkness of the delusion of avidyā (avidyā-moha-tamo-grastasya), in which the seeds of the manifold tendencies of evil pursuit lie latent (antar-līna-aneka-anartha-pravṛtti-bīja-vāsanā-vataḥ). The activity of the controlled mind, on the contrary, is altogether different; in it the seeds of avidyā and other harmful pursuits have been burned away by the fire of the realisation of the truth of the Self (ātma-satya-anubodha-hutāśa-viplushṭa-avidyā-ādi-anartha-pravṛtti-bījasya); it is independent (svatantraḥ), and all the dust of klesha is utterly stilled. Therefore that is not equal to this. Hence the import is: it is fitting that this be known.
MK_C03_K35: In deep sleep the mind is dissolved (līyate); when controlled (nigṛhīta), it is not dissolved. That very mind is then fearless Brahman, an effulgence of knowledge (jñānāloka) on every side.
MK_C03_K35::block-0:
He gives the reason for the distinction in activity. "For" (hi) — in suṣupti the mind is dissolved (līyate); together with all the seed-tendencies (bīja-vāsanā) of the cognitions of avidyā etc., it lapses into the form of darkness, into an undifferentiated seed-state (avishesha-rūpaṃ bīja-bhāvam). But the mind controlled by means of the discriminative knowledge (viveka-vijñāna-pūrvakaṃ nigṛhītaṃ niruddhaṃ sat) does not get dissolved, does not lapse into the seed-state of darkness. Therefore the difference of activity between the deep-sleep state and the samāhita (collected, in samādhi) state of the mind is justified.

When it is wholly free from the twin impurities born of the avidyā of the grasped and the grasper (grāhya-grāhaka-avidyā-kṛta-mala-dvaya-varjitam), then it has become verily the supreme non-dual Brahman; it has been so transformed (saṃvṛttam). Hence "that very" is fearless (nirbhayam), since the cause of fear, the apprehension of duality, is absent. As the śruti puts it: tranquil and fearless is Brahman, knowing which the wise fears nothing whatever. That same is qualified further: jñapti, knowledge — the consciousness that is the very nature of the Self; that knowledge alone is the light (āloka, prakāśa) of Brahman, hence "jñānālokam," of the form of a single homogeneous mass of consciousness (vijñānaika-rasa-ghanam). "Samantataḥ" — on every side, like space, pervading without break, without interval — that is the meaning.
MK_C03_K36: Unborn (aja), free from sleep and dream (anidram, asvapnam), without name (anāmaka), without form (arūpaka), shining once for all (sakṛd-vibhātam), all-knowing (sarvajña) — there is no observance (upacāra) whatever to be performed in regard to It.
MK_C03_K36::block-0:
Since the cause of birth is absent, both within and without, It is unborn (aja); for the cause of birth is avidyā, as in the rope-snake (rajju-sarpa-vat) — this we have already said. And that avidyā has been arrested by the realisation of the truth of the Self; therefore, unborn. Hence also "anidram," since It has awakened, in the form of the non-dual Self, from the beginningless sleep of the māyā characterised as avidyā; therefore "asvapnam" too. For the name and form (nāma-rūpa) of the Self are products of non-awakening (aprabodha-kṛte); on the awakening, they perish like the rope-snake.

It is not designated by any name nor figured under any form; therefore "anāmaka" and "arūpaka." As the śruti says: "Whence speech turns back" (Tai. U. 2.4.1) and so on. Further, "sakṛd-vibhātam" — ever shining, eternally luminous (sadā bhā-rūpam), since It is free from non-perception, otherwise-perception, manifestation, and disappearance. Perception and non-perception constitute night and day; and the darkness in the form of avidyā is the cause of perpetual non-shining; in Its absence, and because Its very form is eternal consciousness-light, "sakṛd-vibhātam" is fitting. For the very same reason, It is everything and is of the nature of intelligence — therefore "sarvajñam," all-knowing.

In this Brahman thus described, no observance (upacāra) such as samādhāna and the like — those that are made in respect of others, beyond the proper essence of the Self — is to be performed. Since Brahman is by nature ever pure, awakened, and free (nitya-śuddha-buddha-mukta-svabhāva), there is no possibility (sambhava) of any thing whatever to be done — "kathañcana" — in any way at all, when avidyā is destroyed. This is the import.
MK_C03_K37: Free from all speech (sarva-abhilāpa-vigataḥ), arisen above all thought (sarva-cintā-samutthitaḥ), well-pacified (suprashānta), shining once for all (sakṛj-jyotis), it is samādhi, motionless (acala), fearless (abhaya).
MK_C03_K37::block-0:
He gives the reason establishing the meaning already stated regarding namelessness and the rest. "That by which it is uttered" — that is abhilāpa, the instrument of speech, of every kind of designation; from this It is set apart (vigataḥ); speech here stands as a token, the meaning being: It is free from every external organ. So too, sarva-cintā-samutthitaḥ — "that by which it is thought" is cintā, the buddhi; from that It has risen up, that is, It is free from the inner organ (antaḥkaraṇa-vivarjita); as the śruti says: "Without breath, without mind, pure, higher than the higher imperishable" (Mu. U. 2.1.2) and the rest.

Since It is free from every object, It is suprashānta. Sakṛj-jyotis — ever the light, in the form of the consciousness-essence of the Self. "Samādhi" — because It is grasped by the wisdom whose cause is samādhi; or, that in which (everything) is well-collected (samādhīyate asmin) is samādhi. Acala — without modification (avikriyaḥ). For that very reason, abhaya — for there is no possibility of modification (vikriyā-abhāvāt).
MK_C03_K38: There is neither acceptance (graha) nor rejection (utsarga) where thought (cintā) does not exist. Then knowledge, established in the Self (ātma-saṃstham), is unborn (ajāti) and has attained sameness (samatām).
MK_C03_K38::block-0:
Since the very Brahman has been declared as "samādhi, motionless, fearless," therefore in It, in that Brahman, there is no graha — taking up, appropriation; and no utsarga — casting off, abandonment. For where there is modification, or being-an-object-of-it, there acceptance and rejection are possible; that pair has no place here in Brahman, since there is no other cause of modification, and since It is partless (niravayava); therefore acceptance and rejection are not possible there. "Where thought does not exist" — every kind of thought is impossible, owing to its mindlessness (amanastvāt); whence then could acceptance and rejection be there? — that is the meaning.

When the realisation of the truth of the Self has arisen, at that very moment knowledge is ātma-saṃstham — established in the Self alone (because of the absence of objects, like the heat of fire abiding in the fire itself); ajāti — devoid of birth; samatām gatam — it has attained the supreme equality (parama-sāmyam). What was promised in the beginning — "Therefore I shall declare what is free from poverty (akārpaṇya), unborn, and attained to sameness" (Mā. Kā. 3.2) — that is here concluded by reasoning and by scripture: "unborn, attained to sameness." From this realisation of the truth of the Self everything else is in the field of poverty (kārpaṇya); so the śruti: "Whoever, O Gārgī, departs from this world without knowing this Imperishable is wretched" (Bṛ. U. 3.8.10). Having attained this, every brāhmaṇa becomes one whose work is done — that is the import.
MK_C03_K39: The yoga called the Touchless (asparśa-yoga) is verily known by name, hard for all yogins to attain. Yogins are afraid of it; in this fearless they see fear.
MK_C03_K39::block-0:
Although the highest reality is thus, yet the asparśa-yoga — so called because it is wholly devoid of every connection that goes by the name of "contact" (sparśa) — is verily celebrated under that name, well known in the Upaniṣads. "Hard to behold" (durdarśaḥ) for all yogins (sarva-yogiṇām) — that is, for those bereft of the wisdom of the Vedānta; the meaning is: it is gained only by the great effort of the realisation of the truth of the Self.

The yogins, indeed, are afraid of it — even of this which is free from every fear; deeming this yoga to be of the nature of the destruction of the Self (ātma-nāśa-rūpam), they entertain fear; in this fearless, they are perceivers of fear (bhaya-darśinaḥ) — habituated to seeing the destruction of the Self, the cause of fear, where it is not — they are the undiscerning. That is the meaning. The schools refuted by name in the Kārikā tradition include the Vaiśeṣika, Sāṃkhya, Buddhist Vijñānavāda and Śūnyavāda — all of whom miss this fearless asparśa due to clinging to their varieties of duality.
MK_C03_K40: For all yogins, fearlessness, the destruction of sorrow, awakening, and unending peace are dependent on the control of the mind (mano-nigraha-āyattam).
MK_C03_K40::block-0:
But for those for whom — apart from the essence of Brahman — the mind, the senses, and the rest, like the rope-snake, are merely imagined and not really existent, who are themselves of the nature of Brahman, fearlessness and the unending peace called liberation (mokṣa-ākhyā akṣayā śāntiḥ) are by their very nature already accomplished (svabhāvataḥ eva siddhā), not dependent on anything else — as is said: "There is no observance whatever" (Mā. Kā. 3.36).

Siddhānta now in regard to others: but those yogins different from these — wayfarers (mārga-gāḥ) of inferior and middling vision — who see the mind as something other, distinct from the Self yet related to the Self, for them, who are devoid of the realisation of the truth of the Self, fearlessness for all yogins is dependent on the control of the mind (manaso nigrahāyattam). Further, the destruction of sorrow too — for among the undiscerning, when the mind related to the Self is in agitation, there is no destruction of sorrow. Further, even the awakening to the Self (ātma-prabodhaḥ) is dependent on the control of the mind alone. So too the imperishable peace called liberation, for them, is dependent on the control of the mind only. The contrast of pravṛtti (engaged action of mind-control) and nivṛtti (the natural, effortless cessation in the realised) is thus drawn.
MK_C03_K41: Just as the emptying of the ocean drop by drop with the tip of a blade of kuśa-grass, even so is the restraint of the mind, accomplished without weariness through unflagging perseverance. (41)
MK_C03_K41::block-0: Even the restraint of the mind, for those engaged in this discipline, is attained without weariness, like the resolve to dry up the ocean by emptying it drop by drop with the tip of a blade of kuśa-grass; that is, for those of unflagging resolve and undaunted inner organ (antaḥkaraṇa), it becomes possible apariкheda-tas, free of fatigue, on account of their freedom from despondency (anirveda).
MK_C03_K42: By the proper means one should restrain the mind that is scattered amid desires and enjoyments, and likewise the mind that is well-pleased in laya (dissolution); for laya is as much an obstacle as desire. (42)
MK_C03_K42::block-0:
Is unflagging perseverance alone, then, the means to restrain the mind? No, it is replied. Even one possessed of unflagging perseverance must, by the means about to be stated, restrain the mind that is scattered (vikṣipta) amid the objects of desire and enjoyment — that is, he must hold it back and fix it in the Self alone.

Further, that into which the mind dissolves (līyate asmin) is laya, namely deep sleep (suṣupta); and in that laya the mind becomes well-pleased (suprasanna), free from all toil. The verb "should restrain" carries over to this case as well.

If it be asked — when the mind is well-pleased, why should it be restrained? — the answer is given: just as desire (kāma) is a cause of evil, so too is laya. Hence, just as the mind that runs to objects of desire must be restrained, so also it must be checked from sliding into laya. This is the meaning.
