MK_C03_K43: Recollecting that all is suffering, one should turn the mind back from the enjoyment of desires; recollecting that all is the unborn (aja), one perceives nothing as born at all. (43)
MK_C03_K43::block-0:
What, then, is that means? It is now stated. Recollecting that all duality, which is but the play unfolded by avidyā, is nothing but suffering, one should, through the cultivation of dispassion (vairāgya-bhāvanā), turn back the mind that has run outward from kāma-bhoga — that is, from the enjoyment that springs from desire and is the object of craving.

And recollecting, by the teaching of the śāstra and the ācārya, that "All is the unborn Brahman (ajaṁ brahma sarvam)," one no longer beholds the contrary world of duality as truly born, since it is non-existent (abhāvāt).
MK_C03_K44: In laya one should awaken the mind; if scattered, one should again calm it; one should know it as still defiled (sa-kaṣāya); when it has reached equipoise, one should not disturb it. (44)
MK_C03_K44::block-0:
Thus, by these two means — practice of knowledge (jñāna-abhyāsa) and dispassion (vairāgya) — one should, when the mind has been dissolved in laya, that is, in deep sleep, awaken it (sambodhayet) by joining it to the discriminative vision of the Self. "Citta" and "manas" are not different in meaning here.

And if again it is scattered (vikṣipta) toward objects of enjoyment, one should once more calm it (śamayet). Thus, by repeated practice, when the mind has been awakened from laya and turned back from objects, but has not yet attained equipoise — when it abides in the intermediate state still possessed of subtle impressions of attachment (sa-rāga), conjoined with the seeds of further activity — one should know it as sa-kaṣāya, defiled.

From that state too, by effort, one should bring it to equipoise (sāmya). When, however, it has reached samya — that is, when it is on the very verge of attaining sameness — then one should not disturb it (na cālayet); one should not turn it again toward objects. This is the meaning.
MK_C03_K45: One should not taste the bliss therein; through wisdom one should remain unattached; if the steady mind tends to move outward, one should with effort make it one. (45)
MK_C03_K45::block-0:
Whatever bliss arises for the yogin who is striving after samādhi — that he should not taste, that is, he should not become attached to it. How, then? Remaining niḥsaṅga, free of craving, by prajñā, the discriminative intellect, he should reflect that whatever bliss is experienced is but a fabrication of avidyā and therefore false (mṛṣā); thereby he should restrain the mind from attachment even to that bliss.

When, again, the mind, having turned back from attachment to bliss and become naturally still (niścala), yet begins to flow outward (niścarat), then, restraining it by the means already taught, he should with effort make it one (ekī-kuryāt) in the Self alone — that is, he should reduce it to the mere existence of pure consciousness in its own form (cit-svarūpa-sattāmātra).
MK_C03_K46: When the mind neither dissolves into laya nor is again scattered, when it is unmoving and without any semblance of object, then it has become Brahman itself. (46)
MK_C03_K46::block-0: When the mind, restrained by the means thus declared, neither dissolves into deep sleep nor is again scattered amid objects; when it is aniṅgana, motionless, like a lamp in a windless place; when it is anābhāsa, that is, no longer shines forth in the form of any object fashioned by avidyā — then, the mind of such a character has become niṣpanna brahma, that is, the mind has come to be accomplished in the very nature of Brahman.
MK_C03_K47: Resting in the Self, peaceful, accompanied by liberation, indescribable, the highest bliss, unborn and one with the unborn knowable — they call it the Omniscient. (47)
MK_C03_K47::block-0:
The supreme bliss already declared, characterised by the realisation of the truth of the Self, is svastha, abiding in its own Self; śānta, of the form of the cessation of all evil; sa-nirvāṇa — nirvṛti is nirvāṇa, kaivalya — accompanied by such absolute liberation; akathya, incapable of being told, since its sphere is utterly uncommon and beyond all communication; uttama-sukha, the unsurpassed bliss, since it is directly known only to the yogin himself.

It is aja, unborn, not born like any object-content; and being non-different (avyatirikta) from the unborn (aja) Knowable — that is, the unproduced object of knowledge — it is, by its own form of omniscient consciousness, sarvajña: this very Brahman the knowers of Brahman declare to be that bliss, that Omniscient One.
MK_C03_K48: No jīva whatsoever is ever born; no origination of it exists. This is the supreme truth, wherein nothing whatsoever is born. (48)
MK_C03_K48::block-0:
All this — restraint of the mind and the rest, together with creation as illustrated by clay and gold, and the various upāsanās — has been taught only as a means to the realisation of the supreme truth, not as itself the highest truth.

The paramārtha-satya, the supreme truth, however, is this: no jīva whatsoever — neither as agent (kartṛ) nor as enjoyer (bhoktṛ) — is ever born in any manner whatever. Hence, of this one Self, by its own nature unborn (aja), no origin (sambhava), no cause, exists at all. Since no cause exists for it, therefore no jīva is born — this is the conclusion.

Among the truths previously taught as means, this is the highest truth: that in Brahman, whose nature is truth, not even an atom of anything whatsoever is born.
MK_C04_K01: I bow to that best among the two-footed (Puruṣottama), who, by knowledge that is like space (ākāśa-kalpa) and non-different from the objects of knowledge, has fully realised the dharmas (selves) that are themselves comparable to space.
MK_C04_K01::block-0:
Through the determination of Om and through the falsity of the difference of external objects, the non-duality affirmed by scripture in the previous chapters has been established. Then, in the Advaita-prakaraṇa, that very non-duality was directly ascertained by both scripture and reasoning, and was concluded with the declaration, "This is the supreme truth." The opponents of that scriptural import, of the vision of non-duality, are the dualists (dvaitins) and the nihilists (vaināśikas, the Buddhist destructionists).

Because their views mutually contradict one another, their darśanas are the seat of afflictions such as attachment and aversion (rāga, dveṣa, etc.); thus their character as false darśanas has been hinted at. By contrast, since the Advaita-darśana is not a seat of such afflictions, it is the right vision (samyag-darśana) — and this is by way of praise of the Advaita view. Now, here in this chapter, after demonstrating in detail by their mutual contradiction that those views are not the right vision, the establishment of the Advaita-darśana through the negation of those views is to be concluded by the method of āvīta-nyāya (the indirect method through refutation of the opposite). For this purpose the Alātaśānti-prakaraṇa is begun.

Among the verses there, this first verse is for the purpose of obeisance to the propagator of the Advaita-darśana — and that obeisance is offered through the very nature of non-duality itself. For at the commencement of a śāstra, worship of the teacher is enjoined for the accomplishment of the intended purpose. "Ākāśa-kalpa" — that which is slightly short of being completely ākāśa, i.e. similar to space; by such knowledge that is comparable to space.

What does He know? The dharmas, that is, the selves (ātmans). Of what kind? "Gagana-upamān" — those of which space is the simile, i.e. comparable to the sky — these dharmas, the selves. The qualification of the knowledge itself is then given: that knowledge which is non-different from the dharmas which are its objects, the selves — like the heat of fire, like the light of the sun — by such knowledge non-different from the knowable, comparable to space, not separate from the very nature of the knowable selves.

He who has fully comprehended (sambuddha) — eternally so — the dharmas that are comparable to space, that Lord (Īśvara) named Nārāyaṇa — Him I salute, I bow to. "Dvipadāṁ varam" — the best of those who are designated by two feet, i.e. of men, the foremost — the meaning is Puruṣottama. Through the offering of obeisance to the teacher, the supreme reality (paramārtha-tattva) free from the divisions of knowledge, knowable and knower — which is to be expounded in this prakaraṇa — is here promised, by way of negating the opposing views.
MK_C04_K02: The yoga known as asparśa (the touchless), conducive to the happiness of all beings, beneficial, free from controversy and free from contradiction — taught by scripture — to that yoga I bow.
MK_C04_K02::block-0:
Now, an obeisance is made to the yoga of the Advaita-darśana, by way of its praise. "Sparśa" means contact, relation; that yoga which has no contact whatsoever with anything, at any time, is the asparśa-yoga — and this is the very nature of Brahman itself. "Vai nāma" — among the knowers of Brahman it is well known thus as asparśa-yoga; this is the meaning.

And it is conducive to the happiness of all beings (sarva-sattva-sukha). Some practices, though endowed with means productive of intense future happiness, are themselves of the nature of suffering — as for example tapas. But this yoga is not so. What then? It is happy for all beings. Likewise, in this world some sense-enjoyments are happy but not beneficial; this yoga, however, is both happy and beneficial, because its nature is eternally unwavering.

Further, it is "avivāda" — "vivāda" means contradictory speech that arises through the taking up of a thesis and counter-thesis; that in which there is no such contradictory speech is avivāda, free from controversy. Why so? Because it is also "aviruddha" — free from contradiction. Such a yoga as this, which has been taught (deśita), instructed by śāstra — to that I bow, I prostrate; this is the meaning.
MK_C04_K03: Some disputants assert the origination of an existent thing, while others, considering themselves wise, assert the origination of a non-existent thing — debating with one another.
MK_C04_K03::block-0: How do the dualists contradict one another? It is said: of "bhūta," of an existent thing, certain disputants — namely the Sāṅkhyas alone, indeed — assert origination (jāti, utpatti); not all dualists do so. For others — the Vaiśeṣikas and the Naiyāyikas — "the wise," i.e. those who imagine themselves to be intelligent (prājña-abhimānin), hold that origination is of "abhūta," of the non-existent. Engaging in mutually contradictory speech, they intend to defeat one another — this is the purport.
MK_C04_K04: An existent does not arise as anything; nor does the non-existent arise. Disputing thus, they, though dualists, in effect proclaim ajāti (non-origination), and so are at one with the non-dualists.
MK_C04_K04::block-0:
What is established by these disputants when they thus mutually negate one another's positions through contradictory speech? It is answered: when the asat-vādin (the Vaiśeṣika/Naiyāyika who holds the cause to be non-existent prior) says, "An existent thing does not originate as anything, precisely because it is already existent — like the Self," he negates the Sāṅkhya thesis of sat-janma (origination of the existent). Likewise, when the Sāṅkhya asat-vādin says, "The non-existent — being non-existent — never originates, like the horns of a hare," he negates the asat-janma thesis of the asad-vādin (the Vaiśeṣika).

Thus, debating with contradictory speech, while really being non-dual themselves in result — these very disputants, by negating mutually one another's theses of the origination of the existent and the non-existent, by implication proclaim, make manifest, ajāti — non-origination.
MK_C04_K05: We approve the non-origination thus made manifest by them; we do not dispute with them. Understand, O disciples, this view that is free from controversy.
MK_C04_K05::block-0: The ajāti thus made manifest by them — we merely approve it, saying, "Let it be so"; we do not dispute with them by taking up a thesis and counter-thesis, as they do mutually with one another — this is the purport. Therefore, that paramārtha-darśana, which is free from dispute and which is approved by us — understand it, O disciples (niboḍhata).
MK_C04_K06: The disputants assert the origination of the very dharma which is in truth unborn. But how can a dharma which is unborn and immortal pass into mortality?
MK_C04_K06::block-0: All these are sat-asad-vādins, holders of the views of the existent and non-existent. This śloka, however, is one whose commentary has already been given earlier.
MK_C04_K07: The immortal does not become the mortal, nor does the mortal become the immortal in like manner; for the alteration of one's own nature (prakṛti) cannot in any way come about.
MK_C04_K08: If a dharma which is, by its very nature, immortal nonetheless lapses into mortality, then having become immortal only through some adventitious cause, how shall it remain unshakable?
MK_C04_K08::block-0: The placing here of these verses, whose meaning has already been explained, is for the purpose of displaying the joyful acknowledgement of non-origination (anutpatti) which is itself made manifest by the mutual contradiction of the theses of opponents.
MK_C04_K09: That which is sāṃsiddhikī (perfectly accomplished), svābhāvikī (belonging to a thing's very nature), sahajā (innate, born together with the substance), and akṛtā (uncreated by anyone) — that is to be known as prakṛti (the intrinsic nature), since it does not abandon its own nature. (9)
MK_C04_K09::block-0:
Since prakṛti, even in worldly experience, never deviates from its own nature, the question arises: what is that prakṛti? The answer is given. Samyak-siddhi is saṃsiddhi (full accomplishment); that which arises therein is sāṃsiddhikī. For example, the attainment of the lordly powers such as aṇimā by accomplished yogins is their prakṛti, and that does not deviate for those yogins either in the past or in the future. Such indeed is it (this established prakṛti).

Svābhāvikī is that which is established from the very nature (svabhāva) of a substance, as the characteristic of heat and light in fire and the like. That too does not deviate at any other time or in any other place. Likewise sahajā is what is born together (saha-jāta) with the self of the thing, as the characteristic of flying through space in birds and the rest. There is also another (kind), the akṛtā, that which has not been made by anyone — as the characteristic of water flowing toward a lower region. And whatever else there may be that does not abandon its own nature — all of that is to be known in the world as prakṛti.

If, even in worldly things which are falsely imagined (mithyā-kalpita), prakṛti does not become otherwise, how much more so in supreme things whose very nature is unborn (aja-svabhāva)? The intent is this: the prakṛti characterised by immortality (amṛtatva) cannot become otherwise.
MK_C04_K10: All dharmas (selves) are by their very nature free from old age and death; yet, desiring old age and death, by that very contemplation they fall away (from their own nature). (10)
MK_C04_K10::block-0:
But what is the subject-matter (viṣaya) of that prakṛti, whose otherness (anyathābhāva) the disputants imagine? Or, in supposing such an alteration, what is the fault? It is answered. Jarā-maraṇa-nirmuktāḥ — devoid of all modifications such as old age, death and the rest. Of whom? Of all the dharmas — that is, of all selves. Svabhāvataḥ — by their very prakṛti.

Therefore, while being of such a nature, the dharmas, as it were desiring old age and death — that is, imagining them in themselves as one imagines a serpent in a rope — fall away (cyavante); the meaning is, they swerve from their own nature. Tan-manīṣayā — by the contemplation of old age and death, that is, by the fault of being affected by the conception of those states.
MK_C04_K11: He whose very cause is (also) effect — for him the cause is (said to be) born. How can what is being born be unborn? And how can what is split (into parts) be eternal? (11)
MK_C04_K11::block-0:
How is the position of the sat-kārya-vāda Sāṅkhyas inconsistent? Speaking against them, the Vaiśeṣika says — for that disputant for whom the cause, having the character of the material cause (upādāna) like clay, is itself the effect — that is, for the disputant who holds that the cause itself transforms (pariṇamate) into the form of the effect — for him, although the cause such as pradhāna is unborn (aja), it is born in the form of the effects beginning with mahat. This is the meaning.

If pradhāna is being born in the form of mahat etc., how is it called unborn by them? It is self-contradictory to say both 'it is born' and 'it is unborn'. They also call it eternal (nitya). And pradhāna is bhinna (split, divided), splintered through one part. How can what has cracked open through one part be eternal? In the world a thing with parts (sāvayava), like a pot, that has the property of cracking through one part, is not seen to be eternal. The intent is that they assert what is self-contradictory — that it is split through one part and yet unborn and eternal.
MK_C04_K12: If for you the effect is non-different from the cause, then the effect is unborn (aja). How can your cause be (eternally) firm, when it is non-different from the effect that is being born? (12)
MK_C04_K12::block-0: To clarify the very meaning that has been stated, he says — if non-difference (ananyatva) of the effect from the unborn cause is admitted by you, then it follows that the effect too is unborn. And this is yet another self-contradiction in your view, namely 'the effect, yet unborn'. Furthermore, when there is non-difference between cause and effect, how can the cause, being non-different from the effect that is being born, be for you eternal (nitya) and firm (dhruva)? For one part of a hen is not cooked while another part is set apart for laying eggs.
MK_C04_K13: For him who holds that (an effect) is born from the unborn (aja), there is verily no example. And if (an effect) be born from what is itself born, no settled position (vyavasthā) results. (13)
MK_C04_K13::block-0:
And further: for the disputant who holds that the effect is born from the unborn, that is, from a thing not arisen, there is verily no example (dṛṣṭānta). And in the absence of an example, it is established by implication that nothing is born from the unborn. This is the meaning.

But if, on the other hand, the assumption is that what is born proceeds from what is (itself) already born, even then no settled position (vyavasthā) results — for that too would be from another that is born, and that yet from another, ad infinitum. The meaning is, there would be infinite regress (anavasthā).
MK_C04_K14: How is beginninglessness (anāditva) of cause and effect described by those for whom the cause (hetu) is the beginning of the fruit, and the beginning of the cause is the fruit? (14)
MK_C04_K14::block-0: By the śruti 'When for him all has become the very Self' (Bṛ. Up. 4.5.15) the absence of duality in the supreme sense (paramārtha) is declared. Resorting to that, he says — for those disputants the beginning (ādi), that is the cause, of the hetu (such as dharma and so on) is the saṅghāta of body etc., the fruit; and likewise the beginning, that is the cause, of the fruit, namely the saṅghāta of body etc., is the hetu, dharma and the like. Thus by those who declare hetu and phala to have a beginning through being mutually each other's effect and cause — by them how can the beginninglessness (anāditva) of hetu and phala likewise be described? It is self-contradictory, is the meaning. For of the eternal, immutable (kūṭastha) Self, the character of being hetu-and-phala is not possible.
MK_C04_K15: For those for whom the cause is the beginning of the fruit, and the beginning of the cause is the fruit — for them the birth (of the cause) would be like the birth of the father from the son. (15)
MK_C04_K15::block-0: How is what is contradictory accepted by them? It is answered — for those who accept the birth of the cause (hetu) from the very fruit which is itself produced by the cause, such a contradiction as has been stated obtains, just as though there were the birth of the father from the son.
MK_C04_K16: If both cause and effect (can) come into being, the order (krama) must be sought by you (the opponent); since, when both arise simultaneously, there is no relation, like (the two) horns. (16)
MK_C04_K16::block-0: If you think that the contradiction stated is not fit to be admitted, then in the arising (sambhava, that is utpatti) of cause and effect a sequence (krama) must be sought (eṣitavyaḥ) and investigated by you — first the cause and afterwards the effect. And further: when both arise simultaneously (yugapad-sambhava), there is no relation between cause and effect through the connection of effect-and-cause — just as between the simultaneously arising left and right horns of a cow.
MK_C04_K17: When (the cause) is being produced from the effect, which is itself unestablished, your cause is not established. How shall a cause that is itself unestablished produce an effect?
MK_C04_K17::block-0:
How is there non-relation? This is what is stated. Being produced (utpadyamānaḥ san) from the effect (phalāt) which is in itself unattained-self-nature (svato'labdhātmakāt), like (something arising) from a hare's horn and the like which is non-existent (asataḥ), the cause (hetuḥ) is not established (na prasidhyati) — that is, it does not attain birth (janma na labhate).

He (the cause), being itself unattained-self-nature (alabdhātmakaḥ), unestablished (aprasiddhaḥ), comparable to a hare's horn and the like — how shall that cause of yours produce an effect? For never indeed has there been seen anywhere — neither in this manner nor otherwise — a relation through cause-and-effect-hood (kāryakāraṇabhāvena sambandhaḥ) between two things whose establishment depends mutually on each other (itaretarāpekṣasiddhyoḥ), comparable to a hare's horn. This is the import.
MK_C04_K18: If the cause's establishment depends on the effect, and the effect's establishment from the cause, which of the two is produced first, in dependence upon which the other is established?
MK_C04_K18::block-0: Even when the cause-and-effect-hood between cause and effect has been refuted by the fault of non-relation, if mutual establishment between cause and effect is still admitted by you, then which of the two — cause or effect — is produced first? Tell me, in dependence upon which prior-established one would the latter (the subsequent one) attain its establishment. This is the meaning.
MK_C04_K19: It is either inability (to answer), or non-discrimination, or else a violation of the sequence — thus indeed in every way ajāti (non-origination) has been illumined by the wise.
MK_C04_K19::block-0:
If you think "this cannot be answered," then this very (silence) is inability (aśaktiḥ), non-discrimination (aparijñānam), non-discrimination of the truth — confusion (mūḍhatā) — that is the meaning. Or else, this sequence (kramaḥ) which you stated — the establishment of the cause from the effect and the establishment of the effect from the cause — characterized by mutual successiveness (itaretarānantarya), would suffer a violation (kopaḥ), i.e., reversal, becoming-otherwise. This is the import.

Thus, owing to the impossibility of cause-and-effect-hood between cause and effect, ajāti (non-origination) — the non-arising of everything — has been illumined, made evident, by the wise (buddhaiḥ), the learned (paṇḍitaiḥ), namely the disputants who, by mutually pointing out the faults in each other's positions, themselves end up disclosing it. This is the meaning.
MK_C04_K20: The example called seed-and-sprout (bījāṅkura) is always equal to the very thing to be proved (sādhya-sama). For a reason that is itself equal to what is to be proved is not fit to establish the sādhya.
MK_C04_K20::block-0:
Now (the opponent says): "By saying 'cause-and-effect-hood between cause and effect,' you have, taking refuge in mere words, perpetrated this trickery (chala) — citing 'as the father's birth from the son' (Mā. Kā. 4.15) and 'and non-relation as in horns' (Mā. Kā. 4.16) and the like. We have never admitted that the effect is established from an unestablished cause, nor that the cause is established from an unestablished effect. What then? Cause-and-effect-hood is admitted in the manner of seed and sprout (bījāṅkuravat)."

To this it is replied — that example called seed-and-sprout — that is equal (sama), parallel, to the very sādhya (the thesis to be proved) for me. This is the import. "But surely the cause-and-effect-hood between seed and sprout is directly perceived, and is beginningless?" No: because each prior one becomes-the-latter (apara-bhāva) for the next, and beginning-having-ness (ādimattva) is admitted. Just as the sprout produced now is beginning-having (ādimān) from a seed, and that seed too is beginning-having from another, prior sprout — being produced in sequence — so each prior sprout and each prior seed is itself beginning-having, beginning-having indeed. Since each individual member of the seed-sprout class is beginning-having, the beginninglessness of any one is impossible. So too with cause and effect.

If it be said: "But the seed-sprout-series (santati) is beginningless" — no, because of the impossibility of (the series') unity. For the series of seed and sprout, distinct from seed and sprout themselves, is not admitted as something single by those who claim its beginninglessness — nor likewise the cause-effect-series. Therefore it has been well said: "How is the beginninglessness of cause and effect to be described by them?"

And thus, otherwise too there is impossibility, and (our argument) is no chala (trickery) — this is the import. And in worldly inference, a reason that is sādhya-sama (equal to the thesis) is not fit, not employed by experts in pramāṇa, as the cause for establishing the sādhya. Here "hetu" is intended as "dṛṣṭānta" (example), because of its conveying-power (gamakatva); for here the topic is the example, not the (formal) reason.
MK_C04_K21: The non-cognition of (which is) prior and (which is) posterior is itself the illuminator of ajāti. For if the dharma which is being born is grasped, why is its prior (cause) not grasped?
MK_C04_K21::block-0: How has ajāti been illumined by the wise? He says: this very non-cognition of cause and effect as prior and posterior — that itself is the illuminator (paridīpaka), the manifester, of ajāti. This is the meaning. For if a dharma being born were grasped, why is its prior cause not grasped? Necessarily, by one who grasps a thing-being-born, its producer too should be grasped, since the relation between produced and producer cannot be set aside. Therefore that (non-cognition) is the illuminator of ajāti. This is the meaning.
MK_C04_K22: No object whatsoever is born — neither from itself nor from another, nor (from both); whether existent, non-existent, or both existent-and-non-existent, no object whatsoever is born.
MK_C04_K22::block-0:
And for this reason too nothing is born: any object that is being born is not born from itself, from another, from both, nor as existent (sat), non-existent (asat), or both existent-and-non-existent (sad-asat). Its birth is impossible by any mode whatever. Not, indeed, does it arise from itself — from its own form which is itself unaccomplished — by itself, as a pot from that very pot. Nor from another, one thing from another, as cloth from a pot. Nor from both, owing to contradiction; as a pot or cloth is not born from a pot-and-cloth.

(Pūrvapakṣa): "But surely a pot is born from clay, and a son from a father." True, the cognition and word "is born" exists for the deluded. But those very word and cognition are examined by the discerning — whether they are real or false; for upon examination, the object that is the referent of the word and cognition — characterized as pot, son, etc. — is mere word, as the śruti says, "a verbal handle" (vācārambhaṇam — Chā. Up. 6.4.4). If it is existent, it is not born, owing to its existence — like clay, father, etc. If non-existent, then too it is not born, owing to non-existence — like a hare's horn etc. If both existent-and-non-existent, then too it is not born, since one (single thing) cannot be (the locus of) contradictories. Hence it is established that no object whatsoever is born.

For those who hold that birth itself is being born — admitting unity of action, agent, and result — and who hold that an object is momentary (kṣaṇika), they are far away from sound reasoning. For they cannot stand in another moment after the moment of determination "this is thus"; and the recollection of what was not previously experienced is impossible (for the momentariness theory).
MK_C04_K23: The cause is not born from a beginningless effect, nor the effect from its own (causeless) nature. That for which there is no beginning indeed has no birth.
MK_C04_K23::block-0:
Further, by you who admit the beginninglessness (anāditva) of cause and effect, the very birthlessness (ajanmatva) of cause and effect would be admitted by force. How? From a beginningless (anādeḥ) — beginning-devoid — effect, the cause is not born. For the birth of the cause from the beginningless, unborn effect is not held by you. And the effect too is not held by you to be born from a beginningless, unborn cause spontaneously, without cause, on its own nature. Therefore by you who admit beginninglessness, the unbornness of cause and effect is itself admitted.

Since in the world, the beginning — the cause — is not found for that whose beginning is not found, and that previously stated birth (jāti) too is not found for that. Indeed, only that which has a cause is admitted to have a beginning, not what is causeless.
MK_C04_K24: Cognition has a cause — otherwise both (cognition and its variety) would be destroyed; and because affliction (saṅkleśa) is experienced, the existence of dependent things (paratantra) is held.
MK_C04_K24::block-0:
Wishing to firmly establish the very meaning already stated, he again raises an objection (this is the pūrvapakṣa of the Vijñānavādin Buddhist). Cognition (prajñāna) is prajñapti — the perception of sound and the like. Its sa-nimittatva — having-cause-ness, where nimitta means cause, viṣaya, object — that is, having-object-ness, having-an-object-distinct-from-its-own-self — this we propound. For perception of sound etc. cannot be objectless (nirviṣayā), since it has a nimitta.

Otherwise, in objectlessness, the variety of cognitions of sound, touch, blue, yellow, red, etc. — the duo (dvayam, viz. cognition and its content variety) — would suffer destruction (nāśa), absence. This is the meaning. But there is no absence of the variety of cognitions or of the duo, because (it is) directly perceived. Hence, since the variety of cognitions, the duo, is seen, the others' tantra (system) — para-tantra, the doctrine of others (i.e., of those who hold external objects). The existence (astitā) of that para-tantra (the dependent), i.e., of the external object that has its support in another and is distinct from cognition, is held to be intended.

For the cognition (prajñapti), being mere illumination by nature, cannot have this variety merely from a difference in its own nature, without the variety of external supports — blue, yellow, etc. The variety of crystal does not come about without the supporting upādhis like blue and so on. This is the import.

For this reason too, the existence of an external object distinct from cognition, based on "the dependent" (paratantra), is established. Affliction (saṅkleśa) means pain (duḥkha). Pain is experienced as having causes such as the burning of fire and the like. If the burning fire and the like — externals which are causes of burning etc. and distinct from consciousness — did not exist, then the pain of burning etc. would not be experienced. But it is experienced. Hence by that we hold that an external object exists. For affliction is not fitting in mere consciousness alone, since it is not seen elsewhere (in pure cognition without object). This is the import.
MK_C04_K25: It is admitted that cognition has a cause, on the strength of the reasoning seen. It is admitted that the cause [itself] is causeless, on the strength of seeing the [real] nature of things.
MK_C04_K25::block-0:
Here it is replied: indeed, it is so. The fact that cognition (prajñapti) possesses a cause is admitted by you on the strength of the reasoning that perceives the dual contamination — namely, the apprehension of object and cogniser together with their defilement. First, stand firm in this very position of yours, that the seeing of reasoning is the ground for accepting things as they are. Now tell us — what follows from this?

It is replied: of the cause, that is, of the pot and the like which you regard as the supporting object (ālambana) of cognition, we admit causelessness (animittatva), that is, non-supportingness (anālambanatva), the absence of being a ground for the variegated appearance. How? "Bhūtadarśanāt" — from the seeing of the real, that is, from the perception of the supreme truth. For when the pot's true nature as mere clay is seen, there is nothing called pot apart from clay — just as there is no buffalo apart from the horse, no cloth apart from the threads, and no threads apart from the fibres. By such progressive seeing of the real, up to the cessation of words and concepts, we never apprehend any [external] cause whatever — this is the meaning.

Or alternatively, the causelessness of the external object is admitted on the ground of its being non-existent in reality (abhūtadarśanāt), as the snake and the like in the rope. And from being only the object of erroneous perception (bhrāntidarśana), the so-called cause comes to be no cause at all; for in the absence of that [error], it does not appear. For in the case of those who are in deep sleep, in samādhi, or liberated, when erroneous perception is absent, no external object distinct from the Self is apprehended. Nor is the thing perceived by a madman cognised in that same form even by the sane. By this much, both the perception of duality and the apprehension of contamination [posited by the Vijñānavādin] stand refuted.
MK_C04_K26: The mind does not contact the [external] object, nor likewise its appearance. Since the object is non-existent, and the apparent object is not separate [from the mind].
MK_C04_K26::block-0: Since there is no external cause, therefore the mind does not contact (na spṛśati) the object that has an external substratum, nor even the appearance of an object — because of being mind, like the dream-mind. For even in the waking state, an external object such as sound and the rest is non-existent, just like the dream-object, by reason of the cause already stated. Nor is the apparent object separate from the mind. The mind itself shines forth as if it were the pot and the other objects, just as in dream.
MK_C04_K27: The mind does not ever contact a cause [object] in the three times. How then will there be a causeless illusion (viparyāsa) of it?
MK_C04_K27::block-0: It may be objected: then the mind's appearing as pot and the like, when no pot really exists, would be an illusion (viparyāsa); and in that case some non-illusory state would have to be specified somewhere. To this it is replied: the mind never contacts the cause, that is, the [external] object, in any of the three times — past, future or present. For if it contacted [an object] anywhere, that would be the non-illusory, the supreme truth, and only relative to that could the appearing as pot when there is no pot be called illusion. But there never is any contact of the mind with an object at all. Therefore, how can there be any causeless illusion of that mind? The intent is that there is no illusion in any way whatever. For this very is the inherent nature of the mind, namely, the appearing as something though there is no [real] cause, such as a pot.
MK_C04_K28: Therefore the mind is not born; what is seen by the mind is not born. Those who see its birth — verily they see footprints in the sky.
MK_C04_K28::block-0:
From "prajñapteḥ sanimittatvam" (MK 4.25) up to here, the words of the Buddhist Vijñānavādin, aimed at refuting the position of the upholder of external objects (bāhyārthavādin), have been welcomed by the ācārya. Taking that very position as the ground, in order now to refute the Vijñānavādin himself, this is said — "tasmāt" and so on.

Since the Vijñānavādin himself accepts that the mind shines as pot and the like even when there is no pot, and we too have accepted this on the strength of the seeing of the real (bhūtadarśanāt), therefore the apparent birth of that mind itself is reasonable only when there is no real birth. Hence the mind is not born. Just as what is seen by the mind is not born, [so the mind itself is not born]. Therefore, those Vijñānavādins who see the birth of that mind, and ascribe to it momentariness, sufferingness, voidness, non-selfhood, and so forth — they, attempting to see by that very mind the form of the mind which cannot be seen [by itself], are seeing footprints of birds and the like in the sky. Therefore they are far more reckless than even the dualists — this is the meaning. As for the Śūnyavādins who, themselves seeing, declare the voidness of all things together with the voidness of their own seeing — they are even more reckless than these, wishing to seize the very sky in their fist.
MK_C04_K29: Since the unborn is [said to be] born, ajāti is therefore [its] very nature. There can be no transformation of [its] nature in any manner whatever.
MK_C04_K29::block-0: By the reasons stated, it has been established that Brahman is one and unborn (aja). What was promised at the outset is now drawn to its conclusion by this verse. The unborn mind which the disputants imagine to be born as Brahman — since the unborn is what is supposed to be born, ajāti, that is, the unborn nature, is its very svabhāva. Therefore, of that nature whose form is unborn, there can be no transformation, that is, no birth, in any manner whatever.
MK_C04_K30: The endingness of the beginningless saṃsāra will not be established. Nor will the endlessness of mokṣa, which has a beginning, come about.
MK_C04_K30::block-0: Now another defect in the position of those who hold that saṃsāra and mokṣa of the Self are real in the highest sense is stated — the endingness, that is, the termination, of saṃsāra, which is anādi, devoid of any past beginning, will not be established (na setsyati), will not attain establishment by reasoning. For nothing whatever has been seen in the world that, being beginningless, has an end. If it be said: the cessation of the unbroken continuity of the seed-and-sprout relation is seen [as such an example] — no, because that is set aside by the absence of [its being] one [continuous] thing. Likewise, the endlessness too of mokṣa, which arises at the time of the attainment of [true] knowledge and so has a beginning, will not be — because such a thing is not seen in pots and the like. If it be said: as in the destruction of pots and so on, mokṣa is non-substantial, so there is no defect — then the assertion of the real existence of mokṣa in the highest sense is given up; and just like the horns of a hare, by its very non-existence, the [supposed] beginning too becomes void.
MK_C04_K31: What is non-existent in the beginning and at the end is just so in the present too. Though similar to the unreal, [these] are observed as if real.
MK_C04_K32: Their purposiveness is contradicted in dream. Therefore, by reason of having beginning and end, they are remembered as verily false.
MK_C04_K32::block-0: These two verses, already explained in the Vaitathya[-prakaraṇa], are recited here in the context of [showing] the absence of saṃsāra and mokṣa.
MK_C04_K33: All entities (dharmas) seen in dream are unreal (mṛṣā), because they are perceived within the body (kāyasya antar-nidarśanāt). In this enclosed, narrow space (saṃvṛte pradeśe), how indeed can the perception of (large) beings (bhūtānāṃ darśanam) be possible?
MK_C04_K33::block-0:
The meaning expressed earlier — "The supposed cause is held to be no real cause, because of the (illusory) perception of beings" (Mā. Kā. 4.25) — is now elaborated through these following ślokas.

That is, the kārikās that follow expand and demonstrate, by reasoned arguments, why the dream-objects (and by extension all objects of cognition) cannot be real causes or effects, since they manifest only within the dreamer's own body and consciousness, and yet appear to occupy vast external regions.
MK_C04_K34: It is not reasonable (na yuktam) that the dreamer actually goes (gatvā) to behold (the distant places dreamt of), because of the absence of regulation of time (kālasya aniyamāt) with respect to such going. Moreover, on awaking (pratibuddhaḥ), no one is found to be in that (dreamt) place (tasmin deśe na vidyate).
MK_C04_K34::block-0:
In the waking state (jāgarite), the time required for going (gati) and for returning (āgamana) is fixed (niyatau), and the place reached is determinable by valid means of cognition (deśaḥ pramāṇataḥ). Of such fixity in regard to dream-going there is non-regulation (aniyamāt) — that is, the absence of any such fixed rule (niyamasya abhāvāt).

The purport, therefore, is this: in dream there is no actual going to another place (svapne na deśāntara-gamanam). For one closes the eyes here and immediately, without the lapse of any travel-time, beholds a distant city; and on waking one finds the body lying just where it lay. Hence the supposed external journey is itself a mental projection, not a literal traversing of space.
MK_C04_K35: Having taken counsel together with friends and others (mitrādyaiḥ saha sammantrya) in dream, the awakened one (sambuddhaḥ) does not actually meet (na prapadyate) with that very counsel; and whatever was received (gṛhītam) — gold and the like — that too the awakened one does not behold (na paśyati).
MK_C04_K35::block-0:
Having taken counsel together with friends and the like (mitrādyaiḥ saha sammantrya), that very deliberation (mantraṇa) the awakened person does not encounter again — the friends are nowhere to be found, and the agreement reached has no continuance. Likewise, whatever was received (gṛhītam), be it gold (hiraṇya) or any other valuable, the awakened one does not actually obtain (na prāpnoti).

From this it follows that in dream there is no actual journey to another place (na deśāntaraṃ gacchati svapne). For if the dreamer had truly traveled, the persons met and the wealth received would persist on waking — they do not. Hence the dream-encounter and dream-acquisition are themselves projections of the mind, not transactions in real space.
MK_C04_K36: And in dream the body (kāyaḥ) too is unreal (avastukaḥ), because of the perception of another, separate (body) (pṛthak anyasya darśanāt — the body lying in bed). As is the (dream-)body, so too is everything that is seen by the mind (cittadṛśyam) — entirely without reality (avastukam).
MK_C04_K36::block-0:
The body which is seen wandering about in the dream (svapne ca aṭan dṛśyate yaḥ kāyaḥ) is itself unreal (avastukaḥ). For there is the perception of another, distinct body — the one resting in the place where the dreamer lies asleep (svāpa-deśa-sthasya pṛthak kāyāntarasya darśanāt). Two bodies cannot simultaneously be the one self; hence the dream-body is established as a mental fabrication.

Just as the dream-seen body (svapna-dṛśyaḥ kāyaḥ) is non-existent (asan), so too is everything cognised by the mind (sarvaṃ cittadṛśyam) unreal (avastukam) — including the objects of the waking state, by virtue of their being equally objects of mental cognition (jāgarite api cittadṛśyatvāt). This is the meaning.

The purport of the section (prakaraṇārtha) is therefore this: because of its parity with dream (svapna-samatvāt), the waking world also is unreal (asat jāgaritam api). The argument is not that dream is real, but that waking, sharing the very mark (cittadṛśyatva) on which dream's unreality rests, must share its unreality.
MK_C04_K37: Because of (its) being apprehended like the waking (state) (grahaṇāt jāgaritavat), the waking is held to be the cause of dream (tat-hetuḥ svapnaḥ iṣyate). But because the waking is the cause (only of the dream of that very dreamer), the waking is held to be real for him alone (tasyaiva sat — the dreamer alone) — (just as the dream is real only for him).
MK_C04_K37::block-0:
And from this further reason too the unreality of waking-objects (jāgrad-vastunaḥ asattvam) is established: dream is apprehended just as waking is (jāgaritavat grahaṇāt) — namely, in the mode of subject-and-object (grāhya-grāhaka-rūpeṇa). Since waking serves as the cause (hetu) of this dream — for dream-impressions arise from waking-experiences — the dream is regarded as the effect of waking (jāgarita-kāryam iṣyate).

Because of being its effect (tad-hetutvāt — i.e., jāgarita-kāryatvāt), the waking is regarded as real (sat) only for that very (dreamer) — for the one who has the dream (svapna-dṛśa eva) — and not for others (na tu anyeṣām); just as the dream is real only for him. This is the intent.

Just as the dream, though existing only for the dreamer (svapna-dṛśa eva san), appears as if it were a publicly existent thing (sādhāraṇa-vidyamāna-vastuvat avabhāsate), so too the waking, being the cause of that very dream-appearance, manifests as if it were a publicly existent thing — but it is not in truth a common, externally established reality, exactly as dream is not. The aim is to show that the waking-world, on its own showing, has no greater ontological status than the dream it produces.
MK_C04_K38: Because origination (utpāda) is unestablished (aprasiddhatvāt), all is declared to be unborn (ajaṃ sarvam udāhṛtam). Nor in any way whatsoever (kathañcana) is there the arising (sambhavaḥ) of the non-existent (abhūtasya) from the existent (bhūtāt).
MK_C04_K38::block-0:
[Pūrvapakṣa]: Even granting that waking is the cause of dream, surely waking-objects are not unreal in the manner of dream-objects. For dream is observed to be exceedingly fluctuating (atyanta-cala), whereas waking is seen to be stable (sthira). Hence the parity asserted is unsound.

[Siddhānta]: True — so it might be for the undiscriminating (avivekinām). But for the discerning (vivekinām), no origination of any thing whatsoever is established (na kasyacit vastunaḥ utpādaḥ prasiddhaḥ). Hence, because origination is unestablished (aprasiddhatvāt utpādasya), the Self alone is everything (ātmaiva sarvam) — and so all is declared as unborn (ajaṃ sarvam udāhṛtam) in the Vedāntas, as in "Verily, He, unborn, is both within and without" (sa-bāhya-abhyantaro hi ajaḥ — Mu. U. 2.1.2).

As for what you suppose — namely, that the unreal dream is born from the real waking (jāgaritāt sataḥ asan svapnaḥ jāyate) — that is untenable. There is no arising in the world of the non-existent (abhūtasya) from the existent (bhūtāt). For the arising of a non-existent thing such as a hare's horn (śaśa-viṣāṇa) has never been observed in any way whatsoever (kathañcid api). Thus what does not exist cannot come into being from what exists.
MK_C04_K39: Having seen the unreal in waking (asat jāgarite dṛṣṭvā), the dreamer, immersed in it (tanmayaḥ), beholds it again in dream (svapne paśyati). And having seen the unreal even in dream (asat svapne api dṛṣṭvā), the awakened one no longer beholds it (pratibuddhaḥ na paśyati).
MK_C04_K39::block-0:
[Pūrvapakṣa]: But you yourself have said that dream is the effect of waking (svapnaḥ jāgarita-kāryam); how then can it be said that origination is unestablished (utpādaḥ aprasiddhaḥ)?

[Siddhānta]: Hear, then, in what manner the cause-effect relation (kārya-kāraṇa-bhāva) is intended by us. Having beheld in waking (jāgarite dṛṣṭvā) what is itself unreal (asat) — a thing imagined like the rope-snake (rajju-sarpa-vat vikalpitaṃ vastu) — one becomes coloured by that (tad-bhāva-bhāvitaḥ), wholly identified with it (tanmayaḥ), and then in dream too (svapne api), in the very manner of waking (jāgaritavat), as subject and object (grāhya-grāhaka-rūpeṇa), continues to imagine and behold it (vikalpayan paśyati).

Likewise, having beheld the unreal even in dream (asat svapne api dṛṣṭvā), the awakened one (pratibuddhaḥ) no longer beholds it (na paśyati), because he ceases to imagine it (avikalpayan); the word "and" (ca-śabda) further intends: similarly, having beheld in waking, one does not always behold the same in dream (jāgarite api dṛṣṭvā svapne na paśyati kadācit). This is the meaning.

Therefore the waking is called the cause of dream (jāgaritaṃ svapna-hetuḥ ucyate) — only as the supplier of imagined contents — and not because it is itself ultimately real (na tu paramārtha-sat). The cause-effect relation here is between two equally projected appearances, not between a true cause and a derived effect.
MK_C04_K40: There exists no non-existent having a non-existent cause (na asti asat-hetukam asat); likewise no existent having a non-existent cause (asat-hetukaṃ sat tathā na asti). And no existent has an existent cause (sat-hetukaṃ sat na asti); whence then could a non-existent (effect) have an existent cause (sat-hetukam asat kutaḥ)?
MK_C04_K40::block-0:
In ultimate truth (paramārthataḥ), no cause-effect relation (kārya-kāraṇa-bhāva) of anything (kasyacit) with anything else (kenacit api), in any manner whatsoever (prakāreṇa), is intelligible (na upapadyate). How so?

[First disjunct]: There exists no non-existent (asat) having a non-existent cause (asat-hetukam) — that is, no non-existent like a sky-flower (kha-puṣpa) etc., having for its cause something equally non-existent like a hare's horn (śaśa-viṣāṇa) etc. (na vidyate).

[Second disjunct]: Likewise, there exists no existent (sat), say a pot or the like (ghaṭādi vastu), having for its cause a non-existent (asat-hetukam), like a hare's horn — for from a non-existent nothing can issue.

[Third disjunct]: Likewise, there is no existent (sat), say a pot, that is the effect (kāryam) of another existent thing (sat) (vastvantara-kāryam) — the satkāryavāda already negates origination of a real from a real, since the effect must pre-exist or be merely a name.

[Fourth disjunct]: How indeed (kutaḥ eva) could a non-existent effect (asat) arise from an existent cause (sat-hetukam)? It cannot at all (sambhavati).

No other variety of cause-effect relation is possible (na ca anyaḥ kārya-kāraṇa-bhāvaḥ sambhavati) or capable of being conceived (śakyo vā kalpayitum). Thus, for the discerning (vivekinām), the cause-effect relation of anything with anything else is entirely unestablished (asiddha eva). This is the intent — the doctrine of ajāti, the non-origination of all that appears.
MK_C04_K41: Just as in waking, owing to misapprehension, one touches as though real things that defy thought, so too in dream, owing to misapprehension, one sees objects there itself. (41)
MK_C04_K41::block-0:
Once again, in order to dispel the suspicion of a cause-and-effect relation between waking and dream, both of which are unreal, he says: "vipāryāsāt" - through non-discrimination; "yathā jāgrat" - just as in the waking state; "acintyān" - things that cannot be thought, that is, beings impossible to conceive, such as the rope-snake and the like; "bhūtavat" - as though they were real, as though existing in truth; "spṛśet" - one would touch them; the meaning is that as though touching, one imagines them - just as some person does in waking.

In the same way, in dream, owing to misapprehension, one imagines as though seeing elephants and similar things. "There itself one sees them" - that is, they do not arise from the waking state. The purport is that the objects of dream are not produced from waking objects, just as the objects of waking are not produced from any prior real cause.
MK_C04_K42: Owing to perception and to practice, the doctrine of "existent reality" is taught; for those who always tremble at non-origination, the wise have taught origination. (42)
MK_C04_K42::block-0:
Whatever "jāti" - origination - has been taught "buddhaiḥ" - by the wise, the knowers of non-duality (advaitavādins), it is taught "upalambhāt" - from "upalambhana" or perception, that is, on account of apprehension; "samācārāt" - and on account of the conduct prescribed by the duties of varṇa and āśrama. By these two reasons it is taught for the sake of "asti-vastutva-vādins" - those whose habit it is to declare "there is reality of substance," who are firmly clinging, faithful, and of feeble discrimination - taught as a means for approaching the truth. Let such persons grasp that taught origination for the time being.

For those who diligently study Vedānta, however, the discrimination concerning the unborn non-dual Self will arise of itself; not by the conviction of ultimate truth taken otherwise. For those Śrotriyas, being of gross intellect, "sadā trasanti" - always tremble at "ajāteḥ" - the unborn Reality, fancying it to be the destruction of the Self - they are non-discerning, that is the meaning. As stated, "Such teaching is the means for descent" (Mā. Kā. 3.15).
MK_C04_K43: For those who, trembling at non-origination, depart on account of perception, the faults of origination will not be established; even if there is a fault, it will be slight. (43)
MK_C04_K43::block-0:
And those who, thus, owing to "upalambhāt" - perception - and "samācārāt" - conduct, trembling at "ajāteḥ" - the unborn Reality, holding "there is reality," "viyanti" - depart contrarily, that is, take to duality, deviating from the non-dual Self.

For them, who tremble at non-origination, who are faithful, who hold to the right path, the "jāti-doṣas" - faults arising from the apprehension of origination - will not become established, will not attain consummation, since they are engaged on the path of discrimination. Even if there be some fault, it too will be very slight, having for its cause merely the non-attainment of complete right vision - this is the meaning.
MK_C04_K44: Just as a magical elephant is called an elephant on account of perception and on account of conduct, so too on account of perception and on account of conduct, reality is said to exist. (44)
MK_C04_K44::block-0:
Pūrvapakṣa: But surely, since perception and customary conduct are valid means, duality does indeed exist as a real thing. Siddhānta: No - because perception and customary conduct are deviant. "How are they deviant?" - it is answered: a magical elephant (māyā-hastī) is indeed perceived as though it were an elephant; people behave towards it with practices appropriate to elephants - tying it up, mounting it, and so on; and it is called "elephant," though non-existent.

In just the same way, on account of perception and on account of conduct, duality, having the form of difference, is said to be a real thing. Therefore perception and customary conduct cannot be the proofs for the actual existence of dual reality. This is the import.
MK_C04_K45: The semblance of origination, the semblance of motion, and likewise the semblance of substance - that consciousness is unborn, motionless, non-substantial, peaceful and non-dual. (45)
MK_C04_K45::block-0:
What then is the truly real thing, on which the unreal cognitions of origination and the rest are founded? - he says: being unborn, it appears as though born; thus it is "jātyābhāsaṃ" - having the semblance of origination - as in "Devadatta is being born." "Calābhāsaṃ" - it appears as though moving - as in "that same Devadatta walks." "Vastvābhāsaṃ" - "vastu" means substance, the substrate of qualities; appearing like that, it is "vastvābhāsaṃ" - as in "that same Devadatta is fair, tall."

Thus "Devadatta is born," "he stirs," "he is tall, fair" - in this way it appears. But in ultimate truth, it is unborn, motionless, non-substantial, non-material. What is it that is of this nature? - "vijñāna" - awareness, mere intelligence; being free of origination and the rest, it is "śānta" - peaceful; and for that very reason it is also "advaya" - non-dual - this is the meaning.
MK_C04_K46: Thus does mind not arise; thus are dharmas held to be unborn; those who know thus do not fall into error. (46)
MK_C04_K46::block-0:
Thus, from the reasons stated, the mind does not arise. Thus the "dharmas" - the selves - are remembered as unborn by the knowers of Brahman. The plural "dharmāḥ" is used metaphorically for the non-dual itself, since it follows the differentiation of bodies.

Those who, in just this way, know the consciousness as described, free from origination and the rest, the non-dual Self-essence (ātma-tattva) - having abandoned outer cravings - do not fall again into the ocean of darkness which is avidyā, into vipāryaya - delusion. As declared by the mantra, "There, what delusion, what grief, for him who beholds oneness?" (Īśā 7) and other mantra-passages.
MK_C04_K47: As the firebrand's motion appears as straight, crooked, and so on, so too the vibration of consciousness appears as the perceived and the perceiver. (47)
MK_C04_K47::block-0:
In order to elaborate the just-stated vision of the highest truth, he says: just as in the world the motion of a firebrand (alāta-spandita), the whirling of a brand, appears in modes of straight, crooked, and the like - so too the appearance of "grahaṇa-grāhaka" - of object and subject - that is, of viṣayī (subject) and viṣaya (object).

What is that? "Vijñāna-spanditaṃ" - it is as though the vibration of consciousness, vibrating as it were through avidyā. For there is no real motion of consciousness which is motionless; for it has been said "unborn, motionless" (Mā. Kā. 4.45). The firebrand-circle (alātacakra) is the simile that refutes the Vijñānavāda Buddhist who admits a real momentary stream of cognitions; in truth, no such vibration belongs to consciousness.
MK_C04_K48: As the firebrand, when not vibrating, is without appearance and unborn, so too consciousness, when not vibrating, is without appearance and unborn. (48)
MK_C04_K48::block-0: "Aspandamānaṃ" - free from vibration - that very firebrand, not arising in the forms of straight and the rest, is "anābhāsaṃ" - without appearance - and "ajaṃ" - unborn; just as that is, so too consciousness, vibrating through avidyā, on the cessation of avidyā becomes non-vibrating, without the appearance of origination and the rest, unborn, and motionless - this is the meaning.
MK_C04_K49: When the firebrand (alāta) is in motion, the appearances upon it do not arise from anywhere else; nor, when it is at rest, do they go forth to any other place from it; nor do they re-enter the firebrand itself. (49)
MK_C04_K49::block-0: Furthermore, when that very firebrand is in motion, the straight, curved, and other appearances do not arise upon the firebrand by coming from somewhere else apart from the firebrand itself; therefore they are not anyatobhuvaḥ, that is, not produced from another. Nor have they gone out elsewhere from that firebrand when it has become motionless. Nor do they re-enter the motionless firebrand itself.
MK_C04_K50: They have not gone forth from the firebrand, because they are devoid of the character of being a substance; in consciousness too they would stand in the very same way, since the appearances are without distinction. (50)
MK_C04_K50::block-0:
Furthermore, those appearances have not gone forth out of the firebrand as one might go out of a house, owing to the connection with the absence of substantiality. The state of being a substance is dravyatva; the absence of that is dravyatvābhāva; "dravyatvābhāvayogataḥ" therefore means by reason of being conjoined with the absence of substantiality, that is, on account of the absence of any real thinghood, this is the meaning. For entry, exit and the like are possible only of a real thing (vastu), not of a non-thing (avastu).

In consciousness (vijñāna) likewise the appearances of class, attribute and the rest stand in the very same manner, because the appearance is without any difference, that is, on account of equality.
MK_C04_K51: When consciousness is, as it were, in motion, the appearances do not come from elsewhere; nor, when it is at rest, do they go forth to any other place from it; nor do they re-enter consciousness. (51)
MK_C04_K52: They have not gone forth from consciousness, because they are devoid of the character of being a substance; and because the relation of effect and cause is absent, they are forever incomprehensible. (52)
MK_C04_K52::block-0:
How is the equality established? It is replied: everything in consciousness is similar to the firebrand; the special feature of consciousness, however, is its eternal motionlessness. The objection then is, by what are the appearances of class and the like brought about in consciousness, which is itself motionless? To this it is said: because of the absence of the relation of effect and cause, that is, because the relation of being produced and producer is not established, and because they are of the nature of non-being, they are inconceivable, since they are forever such.

Just as in the firebrand alone the cognition of straight, curved and so forth is observed even though such straight and other figures do not really exist, so too in mere consciousness the cognition of class, attribute and the rest is wholly false, since class and the like equally do not exist; this is the collective import.
MK_C04_K53: A substance may be the cause of a substance, and one thing of another; but neither substancehood nor otherness can hold of the dharmas (selves). (53)
MK_C04_K53::block-0:
It has been established that the Self-reality is unborn and one only. Yet for those who imagine the relation of effect and cause, a substance may be the cause of another substance distinct from it; it is not the cause of itself. Nor is anything non-substantial seen in the world to be the independent cause of anything.

But substantiality is not possible for the dharmas, that is, for the selves, nor is otherness from anything possible for them, by which one could acquire the status of cause or effect with respect to another. Therefore, because they are non-substantial and because they are non-different, the Self is neither the effect nor the cause of anything, this is the meaning.
MK_C04_K54: Thus the dharmas are not born of mind, nor is the mind born of any dharma; thus the wise enter into the non-origination of cause and effect. (54)
MK_C04_K54::block-0:
Thus, by the reasons stated, the mind is nothing other than the very nature of the Self-knowledge, and so the outer dharmas are not born of mind, nor again is the mind born of outer dharmas, since all dharmas are mere appearances having the nature of consciousness. Thus the effect is not born from the cause, nor again is the cause born from the effect; in this way the wise (manīṣiṇaḥ) enter into, that is, settle upon, the non-origination of cause and effect, the hetuphalājāti.

The knowers of Brahman recognize the very absence of cause and effect within the Self, this is the meaning.
MK_C04_K55: So long as there is the clinging to cause and effect, there will be the rising up of cause and effect; when the clinging to cause and effect is exhausted, there is no rising up of cause and effect. (55)
MK_C04_K55::block-0:
But what then becomes of those who are firmly attached to cause and effect? It is replied: "I am the doer of the cause called dharma and adharma; my dharma and adharma have such-and-such fruit; in another time, born somewhere in some class of living beings, I shall enjoy it", such is the clinging (āveśa) to cause and effect, that is, the seizure by cause and effect, the superimposition (adhyāropaṇa) upon the Self; that is the very citta-state, this is the meaning. So long as such clinging endures, the rising up of cause and effect, that is, the unbroken proceeding of dharma and adharma and their fruits, takes place.

But when, by the vision of non-duality stated above, the seizure brought on by cause and effect arisen from avidyā is dispelled, just as a possession is removed by the power of mantra and herbs, then, that being exhausted, there is no rising up of cause and effect.
MK_C04_K56: So long as there is clinging to cause and effect, so long does saṃsāra extend; when the clinging to cause and effect is exhausted, one does not enter saṃsāra. (56)
MK_C04_K56::block-0: If there is the rising up of cause and effect, what is the fault? It is replied: so long as the clinging to cause and effect is not turned away by right vision (samyagdarśana), being unexhausted, saṃsāra is extended (āyātaḥ), that is, prolonged, this is the meaning. But when the clinging to cause and effect is exhausted, one does not enter saṃsāra, since its cause is absent.
MK_C04_K57: By concealment all is born; on that account there is nothing eternal indeed. By the supreme reality, all is unborn; on that account there is no annihilation indeed. (57)
MK_C04_K57::block-0:
Pūrvapakṣa: "Surely apart from the unborn Ātman nothing whatsoever exists; how then are origination and destruction predicated by you of cause and effect, and of saṃsāra?" Listen. Saṃvṛti — saṃvaraṇa, that is, covering — is the avidyā-sphere, the worldly transaction (laukikavyavahāra); by that saṃvṛti everything is born. Therefore, in the avidyā-sphere there is indeed nothing eternal, nothing nitya. Hence saṃsāra, characterised by origination and destruction, is said to come about (āyate).

But by the supreme reality (paramārtha-sadbhāvena), since all is the unborn Ātman alone, on that account, owing to the absence of birth itself (jāti-abhāva), there is indeed no annihilation (uccheda) of any cause, effect, or anything else — this is the import. The siddhānta is that the very dichotomy of origination and cessation pertains only to the conventional level mistakenly taken for real, never to the paramārtha.
MK_C04_K58: Those dharmas that are said to be born — they are not born in reality. Their birth is like that of māyā, and that māyā too does not exist. (58)
MK_C04_K58::block-0:
Whatever ātmans and other dharmas are imagined to be born — those, ye, of such-and-such kind, that is, in the manner of the saṃvṛti already declared, are pointed at; thus the dharmas are born only by saṃvṛti. They are not born in tattva, in paramārtha. And again, that birth of theirs by saṃvṛti — of the dharmas as already described, that is — just as birth occurs through māyā, so is it to be understood: it is māyā-like (māyopama).

Then, surely, māyā is some thing, an entity? Not so: "and that māyā too does not exist (sā ca māyā na vidyate)." The word māyā is the appellation of the non-existent (avidyamānasya ākhyā) — this is the intent. The siddhānta names and refutes the Vijñānavādin's notion that imagined dharmas have any momentary svalakṣaṇa-svabhāva: their very arising is mithyā, and the very māyā by which they are figured is itself unreal.
MK_C04_K59: As from a māyā-made seed there is born a sprout that is itself made of māyā — that sprout is neither eternal nor subject to annihilation — even so is the construal applied to dharmas. (59)
MK_C04_K59::block-0: How is the birth of these dharmas māyā-like? He says — just as from a māyā-made (māyāmaya) mango seed and the like there arises a sprout (aṅkura) that is tanmaya, made of the same māyā, that sprout is neither nitya, eternal, nor ucchedī, perishable, that is, subject to annihilation. Precisely on account of its being non-existent in truth (abhūtatva), the construal of birth, destruction, and the like upon the dharmas is a mere yukti, an applicable manner of speech, but in paramārtha the birth or destruction of dharmas is not coherent — this is the meaning. Both the alternatives of pravṛtti and nivṛtti collapse together when their substratum is itself unreal.
MK_C04_K60: In all unborn dharmas there is no designation of eternal or non-eternal. Where words do not function, no discrimination is uttered. (60)
MK_C04_K60::block-0:
But in paramārtha, in the ātmans that are aja, having for their being only the eternal one-flavoured pure consciousness (nityaika-rasa-vijñapti-mātra-sattāka), the appellation "eternal" or "non-eternal" does not arise — abhidhāna does not function — this is the meaning. Yatra, where, that is, in those, the varṇas — the words by which objects are described, named — do not vart, do not function in denoting or making manifest, this is the meaning.

"This is thus" — such viveka, such discriminative distinction, is not uttered there as "eternal" or "non-eternal," in accordance with the śruti yato vāco nivartante (Tai. U. 2.9.1) — "whence words turn back." Hence the very pravṛtti of speech that the disputant relies on is, at the level of ajāti, nivṛtta.
MK_C04_K61: As in dream the citta moves through māyā appearing as duality, even so in waking does the citta move through māyā appearing as duality. (61)
MK_C04_K62: The citta in dream is non-dual yet appearing as duality — there is no doubt of this. So too in waking, the citta is non-dual yet appearing as duality — there is no doubt. (62)
MK_C04_K62::block-0: Now, that further state of being a sphere of speech (vāg-gocaratva) is, in paramārtha, of the non-dual mere consciousness (advaya vijñānamātra) — that is only a vibration of the manas (manasaḥ spandanamātra), and not a paramārtha matter. Thus the meaning of the two ślokas has been stated. The siddhānta is firm: discourse and duality alike are spanda of citta, never the very Self.
MK_C04_K63: The dream-seer, moving in dream, in all the ten directions, sees jīvas dwelling there — egg-born, sweat-born, and the like — whomsoever he sees ever. (63)
MK_C04_K63::block-0: And from this too the absence of duality being a sphere of speech is shown — "He sees dreams," hence svapna-dṛk; pracaran, moving, wandering, in svapna, in the dream-place; in all the ten directions, those situated, vartamāna, jīvas, that is prāṇins, egg-born or sweat-born, whomsoever he sees always. Yet none of these has any reality apart from the dreamer's own citta — this is the bhūmikā for the next kārikā's siddhānta.
MK_C04_K64: These jīvas are seen only by the dream-seer's citta; they do not exist apart from it. So too this very citta of the dream-seer is held to be only what is seen by him. (64)
MK_C04_K64::block-0:
If so, what then? It is said — the citta of the dream-seer is svapna-dṛk-citta; by it those jīvas are dṛśya, things seen. From that, that is, from the dream-seer's citta, they are not pṛthak, separate; they do not exist independently — this is the meaning. For the citta itself is figured (vikalpyate) under the diverse forms of many jīvas and the like. Likewise, that very svapna-dṛk-citta is itself only tad-dṛśya, what is seen by him — by the dream-seer it is dṛśya, hence tad-dṛśya. Therefore, apart from the dream-seer there is no thing called citta at all — this is the meaning.

Thus the Vijñānavādin's posit of an autonomous, self-luminous citta independent of its drāṣṭṛ is refuted; both the seen jīvas and the seeing citta collapse into the one consciousness-substrate, and asparśa, untouched non-duality, alone abides as the alātacakra-analogy will further establish.
MK_C04_K65: Moving about in the waking state, in the ten directions of waking, the dweller (jīva) ever sees those living beings—the egg-born, the sweat-born, and the rest—who stand established (in those directions).
MK_C04_K66: These (beings) are objects to be perceived by the mind of the waking person; they do not exist apart from that (mind). Just so, this (mind) too, being the object seen, is held to be (nothing other than) the mind of the waker.
MK_C04_K66::block-0: The jīvas seen by the waker are not different from his mind, because they are objects perceived by that very mind, just like the jīvas perceived by the dream-seer's mind. And that mind, whose nature is the perceiving of the jīvas, is itself not distinct from the seer (draṣṭṛ), because it is what is perceived by the seer (draṣṭṛ-dṛśyatva), like the dream-mind. The remaining purport has already been stated.
MK_C04_K67: These two are mutually objects to each other; (when this is so,) what indeed is it that exists? It is asked thus: both are devoid of (independent) defining mark; in their own view, neither is grasped (apart from the other).
MK_C04_K67::block-0:
The two—jīva (the conscious cognizer) and citta (the cognition)—or, equivalently, citta and caitta (mind and mental object), are mutually perceived, that is, knowable only through each other. For citta is so called only with reference to objects such as the jīva; and the jīva and the rest are termed dṛśya (perceptible) only with reference to citta. Hence the two are mutually dependent for their being seen.

Therefore it is said that nothing whatsoever exists—neither citta nor that which is to be cognized by citta. "What indeed is it that exists?"—thus the discriminating one declares. Just as in dream there is neither an elephant nor an elephant-cognition, so here too, in the view of the discerning, the case is the same; this is the purport.

How so? Because both are devoid of lakṣaṇa. Lakṣaṇā means that by which a thing is characterized—namely, the pramāṇa (means of valid knowledge); both, citta and caitta, are devoid of pramāṇa, since the pair is mutually dependent. Hence in their own view itself—that is, by the very nature of citta-as-such—it is grasped. For one cannot grasp the pot apart from the cognition of the pot, nor the cognition of the pot apart from the pot. The distinction of pramāṇa and prameya cannot be coherently posited there—this is the purport.
MK_C04_K68: Just as the jīva made of dream is born and also dies, even so all these jīvas come into being and cease to be.
MK_C04_K69: Just as the jīva that is made of māyā is born and also dies, even so all these jīvas come into being and cease to be.
MK_C04_K70: Just as the jīva that is conjured up (nirmitaka) is born and also dies, even so all these jīvas come into being and cease to be.
MK_C04_K70::block-0: Māyāmaya is what has been produced by a magician; nirmitaka is what has been brought forth by mantras, herbs, and the like. Just as the jīvas—the egg-born and the rest—conjured up by dream and by māyā are born and die, so too the jīvas characterized as humans and the rest, being themselves non-existent, are merely figments fashioned by citta-vikalpa (mental construction)—this is the meaning.
MK_C04_K71: No jīva whatsoever is born; coming-into-being does not exist for it. This is the supreme truth, wherein nothing whatsoever is born.
MK_C04_K71::block-0: From the standpoint of vyavahāra-satya (empirical truth) it has been said that the jīvas have birth, death, and the like, on the analogy of the dream-jīva. But from the standpoint of the supreme paramārtha-satya, the truth is that no jīva whatsoever is born—this expresses ajāti. The remaining purport has already been stated.
MK_C04_K72: All this duality, having the form of grasper and grasped, is but the throbbing (spandita) of citta. Citta is objectless, eternal, and unattached—therefore it is so declared.
MK_C04_K72::block-0: All duality, having the character of grasper and grasped, is nothing but the throbbing of citta. Citta, in its supreme reality, is the Ātman alone; hence it is objectless (nirviṣaya). By virtue of that very objectlessness it has been declared to be eternal and unattached (asaṅga), as the śruti says, "This Puruṣa is unattached indeed" (Bṛ. Up. 4.3.15). For attachment belongs to that which has an object, and that, with reference to its object. Since citta is objectless, citta is therefore unattached—this is the meaning.
MK_C04_K73: That which exists by imagined convention (kalpita-saṃvṛti) does not exist in the absolute sense (paramārtha); that which exists by dependent convention (paratantra-abhisaṃvṛti) does not exist absolutely either.
MK_C04_K73::block-0:
Pūrvapakṣa: If asaṅgatva (non-attachment) of citta is established only by absence of object, then citta does not become niḥsaṅga, since the object such as teacher (śāstā), scripture (śāstra), and disciple (śiṣya) and the like are indeed seen to exist.

Siddhānta: This is no fault. Why? Because that padārtha which exists in the form of śāstra and the rest exists only by kalpita-saṃvṛti — by imagined conventional usage. The vigraha is: kalpitā cā sā saṃvṛtiḥ ca — it is both imagined and conventional, contrived as a means (upāya) for the apprehension of the highest reality (paramārtha-pratipatti-upāyatva). That which exists by such conventional fabrication does not exist in the paramārtha sense, does not truly exist. As has been said in Māṇḍūkya-Kārikā 1.18: "When the truth is known, duality does not exist" (jñāte dvaitaṃ na vidyate).

Further, that padārtha which would exist by paratantra-abhisaṃvṛti — by the convention dependent upon the procedure of another's śāstra, that is, by the transactional usage adopted from a rival school — when investigated absolutely, does not exist at all. Hence it has been rightly said in Kārikā 4.72: "For that reason it has been declared unattached" (asaṅgaṃ tena kīrtitam).
MK_C04_K74: By imagined convention (kalpita-saṃvṛti) it is unborn (aja); in the absolute sense it is not even unborn. By the dependent establishment (paratantra-abhiniṣpatti), it is born indeed by convention.
MK_C04_K74::block-0:
Pūrvapakṣa: If śāstra and the rest are merely saṃvṛti, then this notion "aja" (unborn) too would be a mere convention, a kalpanā.

Siddhānta: True, it is just so. By the very kalpita-saṃvṛti pertaining to śāstra and the rest, it is called "aja." In the paramārtha sense it is not even aja, since by paratantra-abhiniṣpatti — having recourse to the established procedure of the rival school (para-śāstra-siddhi) — that which is called "aja" is itself born by convention. Therefore the meaning is: even this kalpanā of "aja" does not at all gain footing in the domain of paramārtha. The designation aja is operative only at the relative level as a means to lead to the truth, but the truth itself transcends even the predicate of ajatva.
MK_C04_K75: There is clinging (abhiniveśa) to the unreal; duality does not exist there. Having known the absence of duality, one becomes causeless (nirnimitta) and is not born.
MK_C04_K75::block-0:
Since the object is asat (unreal), there is in the unreal duality only abhiniveśa — clinging. Abhiniveśa here means mere insistent grasping (āgraha-mātram). Duality does not exist there in truth; only the false clinging exists, and that clinging itself is the cause of birth (janma-kāraṇa).

Therefore, having known dvayābhāva — the non-existence of the duality which is the cause — one becomes nirnimitta, that is, one whose clinging to the false dvaya has ceased (nivṛtta-mithyā-dvaya-abhiniveśa). Such a one is not born. The pravṛtti of saṃsāra rests upon this clinging; with its nivṛtti, rebirth ceases of itself.
MK_C04_K76: When one does not obtain the causes — superior, inferior, and middling — then the citta is not born; in the absence of cause, whence the fruit?
MK_C04_K76::block-0:
The dharmas prescribed by jāti and āśrama, performed devoid of selfish desire (āśīr-varjita), being causes of attaining godhood and the like, when pure, are uttama. The dharmas mixed with adharma, aimed at obtaining manhood and the like, are madhyama. The pravṛtti-viśeṣas characterised by adharma, productive of the state of beasts and the rest, are adhama.
