These uttama-madhyama-adhama (causes), all imagined by avidyā, when one — knowing the Ātman-tattva as one alone, without a second (ekam-eva-advitīyam), free from all kalpanā — does not obtain, does not see (just as the discerning person does not see the dirt in the sky which is seen by children) — then the citta is not born, does not arise in the form of the fruit of uttama, madhyama, and adhama through the shapes of deva and the rest.

Indeed, in the absence of cause, the fruit does not arise — like crops and the like in the absence of seeds. Thus the cessation of pravṛtti yields the cessation of phala, since cause and effect are co-extensive.
MK_C04_K77: The non-arising (anutpatti) of the causeless citta is even and non-dual — it belongs to the wholly unborn, since this (duality) is but a perception of citta.
MK_C04_K77::block-0:
It has been said that in the absence of cause, citta does not arise. Now, what is the nature of that anutpatti of the citta? It is being explained: by paramārtha-darśana, the cause of arising — namely dharma and adharma — has been removed; for the citta which has thus become animitta, the anutpatti, which goes by the name mokṣa, is at all times and in all states samā (uniform), nirviśeṣa (without distinction), and advayā (non-dual). It belongs even prior, to the citta which is itself ajāta, unborn, encompassing all (sarvasya advayasya) — this is the meaning.

Since even before vijñāna, the citta and that which is dvaya — namely birth — are mere citta-dṛśya (perceptions of mind), therefore for the wholly ajāta citta, at all times the anutpatti is samā and advayā only; it is not such that sometimes it is and sometimes it is not. It is ever of one form (sarvadā ekarūpa eva). Thus ajāti is not a fresh acquisition but the eternal nature itself.
MK_C04_K78: Having known true causelessness (animittatā), and not separately taking up any cause, one attains the abode that is free from sorrow, free from desire, and fearless.
MK_C04_K78::block-0: By the nyāya stated above, owing to the absence of duality which is the nimitta of birth, having known the animittatā which is true and of the form of paramārtha, one does not separately take up the hetu — namely the dharma and the rest, which are causes of attaining the wombs of devas and the rest. Becoming one who has abandoned the external longings (tyakta-bāhya-eṣaṇaḥ), and who is free from kāma, śoka, and the like, free from avidyā and the rest, he attains the abhayam padam — the fearless abode. The meaning is: he is not born again. Such mokṣa is the natural fruit of the cessation of the cause-fruit pravṛtti.
MK_C04_K79: Indeed, by clinging to the unreal, it (citta) operates upon what is similar; having known the absence of the substance, it turns back unattached.
MK_C04_K79::block-0:
Since by abhūta-abhiniveśa — the determination of the existence of dvaya in the absent dvaya, which is itself the abhūta-abhiniveśa — that is, owing to the form of avidyā-vyāmoha, the citta indeed operates (pravartate) upon what is similar (sadṛśe), upon the form conformable to that clinging.

When one has known the abhāva — the non-existence — of that vastu, namely the dvaya, then, becoming niḥsaṅga (unattached) and nirapekṣa (without dependence), the citta turns back (vinivartate) from the object of abhūta-abhiniveśa. Thus the cessation of pravṛtti follows from the cessation of the false determination.
MK_C04_K80: For the citta that has turned back and does not engage, the state is then unwavering — that indeed is the object (viṣaya) of the awakened; that is sameness (sāmya), unborn (aja), and non-dual (advaya).
MK_C04_K80::block-0:
For the citta which is nivṛtta from the dvaita-viṣaya, and which is apravṛtta in any other viṣaya — this on account of abhāva-darśana, the seeing of non-existence — there then arises a sthiti that is niścalā, free from cālana, of the very form of Brahman (brahma-svarūpā eva). This sthiti of citta in the form of Brahman is characterised as advaya-vijñāna-eka-rasa-ghana — a single dense mass of the one savour of non-dual consciousness.

Indeed, since this is the viṣaya — the gocara — of the buddhāḥ, the seers of paramārtha, that very tat-sāmya, the supreme equality, is nirviśeṣa, ajam, and advayam. Thus the alāta-śānti culminates in the asparśa Brahman, which is verily the Self of all, ajāti and advaita, eternally unconditioned, the abode of mokṣa.
MK_C04_K81: It is unborn, sleepless, dreamless, and shines forth of itself; for this dharma, by the very nature of its substance, is ever-luminous once and for all.
MK_C04_K81::block-0:
Once again, of what nature is that object of the buddhas? To this it is replied: That shines forth of itself, not depending upon the sun or other luminaries; the meaning is that it has self-luminosity (svayaṃ-jyotiḥ-svabhāva) as its very nature.

Sakṛd-vibhātaḥ means "ever shining"; that is, it shines always without interruption. This dharma named the Self (ātmākhyo dharmaḥ), of such a description, is so dhātu-svabhāvataḥ — that is to say, by the very nature of the entity itself (vastu-svabhāvataḥ). Thus its luminosity is not adventitious but intrinsic, established by the inherent character of Brahman as Pure Consciousness.
MK_C04_K82: Bliss is ever covered over and pain is always laid bare; through the grasping of any dharma whatsoever that Bhagavān becomes hidden.
MK_C04_K82::block-0:
If the highest truth is being declared so often, why is it not grasped by worldly people? It is now stated: Because, through the grasping (graheṇa) — that is, by the obsessive seizing — of any dharma whatever pertaining to a dual entity, through the false adherence to it, sukham āvriyate, that is, bliss is effortlessly veiled. For the covering caused by the perception of duality requires no further effort; once duality is grasped, the non-dual bliss is automatically obscured.

And duḥkhaṃ vivriyate — pain is laid open and made manifest, because knowledge of the supreme truth is hard to attain. Bhagavān asau — that is, the non-dual deity, the Self (ātmādvayo devaḥ). Hence, even when proclaimed repeatedly by the Vedānta texts and by the ācāryas, He cannot be known, as the śruti declares: "Wonderful is the speaker of It, skilled the attainer of It" (Kaṭha Up. 1.2.7). Thus the rarity of the qualified hearer is the reason for non-comprehension, not any defect in the teaching itself.
MK_C04_K83: "It is," "It is not," "It is and is not," or again "Not is and not is not" — by the moving, the steady, both, and the absent, the immature one verily covers it over.
MK_C04_K83::block-0:
The graspings of even paṇḍitas, though pertaining to subtle topics such as "It is," "It is not," and the like, are themselves coverings of the Bhagavān, the supreme Self; how much more then are the conceptions of the deluded, which are characterised by ordinary intellect, coverings? With this purpose he says "asti" etc. One disputant — the upholder of permanent reality — maintains "the Self is" (the eternalist position). Another, the Vainaśika (the Sarvāstivāda Buddhist who holds momentary destruction), maintains "It is not."

Another again, the half-Vainaśika, the Sad-asad-vādin, the digambara Jaina, holds "It is and is not" (anekāntavāda). Yet another, the absolute śūnya-vādin (Mādhyamika), holds "Not is and not is not." Among these, the position "It is" is moving (calaḥ), since it is held to be unlike pots and other impermanent things yet still characterised by being. The position "It is not" is steady (sthiraḥ), since it is uniformly nothing throughout. The third position, embracing both, has the nature of being-and-non-being and is therefore mobile-cum-stable. The fourth, "absence," is utter non-existence (atyantābhāva).

By these four — calaḥ, sthiraḥ, ubhayam and abhāvaḥ — the disputant who upholds being or non-being or any combination, every such bāliśa, the undiscriminating, verily covers Bhagavān. Even though the so-called paṇḍita is in truth bāliśa, owing to non-comprehension of the highest truth, what then need be said of the man naturally deluded by his own nature? This is the import.
MK_C04_K84: These four are the corners by whose graspings He is ever covered over; by whom that Bhagavān, untouched by these, is seen, he is the all-seeing.
MK_C04_K84::block-0:
Then what is that supreme truth, by knowing which a paṇḍita ceases to be a bāliśa? To this he says: These four kotis (corners, alternative positions) — "It is," "It is not," and the rest — are the final determinations made by the various pravāduka-śāstras (the schools of disputants); by the graspings of these four corners, that is, by the firm convictions taken as ascertainments, the Bhagavān of those very disputants is sadā always āvṛtaḥ, covered over.

But He, the Bhagavān, is by these four corners — "It is" and so on — aspṛṣṭaḥ, untouched, that is, free from the alternatives of being and the rest. By the muni who has seen Him — known Him as the Puruṣa of the Upaniṣads spoken of in the Vedānta texts — that one is sarva-dṛk, omniscient; he is the paṇḍita in the supreme sense (paramārtha-paṇḍita). This is the meaning.
MK_C04_K85: Having attained complete omniscience, the non-dual brahmaṇya state, free from beginning, middle and end — what beyond this could one strive after?
MK_C04_K85::block-0:
Having attained this aforesaid full and complete sarva-jñatā, omniscience, and the brāhmaṇya pada — the state of being a Brahman in the highest sense — as the śrutis declare, "He is the Brāhmaṇa" (Bṛ. Up. 3.8.10) and "This is the eternal greatness of the Brāhmaṇa" (Bṛ. Up. 4.4.23) — the non-dual state in which ādi-madhya-anta — origination, continuance, and dissolution (utpatti-sthiti-laya) — are anāpanna, never reached, never befallen.

That very pada being attained, what beyond this — beyond this very gain of one's own Self — does one strive after? The implication is: there is no further purpose, it is purposeless. As the smṛti says, "For him there is no purpose to be served by action" (Bhagavadgītā 3.18). Thus the realised one rests in nivṛtti, having transcended pravṛtti, since for the Self-knower no further action remains to be performed.
MK_C04_K86: This indeed is the discipline (vinaya) of the brāhmaṇas; this is called the natural śama; the dama too, since prakṛti itself is restrained — thus knowing, the wise one attains śama.
MK_C04_K86::block-0:
The vinaya of the vipras, the brāhmaṇas, is their being humble — that natural abiding in the very form of the Self. This vinaya itself is also the śama — the prākṛta, natural, uncontrived śama. The dama too is just this, since prakṛti — namely Brahman — is by its very nature restrained, of the form of intrinsic quiescence (svabhāvataḥ upaśānta-rūpatvāt brahmaṇaḥ).

Thus, knowing Brahman as svabhāva-upaśānta — naturally quiescent in the manner described — the vidvān, the knower, attains śama, the natural quiescence whose very nature is Brahman; that is, he abides in the very form of Brahman. Here vinaya, śama, and dama are not external practices but are the spontaneous expressions of the realised state itself, distinguished from the kṛtaka (manufactured) discipline of the unrealised.
MK_C04_K87: That which has substance and has cognition — that pair is held to be laukika; that which has no substance but still has cognition is held to be śuddha-laukika.
MK_C04_K87::block-0:
Thus, since the views of the disputants are mutually contradictory and serve as the seat of the defects of attachment, aversion, and the rest — the very causes of saṃsāra — they are mithyā-darśanas, false views, as has been shown by their own logic. Hence the Advaita-darśana, which is free from the four corners (catuṣ-koṭi-varjita) and is therefore not a seat of rāga and other doṣas, being naturally peaceful (svabhāva-śānta), is alone the samyag-darśana, right vision. This is the upasaṃhāra.

Now, in order to display his own procedure (sva-prakriyā-pradarśana), the discussion is begun. Sa-vastu — "with substance" — means, accompanied by an entity that exists with the reality of saṃvṛti (conventional being); savastu means having the property of being together with saṃvṛti-sat vastu. Likewise, upalabdhi is upalambha, cognition; sopalambham means accompanied by cognition. The pair (dvayam) — that is, the grasped and the grasper (grāhya-grahaṇa) — that is the seat of all transactions including those of the śāstras, this pair, being not separated from the world (lokād-anapetam), is termed laukika; this is the jāgarita state. Such is the description of waking that is held in the Vedānta texts.

Avastu — without substance — for it lacks even saṃvṛti-existence. Sopalambham — having cognition like that of a real entity, even though no entity exists; thus being accompanied by such cognition. Śuddham — that is, pure, distinct, separated from the gross laukika waking — is held to be laukika because of being shared by all sentient beings (sarva-prāṇi-sādhāraṇatvāt), and this is the svapna, the dream state.
MK_C04_K88: That which is without substance and without cognition is called lokottara. Knowledge, the knowable, and the to-be-known — these have been ever proclaimed by the buddhas.
MK_C04_K88::block-0:
Avastu-anupalambham — that which is without substance and without cognition, that is, free from grāhya and grahaṇa (object and act-of-grasping). Hence lokottaram — beyond the world. For the world is the domain of grāhya and grahaṇa, and where these are absent, what remains is the seed of all pravṛtti — namely, suṣupti, deep sleep. Thus has been declared the supreme reality together with its means: laukika, śuddha-laukika, and lokottara, by which knowledge they are known in succession.

That is jñāna, knowledge, and these very three — laukika, śuddha-laukika, and lokottara — are jñeyam, the knowable, since apart from these no further knowable can be established; for all the entities imagined by the various disputants fall within these three. Vijñeyam, the supremely-to-be-known, is that paramārtha-satyam, the absolute truth, named Turīya, the non-dual unborn ātma-tattva. This — beginning with the laukika and ending with the vijñeya — has sadā, always, been prakīrtitam, proclaimed, by the buddhas — the seers of the highest truth, the knowers of Brahman.
MK_C04_K89: When knowledge and the threefold object of knowledge are successively known by oneself, omniscience here verily arises everywhere for the great-minded one. (89)
MK_C04_K89::block-0:
In ‘knowledge’ – which has the laukika (worldly) and other planes as its sphere – and in the ‘object of knowledge’, namely the laukika and the rest, threefold: first the laukika that is gross (the waking sphere); then, by the cessation of that, the pure laukika (the dream sphere); then, by the cessation of that, the trans-worldly (the deep-sleep sphere). Thus, by the successive cessation of the three states, when the absolutely real Turīya – the non-dual, unborn, fearless – is known, then by oneself, that is, by the very nature of the Self, omniscience arises. ‘Sarva-jña’ – he who is all and is the knower – the state of being such is sarvajñatā, omniscience. ‘Here’, in this world, this arises for the great-minded, that is, for him whose intellect is great.

For the one who knows thus, since his intellect has for its object that Reality which transcends all worldly things, omniscience exists everywhere and at all times. The meaning is: once the true nature of the Self has been known, there is no deviation. For there is no rise and setting of knowledge in the knower of the supreme reality, as there is in the case of others, the disputants of various schools.
MK_C04_K90: Things to be abandoned, to be known, to be attained, and to be matured are to be cognised from the very outset. Of these, except for the one to be known, the apprehension in the three is held to be merely conventional. (90)
MK_C04_K90::block-0:
Lest, by the successive designation of the laukika and others as objects of knowledge, the suspicion arise that they really exist, he says: the things to be abandoned (heya) are the three – waking, dream, and deep sleep – to be cast off as non-existent in the Self, like the snake on the rope. The ‘to-be-known’ (jñeya) here is the supreme reality, free from the four alternatives. The ‘to-be-attained’ (āpya) are the means called pāṇḍitya, bālya, and mauna, to be attained by the mendicant who has renounced the three external longings (eṣaṇā-traya). The ‘to-be-matured’ (pākya) are the defects called kaṣāya – passion, hatred, delusion, and the rest – which must be cooked away. All these – heya, jñeya, āpya, pākya – are to be cognised by the mendicant as means.

‘From the outset’ – first of all. Of these, the things to be abandoned and the rest, except for the jñeya which is the supreme real Brahman alone, the apprehension is mere imagination born of avidyā. In the three – heya, āpya, pākya – it is so held by the knowers of Brahman; that is, the three have no absolute reality.
MK_C04_K91: All dharmas are to be known by their very nature as space-like and beginningless; for of them there is no plurality anywhere whatsoever. (91)
MK_C04_K91::block-0:
But in the supreme sense, by their very nature, all dharmas – that is, all Selves – are to be known by the seekers of liberation as space-like, equal to ākāśa in being subtle, untainted, and all-pervading; and as beginningless, that is, eternal.

Warding off the suspicion of difference that might arise from the use of the plural, he says: anywhere whatsoever – in any place – any little, even a particle’s measure – of plurality among them does not exist.
MK_C04_K92: All dharmas are well-determined as enlightened from the very beginning, by their very nature. He in whom such forbearance arises is fit for immortality. (92)
MK_C04_K92::block-0:
Even the knowability of the dharmas is only conventional, not in the absolute sense, he says: since they are enlightened from the very first – ādi-buddha – by their very nature alone; just as the sun is by nature of the form of constant light, so they are of the form of eternal cognition. ‘All dharmas’ – all Selves. Nor is any determination of them to be made; their nature is eternally determined. They are not such that their nature is in doubt – ‘is it thus or not thus?’

The seeker of liberation in whom there is, in the manner stated, an indifference at all times to having to ascertain knowledge – whether for one’s own sake or for another’s – just as the sun is ever indifferent to any other light, whether for itself or for another – he in whom such forbearance, namely indifference to the duty of cognising, exists always in his own Self, is fit for immortality – fit for the state of the Deathless – that is, capable of liberation.
MK_C04_K93: All dharmas are tranquil from the beginning, unborn, by nature wholly extinguished, equal and undivided; the unborn, sameness, the pure. (93)
MK_C04_K93::block-0:
Likewise, there is no duty of bringing about quiescence in the Self either, he says: since they are tranquil from the beginning – ever quiescent – unborn (aja), and by their very nature wholly extinguished, of well-quieted nature, that is, of eternally liberated nature. All dharmas are equal and undivided – samābhinnāḥ – since the Reality of the Self is unborn, sameness, and pure – aja, sāmya, viśārada, viśuddha.

Therefore neither tranquillising nor liberation is to be effected. For of that whose nature is eternally one, nothing done can have any purpose.
MK_C04_K94: But there is no purity for those who ever move in difference; the upholders of separateness, prone to difference, are therefore declared to be miserable. (94)
MK_C04_K94::block-0:
Those who have realised the supreme reality as stated, they alone are not miserable in this world; others are miserable, he says: since they are bent on difference, that is, followers of difference, hence followers of saṁsāra. Who? The pṛthag-vāda – those whose speech is of separateness, of things as many – the dualists. Therefore they are declared as miserable, base, since purity, viśāradya, is not theirs, who move ever in difference, that is, ever abide in the path of duality imagined by avidyā.

Hence their miserableness is fitting – this is the import. The dualist schools (the pṛthag-vādins) are thus named as the school refuted.
MK_C04_K95: Those few, whoever they be, who shall become well-determined in the unborn sameness, they alone in the world are of great knowledge; and that path the world enters not. (95)
MK_C04_K95::block-0:
This supreme reality is unfathomable for the non-magnanimous, the unlearned, those outside the Vedānta – for the small, those of little intellect, he says: in the unborn sameness, the supreme reality, ‘it is just thus and not otherwise’ – whoever, even women and the like, shall become well-determined, they alone in the world are of great knowledge, that is, their knowledge has for its object the unsurpassed Reality. And that, their path, that is, the supreme reality known by them, is not entered into by the common-witted other folk – it does not descend, it does not become an object for them.

In accordance with the smṛti: ‘Even the gods get bewildered, seeking the path of the pathless, of him who, having become the Self of all beings, beholds the One Aim of equality. Just as the track of birds in the sky cannot be traced, so too his course is not perceived’ – and the like.
MK_C04_K96: Knowledge is held to be unborn and unmigrating with respect to the unborn dharmas. Since the knowledge does not pass over, it is therefore declared unattached. (96)
MK_C04_K96::block-0:
How is one of great knowledge, he asks, and answers: in the unborn (aja), unmoving dharmas – the Selves – the knowledge is held to be unborn and unmoving, just as in the sun heat and light. Hence, since it does not transfer to another object, the knowledge is held to be unborn.

Since the knowledge does not move on to any other object, for that reason it is declared unattached (asaṅga), space-like (ākāśa-kalpa), as has been stated. Thus, in line with the asparśa-yoga of non-contact, the knowledge of the unborn (ajāti) is itself unborn, and accords with non-duality (advaita).
MK_C04_K97: For the undiscerning, when even an atomic difference (vaidharmya) is born—whether in things outer or inner—non-attachment (asaṅgatā) does not exist at all; how much less, then, the falling away of the veil!
MK_C04_K97::block-0: Among the disputants other than ours—those who, even after rejecting external objects and resting in mere cognition (vijñānamātra), still admit the difference between cognitions and their objects—when even an atomic, that is, the slightest, vaidharmya (difference of nature) is born or arises in any thing, whether outwardly or inwardly, in such avipaścit, undiscerning ones, asaṅgatā, the state of non-attachment, never exists at all. Where this minute admission of difference is itself the seed of bondage, what need is there to speak (kim uta vaktavyam) of the āvaraṇa-cyuti, the falling away of the bondage of avidyā? That cannot exist for them in any way.
MK_C04_K98: All dharmas are free from any veil and intrinsically pure; they are awakened from the very beginning and likewise liberated. Yet they are spoken of as awakening because they are masters (nāyakāḥ) capable of awakening.
MK_C04_K98::block-0:
Pūrvapakṣa: When you, who say that there is no falling away of the veil for the dharmas, has it not then been admitted in your own siddhānta that the dharmas do possess an āvaraṇa, a veil? Siddhānta: It is not so, says the Master. Alabdhāvaraṇāḥ—those by whom the āvaraṇa, the bondage of avidyā and the rest, is alabdha, that is, never attained or possessed—such dharmas are alabdhāvaraṇāḥ, devoid of bondage; this is the meaning. They are prakṛti-nirmalāḥ, pure by their very own nature, ādau buddhāḥ, awakened from the beginning, and tathā muktāḥ, liberated as well, for they are by nature eternally pure, awake, and free.

If so, how then is it said that they are buddhyante, awakening? It is said because they are nāyakāḥ, masters, sovereigns, by nature capable of awakening, possessing the power of awareness (bodha-śakti); this is the meaning. Just as the sun, though by nature ever-luminous, is yet spoken of as ‘shining’; or just as the mountains, though their motion has eternally ceased, are still spoken of as ‘standing’—so too here. The expression of activity is only a courtesy of speech where the nature is eternally accomplished.
MK_C04_K99: The knowledge of the awakened protector does not move toward dharmas; all dharmas are like that knowledge. This was not declared by the Buddha.
MK_C04_K99::block-0:
Because the jñāna of the buddha—the seer of the supreme reality—does not krāmate, does not move into other dharmas, into other objects standing in their own places, as the radiance of the sun moves outward into things illumined. Tāyinaḥ: tāya is the continuous, unbroken, ākāśa-like extension—he in whom this exists is tāyī; the meaning is, of him whose nature is uninterrupted continuity, like space; or else, of one worthy of worship, or one possessed of prajñā. All dharmas, that is, all selves, are likewise: like that very jñāna, being ākāśa-like, they do not move toward any other thing.

What was set forth at the beginning—‘by knowledge that is space-like’ (Mā. Kā. 4.1) and the rest—is precisely this: for the ākāśa-like Tāyī Buddha, since the dharmas are non-different from him, his ākāśa-like jñāna does not move into any other object. Likewise, the dharmas—the Brahman-Self reality—are like ākāśa: motionless, changeless, partless, eternal, non-dual, unattached, unseen, ungraspable, beyond hunger and the rest, as the śruti declares, ‘There is verily no cessation of the seer’s seeing’ (Bṛ. Up. 4.3.23). This supreme advaya reality, devoid of the divisions of knowledge, knowable, and knower, was not declared by the Buddha.

Though the rejection of external objects and the postulation of mere cognition were said to be a near approach to the non-dual reality, the true paramārtha-tattva, this advaita, is to be known only in the Vedānta texts; this is the meaning. The schools of Vijñānavāda and the rest fall short of it; only the upaniṣadic vidyā discloses it.
MK_C04_K100: Having known that station which is hard to behold, profound, unborn, equipoised, lustrous, and free from manifoldness, we offer obeisance to it as best as we can.
MK_C04_K100::block-0:
At the conclusion of the śāstra, an obeisance is uttered for the praise of the supreme reality. Durdarśam: it is seen with difficulty—durdarśam. It is hard to know, because it is excluded from the four alternatives of ‘is’, ‘is not’, both, and neither—this is the meaning. For this very reason, atigambhīram, exceedingly profound, hard to enter into, like the great ocean for those whose prajñā is unformed.

Ajam, unborn; sāmyam, of equipoise; viśāradam, lustrous and clear. Having buddhvā, known, such a pada (station), anānātvam, free from all manifoldness—becoming one with that—we offer namaskāra, obeisance, to that pada. Although it is beyond all empirical handling, drawing it for the moment within the field of speech, we bow yathābalam, that is, to the measure of our capacity; this is the meaning. Thus the entire teaching of the four prakaraṇas culminates in surrender to the asparśa, ajāti advaya Brahman.
MK_C04_OUTRO1::block-0: Maṅgalācaraṇa 1: Although it is unborn, by the union of its sovereign power (aiśvarya-yoga) it appears to attain birth; though motionless, it appears to attain motion; though one, it appears as many. To that Brahman which dispels the fear of those who bow before it, but which is grasped only as the variegated dharmas of the world by the eyes of the deluded, I offer my salutation.
MK_C04_OUTRO1::block-1: Maṅgalācaraṇa 2: From the great ocean of the Veda, churned by the churning-rod of his prajñā, beholding all beings sunk in the dreadful sea of unceasing birth which is its terrible crocodile, out of compassion he drew up this nectar—this knowledge—hard to obtain even for the immortals, for the sake of all beings. To that supreme guru, worthy of being worshipped by the worshipped themselves, I bow with prostrations of my feet.
MK_C04_OUTRO1::block-2: Maṅgalācaraṇa 3: Whose splendour of prajñā extinguished the deep darkness of moha within my own heart; in whose dread ocean of repeated birth, where I sank and rose again and again, the resort to whose feet brings unfailing attainment of śruti, peace, and humility—those purifying feet, dispellers of the fear of saṃsāra, I salute with my whole being.
